review_text: Invaluable collection. Big, but it could easily be larger. If I were in charge, I would have left out some of the more easily-found texts.
very nice Penguin reissue of the 1855 edition, with an introduction by Harold Bloom
This was a really good novel that started out one way, and ended a way that was very, very satisfactory.
20 years' worth of one of this island's most inventive practioners
This recent edition is the "real," supposedly less edited version.
I love this little pocket dictionary because it's one of the few which indicate the pitch accent so you don't confuse "flower" and "nose".

This was a gift from somebody who mistook my collecting The Alchemist in different languages for a fanatical love of all things Paulo Coelho. Sadly it doesn't have the qualities that give the other book appeal outside the New Age movement of which I am not a part.
It's interesting that an Australian raised in Mexico can imagine an "America-as-imagined-by-Brits".This could be destined to become one of my all-time favourites.

This is the first ever and, as far as I'm aware, still the only pocket dictionary of any indigenous Australian language. I can only hope for something similar for Warlpiri, Arrernte, and Kala Lagaw Ya in the future.

The worst of the old-style Lonely Planet phrasebooks. Where their Spanish and German books were enough to get me started when travelling in countries speaking those languages, this one failed. The omission of some system of phonetic pronunciation to help deal with the very difficult French spelling system is unforgiveable.

This book served me well during a month in Morocco. Locals were often impressed that I used the Moroccan word "zhuzh" for "two" rather than whatever the usual Arabic word is. There's even a brief section on French for when you can't get your tongue around the Arabic.
This book gave me amazing insights at the time, but I wonder how relevant it still is these days.

I spotted this book using some 6th sense in a warehouse-like used bookstore in Newtown, Sydney from a long distance in the wrong section without its dust jacket and with my poor eyesight. The layout and typesetting are exceptionally fine. As for the content, I would not recommend trying to read this from cover to cover but it is a joy to pick up and read a random few pages. Always gives me something to think about. But I'm much more interested in translation than in poetry.

Jennings was one of the first historians to assimilate the new understanding of what had happened to the thriving Indian civilizations of America when Europe crashed into them; the book fairly sizzles with his outrage, and it's an unforgettable read.

This book takes the issue of class seriously and discusses how war and peace affected the working folk, widows, and other non-elites of colonial NYC, Boston, and Philadelphia. Detailed and convincing.

Ostensibly a biography of Facundo Quiroga (1790-1835), this classic is an attack on the dictatorship of Juan Manuel de Rosas (who may have had Quiroga assassinated) and a vision of eternal war between civilization and barbarism.
A great "intellectual" mystery - goes back and forth in time and covers all sorts of interesting material.  Like The Da Vinci Code but better.
Wide-ranging, idiosyncratic, endlessly appetizing... and very British; it does not contain the term "bologna."

This is one of the best technical books I've ever read. In a strange way it's still the best introduction to Linux, even though there are many outdated details. After all, _all_ technical are full of outdated details -- but it's the rare book indeed that can rise above implementation and express an entire philosophy of development concisely and readably.

Excellent anthology of macabre 19th-Century fiction, slightly spoiled by its editors’ pretentious introduction. Includes such firsts-of-their-kind as Polidori’s The Vampyre, and J. Sheridan Le Fanu’s Carmilla; along with Charles Nodier’s bizarre Smarra; Théophile Gautier’s The Beautiful Dead aka “Clarimonde” Poe’s Ligeia; etc., etc. Seek out the larger-format first edition if you can: later printings were much more cheaply & nastily made.

Book devoted to the reproduction of a single very large (3m x 4m) drawing entitled Nobson Central by the English artist Paul Noble. The drawing is part of a series of works depicting the imaginary city of Nobson. It presents ‘acres of ruination that might belong in bombed-out Baghdad or Kabul or an earthquake zone, row upon row of what appear to be modernist slums, concrete dwellings whose walls are breached and pocked, their flat roofs gone […] The configuration of the rows upon rows of buildings actually spells out the opening lines of T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land. But why board up the windows of a house whose walls are open? Why put out the neatly tied binbags when everywhere is rubbish strewn?’

Volume of mostly short, simple, but enjoyable and memorable (if sometimes a tad over-earnest) poems,  interspersed with &#8216;chants, spells and invocations&#8217; in Nahuatl, (with verse translations in English), drawn from a treatise compiled in mid-17th-Century New Spain by Hernando Ruiz de Alarcón, sections of whose Spanish commentary are also quoted, again, with English translations, making for a rich trilingual mixture.

Defining the Italian of Giordano Bruno in the English of Shakespeare, and compiled by a man who knew both, A Worlde of Wordes is the aptest of titles for this uniquely evocative Elizabethan document, here presented in facsimile. The book has no English-Italian section, hence limiting its usefulness as a work of reference, and is not cheap, but nevertheless may be strongly recommended to the studious and the idly curious alike.

Intriguing collection of fantastic tales by a largely-forgotten author. The best of these pieces are first-rate: Fireman Flower is a brilliant and intense hallucination of a story; The Forbidden Lighthouse is memorably evocative; and The Long Sheet is a brief, bitter fable Kafka would have been proud of. Several other of the stories struck me as workmanlike by comparison, but nevertheless, this is a desirable, handsomely-produced book.

What the title says. The graphic works of both artists are fully reproduced, in some cases with additional life-sized details. Lavalleye provides introductory texts for each artist, as well as an annotated catalogue of the works in question.

Limited edition (1000 copies) volume reproducing four beautiful alphabets in full. I bought this for de’ Grassi’s figrative alphabet, and for Mitelli’s marvellous Alfabeto in Sogno (‘Dream Alphabet’). Rossi provides some introductory texts (in Italian).

Privately-printed catalogue of graphic works by the Hungarian artist István Orosz (1951-), an illustrator, theatre-designer and animator, who has produced numerous poster-designs and series of woodcuts and engravings. His smaller-scale prints  are notable for their optical trickery, and brain-twizzling Escher-like illusory effects. Orosz’s works employing anamorphosis (meaning, in this context, the inclusion of images distorted such that they only become clearly visible when reflected in a suitably-shaped and positioned mirror), are the most satisfying and accomplished of their kind that I have seen.

Catalogue of an exhibition at the Accademia di Francia in Rome, in 1993: still the best single book about Velly, featuring a fine selection of his paintings, drawings and prints. Features texts (in Italian) by Jean-Marie Drot, Marisa Volpi, Leonardo Sciascia and Michel Random.

Fascinating & inspiring illustrated account of the creative and personal partnership of the film director, sculptor and graphic artist Jan Švankmajer, and his wife, the painter Eva Švankmajerova. To quote the back-cover blurb, 'their paintings, masturbation machines, poems, formative meetings, screenplays, tactile objects, diaries, films, pottery, games, puppets, collages, texts and dreams represent the imaginative activity of contemporary Czech surrealism.' For me, Jan's works are of considerably greater interest than are Eva's, but, as the book continually reminds us, neither body of work could exist without the other.

Comprehensive, richly-illustrated monograph about the Norwegian painter’s work (up until ’94), with accompanying text (in Norwegian). Especially interesting (to me) were the illustrations of Nerdrum’s first mature works from ca. 1972-9.

A fictional love affair between Elizabeth Stuart, the exiled queen of Bohemia (her husband, the Elector Palatine, accepted the throne of Bohemia in 1619 and held it for one winter before being defeated in 1620) and Pelagius, a West African prince and former slave.
Good historical novel about a woman doctor in the 370s, with a nicely drawn Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria as an old man.
A fine novel about the emperor Hadrian, which too many people quote as if it were history.

The cover is crumbling so badly I have to keep the book in a ziploc plastic bag, but this was a wonderful find (at Acres of Books in Long Beach, one of my favorite used book stores). A "teach yourself Russian" book for the use of Baltic Germans in the time of Catherine the Great.

A wonderful book that not only gives thorough etymologies but explains the history of the popularity of names; under Elmer: "This has been used as a given name in America since the 19th century, in honour of the brothers Ebenezer and Jonathan Elmer, leading supporters of the American Revolution." Has appendices of Arabic and Indian/Pakistani names.
This is Wolfe's second book on tai chi. It is another gem. Can't wait for the third!
This is one of the best books on tai chi that you can read. You can read it over and over again and always find something new inside of it.

A product of old age, this isn't Partridge at his best (it's "here come de judge," not "there come...," Eric), but full of good stories and obscure allusions (especially helpful for Yanks who didn't grow up with ITMA)

As useful and maddening as all of Room's productions; you can't trust it (under Peking/Beijing: "alternative name of Peiping has same meaning"), and there are bizarre inclusions (Cortina d'Ampezzo, Costa Smeralda, Costa Verde) and exclusions (Babylon, Carthage, Lhasa), but I refer to it all the time.

This is absolutely one of my favorite compilations of historical letters from 19th century Kentucky. True, the letters come from one family, and a wealthy family at that, but the variety of letters from both the men and the women make for an enlightening experience. The letters come from the famous Clay family of Kentucky, but not the direct family group of Henry or Cassius Clay. These letters come from the Brutus Clay and Amelia Fields family of Bourbon County (Brutus was Henry's brother). Stretching from the early 19th century into the early 20th century, the many family members and their accounts of daily life are invaluable. However, the letters surrounding the coming and arrival of the Civil War are wonderful. While Brutus Clay was in Washington as a government representative, his wife Amelia was back home at Auvergne, managing their large working farm or plantation. This required directing the field work and handling such things as breeding the cattle. While her husband was critical of her efforts, it really demonstrated the difficulties that women on the homefront encountered. Being in Kentucky, Amelia had to watch for both armies and had to host at least one side before the close of the war. The rest of the collection includes many poignant tales of successes and failures and the fragility of life in 19th century America.
An unsatisfactory edition made obsolete by the Penguin Complete Poems in 1985, but I was sure glad to have it at the time.

Richly-illustrated (mostly in b&w) account of Piranesi’s life & work. Includes the Vedute di Roma and the Carceri reproduced in full. This is an Italian translation of an English work originally published in 1978.

This stout, deceptively-dowdy volume, one of a series issued by an Italian bank, contains a full catalogue of the graphic works of the Bolognese artist Giuseppe Maria Mitelli, and a generous selection of illustrations. Mitelli's series of prints include the remarkable Alfabeto in Sogno (Dream Alphabet); Le Ventiquattr’Hore dell’Humana Felicità (The Twenty-Four Hours if Human Happiness); and Proverbi Figurati (Illustrated Proverbs). He also executed etched and engraved copies of paintings, particularly of the work of the Caraccis. He issued a large number of popular single prints on various subjects (oftentimes satirical ones), designed a deck of Tarot cards, and several board games, and issued alarmist propaganda on the occasion of the 1683 siege of Vienna... Varignana provides an introduction, commentary and notes (in Italian).

This exhibition catalogue is the Italian version of a joint venture between the Tate Gallery and the Comune di Roma. The English edition was published first (in 1996), and, as the exhibition was transferred to Rome, this edition was issued the following year. In addition to reproductions of the works exhibited, it includes ten essays by various authors discussing the 18th-Century grand-tourists, their itineraries, and the art they admired and purchased.

A box containing a booklet (in Italian) and 33 unbound prints reproducing card-games, dice-games and board-games invented and published by the Bolognese graphic artist Giuseppe Maria Mitelli (1634-1718). These include a deck of tarot cards, a ‘patience’-style card-game (Il gioco di Passatempo), and board games such as Il gioco delle Monete—‘the Game of Coins;’ Il Gioco Importantissimo del Fornaro (‘The Very Important Game of the Baker’), and Il Gioco dei Mestieri (‘The Game of Trades’).Of particular historical interest is Mitelli’s 1712 Il Gioco Nuovo di Tutte le Osterie (‘The New Game of All the Hostelries’), a board game where each square represents one of Bologna’s inns or eating-houses. Every osteria is represented by its sign, under which Mitelli has noted a particular speciality of the establishment. For example, L’Orso was known for its Buon Vin Dolce ‘good sweet wine,’ whereas L’Angelo was noted for Buone Sfoglie ‘good pastries.’
A fairy-tale, but for adults.  Inexpressibly sad and beautiful.
This is one of the best books I've ever read.  It flows so well, and the little bits of discovery as the story progresses are fulfilling.
Superb introduction to mythology for the layman in layman's terms.  Campbell was a genius in this subject.
This book introduces the Austin family.  It is perhaps weaker and simpler than the later books in the series, but still a good read.

Boring, you say? Hah! I open at random and find: "Thus, in the Balme library, much breath was wasted on the problem of whether to include in the catalog entry such appellations of chiefs as Otumfuo, Osagyefo, and Nama. The decision reached is that they should not, being the equivalent renderings of titles of esteem like His Majesty or His Grace. Nana (Ga equivalent Nii, Ewe Togbe, etc.) is a most common appellation. It is one of respect, used to precede the name of any chief, the very elderly, or one's grandparents. These days it is coming into vogue as a forename, and only when it is used as such should it appear in the catalog entry." If you can resist that, you're a better man than I.

Terms used by printers, bibliophiles, and others. Some jerk in the Barnes and Noble Sale Annex (former NYC bookstore) showed me an armful of these and told me they were very hard to get and he'd taken all the store had and would resell them for a good profit. I found a copy he'd missed.
If it bothers you that so many sayings are attributed to the wrong people (often Churchill or Mark Twain), this is the book for you.
I've become bored by these "terms of venery," most of which are nonce or silly or never in general use, but can't bring myself to give up this thin, pleasantly illustrated volume.
George Seldes was an amazing guy, a freelance journalist who really did "tell truth to power," and this is much more interesting than most collections of quotations.
Not particularly necessary now that the internet can tell us what "Cowes Week" or the "Coyote State" is, but still fun to flip through.

I don't want to visit Afghanistan or Liberia, but I enjoy reading about what you need to know for the trip. "If you don't like what you read or want a better description, please send a certified check to the author for $500,000 and include the corrections, additions, or adjectives you feel describe your rebel group, manifesto, or leadership more accurately."

Davis reports on the coronation of tsar Nicholas II, the millennial celebration of Budapest, the war with Cuba, the inauguration of President McKinley, the Greek-Turkish War of 1897, and Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee.
exhaustive and very entertaining dictionary of onomatopoeic French, with historical citations, from ah! and ai ai! to zip! and zzz!, not forgetting couic!, flonsflons! and plouf!
wonderful, scholarly book on exotic items imported into China during the T'ang Dynasty, and their influence on Chinese life: intoxicatingly rich and strange...
account of a Dutch adventurer who went looking for an arctic trade route to China: full of the period's mix of arcane belief and empirical science

A superb feat of lexicography, and beautifully produced as well -- one of the few expensive books I haven't been able to resist buying at full price when I saw it in a bookstore (the excellent Chaucer's, in Santa Barbara). Incidentally, Gudde is pronounced "Goody."
Not to be confused with the 1991 novel that is, unfortunately, the first Google hit for "Lempriere's Dictionary."

If I could keep just one movie book, this would be the one: bilingual screenplay of one of my favorite movies, multiple shots from every scene, detailed analysis. If only there were books like this for other Godard movies.
see &quot;Three by Perec&quot; for brilliant English translation by Ian Monk (as &quot;The Exeter Text&quot;)
crosswords, word-games, puzzles,and quizzes with a Parisian theme devised by Perec for a French magazine, 1980/81
thematic selection of colour definitions from Furetière's Dictionnaire universel
Bisexual Edwardian secret-agent and a plot to blow up Italy.  Gatiss didn't quite hit the mark often enough in this comedic novel.

Definitely on the creepy/ghoulish side, this book is a travel guide to those parts of Poland not directly annexed into Germany proper - or "Greater Germany". The edition was published at the invitation (read "command") of the Nazi Governor-General, Hans Frank. There are 3 editions of this book existing from 1943; one edition is undated. They are differentiated by the maps included.

I like the format which is much thinner and taller than pocket dictionaries from Collins and Larousse - which makes it much more practical for squeezing into a traveller's pocket. There are some surprising omissions such as "wallet" from the English section and "cuchillo" and "cuchara" from the Spanish section (knife and spoon).One problem is the very quirky pronunciations. It tries to give both US and British versions, but it seems this work was done by British people who are not experts in American speech. Many words give only a "US" pronunciation but include quirks such as the BBC-accent "short i" for the 2nd syllable of "chicken": /'ʧɪkɪn/ (CHICK-inn)!
Zinsser's classic handbook for writing non-fiction covers everything a would-be writer needs to start writing articles. The sections on editing and re-writing are eye opening.
These Christmas stories can be a bit saccharine, but they're perfect for evoking that old-fashioned Christmas feeling.
The "Shoes" books are one of my favorite British children's series.  They're a bit quirky, but so much fun.
I like it enough to keep from dropping it. Watase has that effect on me. I never quite manage to love it, but I never quite manage to hold on to my money, either. Pesk.
The lesser-known sequel to Eight Cousins.  It follows Rose as she grows up and deals with some interesting social issues of the day.  The ending is perfect for hopeless romantics.
Only knocked off that half-a-star because the valley-speak *occasionally* gets annoying.  Otherwise, a concise retelling of Goddesses who get what they want when they want it!  Brava!

Tactics of MistakeGordon R. Dickson (1998)ISBN: 0812545311[i]The young lieutenant-colonel was drink, apparently, and determined to rush upon disaster.[/i]From the moment when young Alliance Officer Cletus Grahame makes his drunken entry into the ship's dining hall and introduces himself to the enemy -- the very powerful Dow DeCastries -- the reader is swept up into the world of intrigue.  Grahame and DeCastries represent the battle between the Collation and the Alliance.  Cletus has the difficult job of bringing down a man who holds the lives of billions in his hands, and he's not off to a good start.  In a game of wits, it would seem that Cletus is out of his league from the start.And he can't foresee the future and know that his family will go on to be the power Dorsai warriors whose exploits Dickson would continue to write about for many years to come, tracing them from their early days in the Chantry Guild and on to The Final Encyclopedia and an attempt to reconnect man to his history, no matter how far he's roamed.I loved the Dorsai books, especially Tactics of Mistake and Lost Dorsai.  Gordon R. Dickson had a wonderful ability to create characters and fascinating situations.  Tactics of Mistake is one of the best of the set.

Magic?  Science?  In the post Holocaust world of City of Bones, it might all be the same.  Whatever it is, it means power and the people will do anything to collect the lost treasures of civilizations and bring them to the towering city of Charisat where they can make their fortune.  Selling, trading...stealing are all part of a day's work, and there are fortunes to be made.At least that's the myth.  Khat and his human partner Sagai aren't having much luck in that department, at least until Khat drags them both into danger over relics, lost cities, and enemies they may not know until it's too late.  Like the layers of the city in which they live, the story in  City of Bones grows in twists and turns and unexpected leaps.  And it's a good thing Khat, unlike his human friend, can survive in the dangerous desert outside of  Charisat because it looks like he's going to run out of options before long.Martha Wells has told a wonderful tale in this book, alive with action, good characters, an interesting world, and solid plotting.  This is an adventure story well worth reading.

World with super-power characters (based on the four elements of fire,air,water, and earth) and a few extraordinaries (normals) and a big storm.  Three viewpoints - well done.  Action scenes a bit weak.
Just comprehensive enough to make you want to explore these complex characters in greater depth.  A great off-the-shelf resource.

While I found The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle to be meandering, these stories show exactly how good Murakami is. His stories are weird, wonderful and enlightening. I may have to reread this now after the tragedy in New Orleans. It seems appropriate.
One of the more useful Russian books for the North American cook. It is somewhat dated - lots of references to "Soviet", etc., but excellent recipies, especially for pilaf.
As a non-architect, I enjoyed some aspects of this book, but frankly, it can't be abridged enough.

Joan Cooper, a Californian by birth, lived and worked at Culbone on Exmoor in Somerset. She is buried in the churchyard there. She exerted spiritual influence not only by her teaching but by her life.

All poems that at one time Lord Wavell could repeat from memory. He compiled it during WW II when he was a serving General in the British Army. As with much attractive poetry, to some degree it remembers itself; who, having once read it, could forget the lines he quotes from his friend Julian Grenfell, killed in WW I, beginning "The sun like a bishop's bottom, rosy and round and hot..."?
Fun, sweet, and yet sassy, story. Might appeal to fans of Agatha Christie's Tommy and Tuppence Beresford series and fans of sweet historical romance.

I thought this would be interesting to read (seeing as this is Terry Jones the comedian we're talking about) but it was actually rather dull and scholarly, albeit fascinating from an informational perspective. Very helpful for an extensive research paper that I wrote once.
Yes, this is a kids' picture book of a rather silly poem by Southey, but the pictures are seriously beautiful! I use to love to read this aloud to myself when I was younger.

Well, yes, only the best book ever! I don't think anyone else could ever come close to approximating Stephen Fry's style. It's so distinctively funny and makes you feel intelligent while reading it. He slips in a reference to literature or history and you feel very elite, as if only you and maybe a few select other people know what he's talking about. For a hopeless Anglophile like me, The Liar is the sort of book that I almost wish I lived in (though perhaps, in this case, it's better just to read about it). This world of Oxbridge and English society that's of course not real at all but does a very good job of pretending - practically a modern version of Wodehouse, except maybe a little less benign and more sinister. Anyway, highly recommended, etc. etc.

Meet Fluffy and PKP -- Princess Killer Pinknose -- two cats who should never be left alone, especially if there's any chance that they'll find something to entertain themselves.  Their humans unexpectedly have to take jobs away from the home, leaving the two without quality pets and food on command.  It's going to be a difficult change for the two spoiled felines, but cats can always find a way of making such a horrible event somewhat better.And guess what?  They found the joys of the Internet!  Surfing, chat rooms... on-line trading services and pizza delivery.The world is not safe.Fluffy has her hands -- a, paws -- full when her psychotic sister PKP learns the power of the Internet.  But with a lot of luck, and some Insider Information on Trading, the two may well make their humans rich... or possibly get them sent to prison.Beth Hilgartner did an excellent job of bringing too delightful, and neurotic, cats to life.  Their adventures with the Internet, a visiting dog, and their poor, befuddled humans make this a joy for cat lovers.The book also has an introduction by S. L. Viehl.

I read this book when I was younger and just fell in love with it. The romanticism charmed me at the time, and I memorised the "They seek him here, they seek him there..." chant. A great book for anyone, especially me when I was growing up!

A fascinating history of some of the early congressional debates about slavery. For the most part these were debates about whether it would even be permissible to discuss the "peculiar institution" of the South in the U.S. House of Representatives. Miller makes excellent use of the original records of these debates and does a good job portraying the debates in terms of the concerns of the participants, people who had no foreknowledge that this issue would ultimately lead to the American Civil War. The book also provides a larger-than-life look at the last stage of the career of John Quincy Adams, the only former U.S. President to serve in the House of Representatives.
Wonderful story—absolutely thrilling. A classic. It's so good you can almost ignore the often flabby writing.

Study of the lives and works of two female painters in late 19th-Century Sweden. I bought this book having seen a small, sketchy portrait by Eva Bonnier in the municipal art-gallery in the town where I live, which, despite its diminutive size, easily outshone anything else on the gallery's walls. Both Bonnier and Hirsch-Pauli excelled as insightful portraitists.Supposing I've gleaned the information from the book correctly (my Swedish is still quite poor), both artists had to navigate social obstacles, and overcome prejudices, in order to continue painting - despite coming from relatively wealthy and libreral family backgrounds. Even so, Bonnier apparently felt obliged to give up painting after a relatively short career.
This was highly recommended by the proprietor of the bookshop in Barcelona when I asked for the best novel in Catalan - after he convinced me of the problems with Tirant lo Blanc.
Very difficult to get into, but I'm a very slow reader. I've put it aside for now.

This is my favourite manga series, bar none. It's not wacky and it's not fantasy; it's hard science fiction, but not space opera. This is low sf, about garbage collectors. I would love it if it were a novel. I wish there were more manga in this subgenre.

Good reference for basic farm cooking in the Midwestern United States. Mrs. Myhre did have an odd, presumably unrequited, love for butter flavored "Crisco" vegetable shortening, though, bless her soul.
One of the few acceptable semi-authentic Chinese/Jewish Cookbooks
This books is evil. Too many books that slipped past my radar, all conveniently listed at the back

This book proves that ancient religions (plural) are true. And how does it do that? Simply: quoting their orthodox and authoritative sources. Simply reading the book makes you perceive three things: first, that these ancient sages really grasped something; second, that this "something" is the same for all of them; and third, that no modern (post-XV century) religion did so.
A readable and useful work, concentrating on the mystical side of things; it must be kept in mind that Glassé was a follower of René Guenon, with his, um, unusual ideas about "universal religion."
A strange, idiosyncratic book full of unusual, thought-provoking readings.
Ann Coulter may have extreme positions regarding some subjects, but one thing she manages to do very well: to show that liberals are, simply put, wrong.
One of my all time favorite books. The perfect read for when you are on the road.

In this book Mr. Horowitz explains what's deeply wrong with the liberal reasoning, and why. Having been one of the most important New Left intellectuals of the 60's, as well as a distinguished Civil Rights activist (what he continues to be), and now turned to libertarian and conservative thinking, he speaks from direct personal experience. A must read!

In 1982 Mr. Golitsyn, an ex-KGB spy, made 148 specific and falsifiable predictions about the future of the communist bloc, and 139 turned out to be right, a success rate of 94% in a time when other analysts managed a perfect 0% score. Not only that, but his biography (unfortunately almost absent in the book) is so interesting that even Alfred Hitchcock made a movie about him. In short: this book is a must read for anyone interested in both Cold War current world affairs. Just read it.

To have militant politics, militant judges and militant NGOs is bad enough, but to have militant journalists is simply ridiculous. Goldberg thus shows that liberals not only think wrong, they also do wrong, and worse, they do wrong where they shouldn't "do" anything at all. No wonder most americans distrust Big Media...
A short and well written, although somewhat too materialistic, biography of the Buddha.
Since I'm not a native English speaker, this ilustrated and very well organized English-English dictionary for foreigners helps me a lot!
This is more or less the core of libertarianism. A true classic.
This is a book that teaches a fundamental lesson: to never, ever, lose hope.
Fascinating diary of social and literary life in tenth-century upper-class Japan by a lady-in-waiting to the young Empress Sadako.
Classic whirlwind tour of Crusades history. Mayer has no political but only scholarly axes to grind.
Miscellaneous collection of material online, but in convenient and modern new format.
Richard is married to an Iranian woman as well as being a professor of Iranian studies at the Sorbonne, and knows the subject as well as anyone could.
The first serious account available in English of the writings and thought of Ibn Arabi, one of the most important thinkers of Islam.
Asad's edition is especially useful because he includes copious notes taken from the traditional commentaries.

A good selection by a guy who was Afghanistan's Minister of Education (in the '50s?) as well as ambassador to India, Great Britain, and the U.S., but about whom I can find nothing online except that he's also known as Najib Ullah Khan.
Novel (by an actress/author popular a century ago but forgotten by her death in 1937) about Shamil's fight for freedom from Russia; book also includes story "Tsarskii gnev" [The Tsar's anger].
A riveting book that gives an idea of what being a serf was like (you'll never think fondly of the Sheremetev family again); based on his memoirs, first published in 1888.
Excellent, detailed history of Syrian politics between WWII and the union with Egypt; Seale knew many of the main actors, and the footnotes are peppered with references to conversations.

A fine biography; Seale has been accused of being insufficiently hard on Assad, but he could hardly have had such informative conversations if he'd been a firm critic, and I can get my condemnation elsewhere.
Contains essays by Mahdi, Berque, Rosenthal, Hossein Nasr, Schimmel, Baalbaki, King, Roper, Eickelman, and others.

This is a very good book, if meandering. I take it as a sword & sorcery novel, even though I think she's aiming for something more literary. Nevertheless, the bones of Fritz Leiber and Robert E. Howard can be seen in the actions of Gwynn.
This was very disappointing. Goingback's writing is just poor. It's too bad because he obviously has a passion for St. Augustine, Fla., and has some interesting ideas.
Vandermeer is a fantastic writer. I have two versions of this book, the hardcover Cosmos edition includes many things not in the original Wildside edition. Still, either is worth your while.
The foundation stone of Persian literature; this heavily abridged prose translation at least provides the stories.

Langewiesch is an American author who writes for the Atlantic Monthly magazine. This is travel literature about his solo trip through Algeria, Niger and and Mali in the 1990s by way of public transportation, crossing the Sahara. As with all great travel/adventure books it is more than just exciting stories, it offers insights into life, how we live it, the choices we make. All the while providing unforgettable stories about life in the desert on a personal level from the people who live there.

Thesiger was one of the last British "gentleman explorers" and spent a lifetime traveling the globe, but found no other place as beautiful as Arabia. He traveled through the desert within a desert, the Empty Quarter of southern Saudia Arabia, living with, and as, the Beduin nomads for 5 years and 10s of thousands of miles by camel. He was the first European to see and map many parts of the desert. Incredible insights into Arabian culture and mindset. I suspect this book was the inspiration for Frank Herberts "Dune", it is very other-worldy, yet real and gripping. A short book at 300 pages covering 5 years of high adventure it can be an exhausting read. It is considered an all-time classic of the travel literature genre.As Thesiger says the most interesting part of his journey was not the trip, but the circumstances. Since "infidals" are not allowed in many parts of "The Sands" he was constantly under-cover, on the run, fighting raiders, jailed, sailing on ships maned by African slaves, dealing with quicksands, starvation, wolves, cold, thirst, etc.. he understates much of it, but the number of close calls and near-death encounters and sheer luck are amazing. As well the Arab culture, mindset and way of life is revealed here in a way I have never read or seen before.A common theme throughout is how modern industrial culture is destroying the nomadic way of life, how Thesiger saw in those 5 years the first oil exploration companies changing the way of life for people who have not changed in 7000 years or more. Thesiger documented a culture and society at the cusp of its destruction, that no longer exists. Although the book was written in 1959, much of the current world events involving radical Islam can be better understood by understanding where the Arabian, and Muslim, culture used to be not so long ago.
Beautiful poems, with the original Japanese, romaji and French translation side by side. French translation is excellent.
If there is one Ford book to buy, this is it. There simply is no one currently writing short fiction better than Jeffrey Ford.

This book was terrible, and I like Palahniuk's books. Some of the stories are quite good but are lost in this unrelentingly dark book. No two characters write or speak any differently and they all act stupid beyond the point of credibility.
An incredible book, well worth its price. Excellent biographical and artistic information.
The great Lester Bangs, his work is so good, it's too bad his influence has been so bad on up-and-coming reviewers. Still, that doesn't change how good these articles are.
I've found it to be quite accurate and always recommend it to people coming to the country.

Fascinating non-fiction account, written by the mother of Lauriane. She gives her side of the media circus created by her ex-husband (the first French person to get asylum in the US), with support from every single legal decision in her favor (not one in favor of Kamal, the ex-husband). Several publications had to pay the mother fines for defamation - they never asked her side of the story, and until now she kept a very low profile out of concern for her daughter's well-being. (Lauriane is now 16.)
Wonderful book for anyone interested in the Nez Perce or Native Americans in general. I've read it several times, the author is an excellent observer and writer.
Pretty much what you'd expect a Coen brother's poetry to be.  Obscene, hilarious, and deeply weird.
One of many beautiful, satirical, bawdy, and gently ironic fantasies.  Cabell was a notable literary figure at one point, but his mannered language seems to have fallen out of style.
This book bugs me on many levels, but it would be useful to people who really don't want or need to delve deeply into English. Still, I wish the author himself appreciated English in more depth.
A beautiful book, half fantasy novel and half folktale. More melancholy and serious than you might expect from the back blurb. Underrated and highly recommended.
I haven't read Empire Star, but Babel 17 is excellent: intelligent, fun, fast-paced SF with a nice kick of interesting ideas.
the Egytian-Wahhabi War of the early 19th century over the Hijaz
Writing "this book changed my life" can be a cliche, but in this case, it's true.  I'm a sucker for organizational schemes, and have tried many over the years, but this one works best for me.
Articles "concerning top leaders of the three revolutions of modern China; the Taiping Rebellion, the Republican Revolution, and the Communist vement.
It's easy now to criticize Mao and the Cultural Revolution, but Leys was vilified for doing so thirty years ago. Still vivid, excoriating reportage.
This thick book provides alternative medical to conventional methods of medical treatment.  Very good reference book to have around.

This is a collection of Ashton Smith's fantastic, horrific poetry.  He considered himself a poet first and foremost, and there is really very little like it in the world.  Linguistically excessive, over-ornate, overwrought, but... still somehow fascinating.

Mrs. Ashdown's book is fun, but not very reliable as a source. One can't entirely blame her for this; costume research was still new and full of Victorian misconceptions when this book was written (early 20th century). The book includes several lovely full-color photo plates in which people wear reconstructed costumes of various periods. We now know that many of the details in Ashdown's book are not correct, but the effort put into these photos is still admirable. (Note that the woman on the cover wearing a 14th century cotehardie is clearly wearing a turn of the 20th century corset!) I suggest that you not use this as a main source for costuming research, but it is a fun book to look through if you can avoid the pitfalls.

Dense, dark, dismal and almost opaque.  Don't give up on Davidson after bouncing off this one.  For Vergil fanatics, though, there's a lot of really interesting stuff in here.  Just be prepared to fight for it.
I enjoyed some of the setting and details, but it felt like the author didn't quite know what she wanted to do with the novel. It needed a bit more of a spine.

Ultimately unsatisfying... Moorcock's argument against Tolkien and his ilk is unconvincing when it is on the basis of writing and immaterial when on the basis of politics.  Many of the more recent fantasy fictions influenced by the British left have been equally silly.  Also, dismissing Cabell and Vonnegut as contrived?  I shouldn't really bring up Moorcock's own writing, but... dude shouldn't front.

An unusually focused collection for Wolfe: each story has some connection to a holiday or anniversary. Despite this, the stories are typical Wolfe; vivid, precise, and strange. Recommended, if you can get your hands on it.

An extensive collection of fictional diseases and disorders, each one written by a different author. Some are whimsical, others horrific. Most are a little bit of both. An excellent book to pick up on a rainy afternoon, and it's worth owning just to see the puzzlement on guest's faces as they try to figure out just what it is.

A set of novellas set in an iconic, somewhat unreal city (weird fiction seems to have strong urban tendencies). The novellas hold together so well that it's hard to believe they were ever published separately. Has a truly outstanding fictional history stuck in the middle. There's supposedly a new edition with even more content, but I haven't the money to buy a book I already own.

Naples in an impossible Roman age as only the superstitions of the dark ages would have imagined it; the poet Virgil as a puissant alchemist and sorcerer. A very enjoyable adventure with a well-realized mystical order. First in a series. The second novel, Vergil in Averno, is extremely weird and can be difficult to read, but has the usual Davidson virtue of being impeccably written. The third novel in the series, The Scarlet Fig, has been posthumously edited to completion and should be available in 2005.

This book is along the same lines as the Vergil series in being a sort of idiosyncratic re-imagining of ancient history and legends. Like the Vergil novels it is quite strange, but rewarding. Set in the mythical far-northern land of Ultima Thule, it explores themes of animal transformation and forge mysticism.

The second (chronologically) collection of Bester's short stories, after Starburst.  Bester has a way with pulp SF stories... like lesser authors he uses a strong, sometimes overpowering concept, and hammers it into the reader.  But Bester's clockwork stories flash with wit, style and glimpses of literary brilliance.  A fun, brief collection for a slow weekend.

Librarything apparently won't allow me to review each edition separately.  Oh well.  I keep the Waley edition for his notes and his bare, literal, somewhat political translation.  The Feng-English has a good balance between poetics and literalism and generally comes in a nice edition with Jane English's photographs.  The Le Guin edition has the most beautiful English poetry I've seen in a translation and she has an interesting take on the text.  Her notes are also funny, humble, and helpful.It's good to own multiple English translations, as the thing is basically untranslatable in any perfect fashion.As for the Tao Te Ching itself... I've read many philosophical and religious texts, and this is the one that speaks to me the most.  Simple, humble, strikingly conservative yet almost revolutionary in this day and age.  I go back to it as often as I can.

A precursor to Lone Wolf and Cub, this follows the exploits of Decapitator Asaemon before his appearance in the latter series.  Drawn and written with the same care and elegance, it plays less as an epic revenge story and more as a revealing sort of episodic procedural, with Asaemon intersecting with (and ending) the lives of a host of intriguing characters.

Light, humorous novels by a good pair of authors who were close friends.  The main character finds himself stuck in various mythological worlds (ala A Connecticut Yankee) and gets out of jambs via wits and technological know-how.  Good vacation read.

A character-driven, low-action manga series detailing the lives of orbital trash collectors. Less a continuous story and more a series of linked vignettes. Recommended for lovers of hard SF, excellent artwork, or detailed characters.

Le Guin explores the fear of death and change in this elegant novel.  It's the last in the unofficial "original" trilogy... the books written later, while good, diverge from these first three in some important respects.
A beautiful parable of taoism hidden in a perfectly-written exploration of a compelling, unique fantasy world.  One of the very best.

Immaculately realized secondary world that goes beyond swords and sorcery. Something of the vivid details of Vance but with a less mannered tone. The central conceit of the novel, the Blue Star's magical properties, is a good one, though the characters are somewhat slight.

First in a trilogy of YA novels by Tripods author Christopher.  They take place in post-apocalyptic Britain, and are a fairly dark and sobering look at society, particularly for YA readers.  I enjoyed them quite a bit as an adult.
A crazy fun suspense SF from the olden days.  One of the best examples of Bester's genius: perfect storytelling efficiency.

The "Camel Book", as this book is often called, is the Perl Bible.  It's not only an exhaustive reference, but clearly written any *funny* to boot.  The humour pervades the text, making a sometimes dry subject much more approachable.No Perl programmer can afford to be without this book, and anybody considering writing a technical reference should refer to this book to see how it's done.

This book is basically a best-practice manual for systems administration.  It's extremely well written, covering both technical and policy issues with examples and short case studies throughout.  One really nice feature is that each chapter is broken down into "The Basics" (what you need to do to get something working), and "The Icing" (additional things you can do  to be a cut above the rest).One day I will make time to read this book cover to cover, but in the meantime it's an excellent reference - especially when attempting to communicate with management on sysadmin issues .
A humorous picaresque set in a mythical Latter Rome (though not that of Davidson's superior Vergil Magus series).  Light, but amusing and full of Davidson's strange wit and inventions.

So incredibly excessive, but so wonderful all the same. Smith, a poet by trade, has a way with words which he may go a bit far with, but it's all in the name of vivid, evocative madness. These stories are from an old and dying world, drenched in wickedness and ancient gods. Somewhat in the vein of Lovecraft (and they walked in the same circles, Smith writing sometimes in the Lovecraft canon), but more fantastic and less horrific. Ashton Smith's fantastic poetry (collected in The Last Oblivion) is... interesting, if nothing else.
Probably the only great book about heavy metal. Essential to all headbangers.

Great just for the story of the California sorcerors, the group of writers including William Nolan, Richard Matheson, Beaumont, Ellison, who worked together writing stories for TV and for the science fiction magazines of the day. There's some classic stories in here too.

Somtow is a good horror/science fiction writer, but this autobiographical story is one of his best. I don't think this is the edition I own, which is paperback and came my way via a friend in Thailand.
Painfully slow, it tries to hard to be something more than scary and ends up something less.
People seem to either love or hate this one...I didn't love it.
Really couldn't relate to this book at all...the only good thing about it was the title.
Best book for both adults and children. Meant to be re-read often.
Great series, but the illustrations in this one are my favourite.

Il titolo è tratto dal &quot;Riccardo III&quot; di Shakespeare: è la maledizione che il fantasma della regina Anna scaglia sul re che l'ha fatta uccidere. Ma la storia è ambientata nella Madrid dei nostri giorni, dove l'io narrante, Victor Francés, sceneggiatore per il cinema e la tv, vive facendo il &quot;negro&quot;, in proprio o per conto terzi. Victor conosce Marta, una donna sposata che gli muore tra le braccia proprio la notte del loro primo convegno amoroso. Fugge, ma resta prigioniero del passato della donna e decide di ricostruirlo. Sarà un viaggio di esplorazione nei misteri del cuore umano, ricco di sorprese, drammi, colpi di scena.

The Nuremburg goldsmith Wentzel (or Wenzel) Jamnitzer’s Perspectiva Corporum Regularium was one of a number of fascinating books of elaborate polyhedral designs issued in mid-16th-Century Germany. Jamnitzer has been rated as ‘one of the most creative polyhedral artists of all time.’ This slim paperback reproduces the complete work, with a contemporary introduction in Spanish.
This beautiful volume, nº 8 of the Serie Mayor in in Siruela’s La Biblioteca Azul, reproduces hundreds of the most notable illustrations from Kircher’s books, with notes and commentary in Spanish.
The best value for your euro as far as smaller French-French dictionaries go. Excellent detail for its size.
A very thorough overview with tips that sewers of any level can use. This 1982 edition is full of vintage fun too (color photos!).

A nice introduction to adding a Japanese touch This book is full of ideas for sewing projects with Japanese flair. It does seem to be meant more for beginner-intermediate sewers, as there are quite a few pages on how to do piecing and appliqué (by hand and machine), as well as basic embroidery. However, the introductions to dip-dyeing, stenciling and gilding are nice extras that you don't often see in quilting books. Overall the designs are fun, elegant and easy to make. My favorite part of the book is the templates and motifs - they're rather simple, but still good additions to a design library. I give this book four stars out of five because although it's well done, it lacks depth and inspiration, especially compared to other books on the subject. Wonderful as an introduction and for beginner-intermediate sewers and quilters, but those already familiar with Japanese motifs and textiles will gain only a little new insight.

Valuable resource An excellent book for someone with previous sewing experience, especially hand sewing. (You don't need a machine to make these garments, in fact, it's better to do it by hand.) I very much appreciated the background on Japanese sewing, however, the stitches are not as clearly illustrated as they could be, and would probably be very difficult to understand for a beginning sewer. As for the other illustrations, arm yourself with patience and re-read the explanations several times through. Overall I'm happy with this book after looking everywhere for traditional Japanese kimono patterns. I was able to successfully complete a kurotomesode (formal black kimono) thanks to it.

Inspiring A beautiful book, with story-like descriptions that go along with each design. I'm an intermediate sewer/quilter and found that while giving easy-to-follow instructions, Kumiko Sudo also leaves plenty of room for the imagination, and her designs are sure to spark creativity! I've successfully completed two different blocks: they're enjoyable to make and a pleasure to contemplate once finished. This is one of my favorite quilting books - one I'll use for years and years, thanks to the quality of the designs and instructions.
Lovely designs, as always from Sudo. If you get the Dover book of Japanese crests (mon), this book definitely inspires you to design your own.
Charming little projects ranging from simple to intricate. A lot of small purses, as well as boxes and charm-holders. They all should be hand-sewn (it's much faster and more accurate).

Much more than a simple cookbook, the author truly teaches you how to cook, in authentic Thai style and in general. I've adopted so many techniques from this book that it has truly changed my cooking style for the better.
Nice little pocket guide, only scratches the surface though. Good for the major AOCs.

Capitalism uber alles, because socialism must always equated with central planning.  or at least that's what reagan and thatcher took from this book.  Honestly, I need to finish it, but if you can draw the connection between James C. Scott's use of 'Metis' as a contextualised form of knowledge suppressed by modernist capitalism (or capitalist modernism?), and Hayek's use of "the businessman's knowledge" (paraphrase) as a form of knowledge suppressed by modernist socialism, you'll win a big internet hug.A must read for anyone who dares use that word 'market' or call themselves 'liberal'

Great book, but beware the publisher, they're extremists (very right-wing). I made the mistake of signing up for their (postal, not email) mailing list thinking I'd discover interesting publications, and was instead faced with right-wing screeds... However, while tinges of such a mindset can be discerned in "Mon", the book doesn't suffer from it. I've found it to be a good reference for mon-specific symbolism.
A good book. Gives good description of life inside the SAS and the British army in general.
Very good for English speakers since the Chinese section is in Latin alphabetical order by pronunciation (in other words, you don't need to know ideograms to figure out what someone's saying to you).
Perfect for travel in Italy; there's also a "guide de conversation" in the back.

This book is incredible. If you speak French and plan to go to China, you MUST get this, it explains Chinese to beginners better than anything else I've found. When I was in China, even Chinese people were impressed by it (and not by any others we had!). The publisher, You Feng, is Chinese, based in Paris.
Good overall for the country. (For Beijing, a friend had the Lonely Planet Beijing guide, and we found that the Rough Guide to Beijing was more thorough.)
Stephens, long-time editor of The Statesman in India, knew the situation and the people involved well. The book goes up to 1962.
Quite a large book compared to the size of the point that's being made. Overrated.
Probably not as good as The Minotaur Takes A Cigarette Break, but worth reading.
Thumbs down. These crosswords are too easy, despite the culturally-specific content. Also, they frequently include two-letter words, or non-crossed letters.
Rates up there with Calvin & Hobbes and Far Side as far as I'm concerned.
My first introduction to anarchism; a wonderful collection of essays.

I found it in a used bookstore, noticed that it was part of a long series, and thought "hmmm, it can't be too horrible if they published this many sequels".  As the astute reader can tell, I was quite young at the time and hadn't realized just how many truly awful sequels are published every year.The Gor series seems to be written as erotica for 1930's era mysogynasts.  There aren't even any sex scenes as payoff for reading all the turgid prose promoting the idea that women are sex slaves by their essential nature.Modern books offer better philosophy, better storytelling, and better sex.  My advice is to ignore the Gor series.
I can't believe I've lugged this huge book (it weighs ten pounds!) through all my moves over the last thirty years, but I got it in Dublin and I love Irish even though I'll never use it.
Highly recommended to ambitious fans of fantasy, as it contains the best meta-discussion of fantasy writing I've ever seen.  It's also a good conclusion/summation of Cabell's novels overall.
A dystopic alternate history, mixed with metaphysics. Extremely effective and disturbing. It will stay with you for a long time.
Perhaps someone will disagree, but I found this to be simply too weird and disjointed to enjoy.  I think this happened to Dick novels after a while, unfortunately.
Small, mysterious novel, somewhat reminiscent of Bradbury. Highly recommended by some: I was impressed, though it isn't my favorite novel. Very good for a change of pace.

An eccentric collection by an exceedingly eccentric author.  It's an excellent volume to pair with The Avram Davidson Treasury.  Most of these stories are weirdly skewed peeks at a recent past that never quite was or just might have been.  In the Davidson tradition, some stories are impenetrable, and you put the book down shaking your head.  Others (like Twenty Three, The Peninsula, and Dragon Skin Drum) are just brilliant.  Davidson fans will certainly want to own this.  Newcomers might want to start with the Treasury (or might I suggest The Phoenix and the Mirror?).
A fun little detective story, colorfully illustrated and populated with interesting characters.  Would like to find some other work by this creator.
Excellent, serious-minded Gekiga, with an episodic plot that nevertheless references itself throughout.  Think of it as hard-sf short stories with beautiful art.
The most recent Earthsea novel, it is good reading but follows the recent trend of Le Guin novels feeling a bit too gentle, and without a storytelling spine.

Endlessly complex, endlessly debated (I think Wolfe has to be the most comprehensively discussed SF/F author on the web). Worth reading for Wolfe's unmatched mastery of prose and the intricate, mysterious secondary world. I like Wolfe's short stories most of all, but this comes as a close second.

Big, splashy mission statement of the new weird. Highly grotesque steampunk-esque urban fantasy with some truly frightening, distinctive antagonists. The main characters are oddly irritating at times. Mieville's sequel, The Scar, is also good, but is somewhat anticlimactic and suffers from a truly odd choice of protagonist. The third novel in the series, Iron Council, has much better pacing and more interesting characters. All three novels are great fun but can grate at times because they try to be thrillers and social commentaries, and don't really succeed at both.

Painstakingly written as a Regency-Era fantasy novel.  Superb for those whose ears perk up at this concept... probably a bit baffling for everyone else.  I enjoyed it for the wonderful secondary world, though it isn't quite a full-course meal like Little, Big.

A historically significant and very enjoyable collection of edgy SF stories.  Represented the up-and-coming talent of the time in a way that few collections have before or since.  Essential for any collector of SF short stories.

The shortest and most tightly written of the Culture novels.  Probably the finest in terms of pure enjoyment... the novel is both a fascinating exploration of an exotic culture and a terrific, suspenseful puzzle.

Banks keeps some of his "character-study-inside-space-opera" method going with this Culture novel, but it's headier and more concept-driven than his previous novels.  I'm not sure I believe in his particular conception of AI and it isn't QUITE as good as the first 3 or so, but it's an enjoyable read and definitely should be on your list if you like the Culture novels.
Excellent cinematic, suspenseful SF.  The first and in some ways the best of the Culture series.  Banks is a master at exploring a work that is utopian in some ways, and unremittingly dark in others.

Seems to have been meant as a sort of spiritual sequal to Consider Phlebas.  Seems somewhat indulgent for a Culture novel, and doesn't really cover any new ground.  It also lacks the strong internal structure that Banks' earlier novels boasted.  Perhaps he's tiring of the setting?

Tremendous premise and ideas, excellent writing, incoherent ending.  Basically, the problem is that Stevenson writes narrative checks the second half of the book can't cash and there's just too much to resolve or explore to fruition.  Still an excellent novel, although the more indulgent aspects of his writing, especially after the relatively tight Snow Crash, were to be a bad sign for his later works...
Definitely full of interesting ideas, but I found it a bit too cold to be engaging.

This is a collection of three somewhat early hermaphroditic fantasy novels by Australian writer Constantine.  While not perfectly written (the first one is pretty rough, the latter two are better), they are unique and absorbing post-apocalyptic fantasies with some great characters.  The squeamish need not apply, as there is extensive discussion of hermaphroditic sexuality.
The beards on the so-called Jews on the cover couldn't look more fake if they came with a strap.
What a delightful old-school novel! (It's old-school because it's old.) Story of some boys who build a spaceship. Includes little green men and pet chicken!
Worth reading for the menus alone - where else could you find out what was served at Lawrence Welk's 75th birthday?
This is my favourite Kate Wilhelm book.  Her gothic paranormal suspense ones didn't do anything for me.  I should probably reread it so I can be more specific about the fun dorks' romance + spy plot.

Really a very heterogenous collection, as it spans decades, writing styles, and themes.  The Dying Earth was one of Vance's earliest works and has an episodic, contemplative quality that is missing from his later works.  The two Cugel novels are vintage Vance: strange, cynical, and darkly humorous.  I've yet to read Rhialto the Marvellous.

I should probably disclose that I am a Vance collector and die-hard. While most of his work is science-fantasy, the Lyonesse series is a historical fantasy, and a very good one. Vance's prose style is unusual and can be a hard sell; think P.G. Wodehouse with laser guns and ogres. I recommend giving it a try, though; you might very well find yourself as miserably addicted as I am.

A pretty good Gaean Reach one-shot, with some good character chemistry and a Vance protagonist that isn't quite the usual you expect from him.  How fantastic is it that Ibooks is making these available again.

A somewhat interesting anthropological "social SF" novel, in the vein of The Dispossessed, but inferior to most of Le Guin's better works.  It's not offensively bad, but it's probably only for Le Guin diehards.
One of the best Sacco comics, partially because of its strong internal structure.  This is an example of a book leaving you with a profound ambivalence, and that being a good thing.
Short biographies of animation greats from America, Europe and Japan.  It's pretty good reading, and the presentation is nice.  A good coffee-table book for an animation geek.

Not much to say; it's a dense book that I read many moons ago. Not the best for reproduction of period poetical forms, as it talks more about the cultural aspects of the form than about the poetry itself. Focuses on early Islam, up to 'Abbasid era.

The famous characters of Victorian novels, effortlessly translated into retro superheroes by the fabulous Alan Moore.  And did I mention that the art is really excellent?  Both volumes are highly recommended for the discerning adventure fan.
Agatha Christie wins. She always beats me. I suspected the murderer at one point in the book, but I think that I suspected everyone at some point or another. AC's always a good read.
Brilliant novel. The story at the center is the best part, but all the layers of narrative add more and more to the novel.

Very impressed. This is the first book by G.G. I have read. I do not like the neither USA or USSR is bad or good moral relativism which is expressed by several characters (particularly Daintry), but it is so well written that I do find myself rooting for the traitor Castle.
Fun stuff. Tasty sci-fi martial art, bartending, one man rebellion goodness.
Not really useful as a reference, but good to flip through when you're bored. Nice odds and ends. You'll pick up a few things.
This really isn't fantasy at all. There are a few eerie moments, when the narrator is superstitious, but that's it. Still, "low fantasy" fans will probably enjoy the setting.

Since it had been many years since I had read some of the earlier books in this series, I decided I wanted to go back and reread each of them, in order, before beginning this book. I felt I'd enjoy it the most in that manner. Rereading helped remind me of many details I'd forgotten. In all honesty, I'm very impressed with Jordan's continuity. He must keep good notes... for if there are discontinuities, they certainly are not obvious. During this reading, I was focusing on the details. There are many side- and sub-plots to this series. Jordan certainly has an effective way of moving from scene to scene in a manner that is effective, rather then jarring. (As compared to, say, Martin's Fire and Ice series. I'm not sure what quality of his writing it is that bugs me, but every change of scene there makes me feel like it's a whole new book.) Perhaps it's the way Jordan blends people from different groups into some of the same scenes, though  various means, be it the dreams of the women, or the "colors" that have entered the latest books through the men. It's just a much more smooth transisition each time.I'm enjoying the way that many lines are being tied, while others are continuing and even a few beginning. I'm going to hate to see the end of this book, and, honestly, I don't get the feeling at all that it's being "dragged on". I'm much more worried that as the end nears, too many lines will have unfinished or rushed endings... An abrupt, pasted-together final book, just to have an END, would be a disappointment after such a wonderful series.

This is a very slim little book, but it’s a lot of fun! It tells the story of a girl who remembers the line from Peter Pan about how a fairy dies every time someone says “I don’t believe in fairies” as she is getting attacked by the Fairy of Frequent and Painful Pointless Antagonism. So she says it until the fairy falls dead (seven times), at which point a hobgoblin shows up and accuses her of murdering seven fairies, some of whom were actually good. So the girl travels around the world with the hobgoblin to fix the damage that she caused by killing the fairies (and yes, she could just clap her hands a lot and say “I do believe in fairies, I do, I do”, but then the Fairy of Frequent and Painful Pointless Antagonism would come back to life right in front of her and angry). The journey is very funny and the solutions that the girl comes up with are very entertaining.The writing is very good and incredibly funny. This writer has a wonderful style, which is very impressive since this is his first book. The book is peppered with great phrases like “dropped dead as a gossamer-winged doorknob” and the level of language craft is extremely high throughout the book. That said, there isn’t a whole lot of depth to the story, which is why the book is so short. I really didn’t think that hurt the book, though, since it was a blast to read. Not every book needs to be deep. The main character (Clemency Pogue) and the hobgoblin are wonderfully drawn. Besides, how can a book that advertises itself as doing “for burlap pants what holes have done for Swiss cheese” be anything but pure fun?The illustrations are perfect for the book. They are black and white, mostly full-page pictures of scenes from the book. The style is a believable cartoonishness that resembles the illustrations of Tony DiTerlizzi in the Spiderwick Chronicles. I loved the picture of the little boy pretending to be a dog, chewing on pillows and jumping on the bed. The scenes illustrated are well chosen and generally properly placed, which is much appreciated and not common enough in books.This book is great. It’s light reading and will take maybe an hour to read, but it’s well worth it! I very much look forward to more books from this author!

This book is light and funny and thoroughly enjoyable to read. The plot is a novel idea - a demon tries to set up a fairy tale (Sleeping Beauty) so that it comes out wrong to prove that evil is more at work in the world than good. To do this, he constructs the principle characters (Beauty and the Prince) from parts of other people that are expressly chosen to make their task unlikely (cowardly legs for the prince and a scorned woman’s head for Beauty). Through it all he is fighting a bureaucratic system of evil (of course evil is entirely bureaucracy, it only fits) and an angel who can summon whatever he needs at a moment’s notice. The book and the writing are delightfully funny.This is a very well written book. The plot is paced well and the pace is generally good, varying from laid back to fast paced. The characters are also extremely well done. Azzie, the demon, is creepy and very much trying to be evil, even if sometimes one can’t help but feel for him. His “assistant”, Frike, is perhaps creepier than the actual demon, although his is human. His desire to partake in any questionable activity that Azzie can come up with is endlessly entertaining. Babriel, an angel set to make certain Azzie doesn’t cheat, is another fascinating character. He isn’t good as one generally thinks of angels, but he is good to a fault and the dichotomy there (he helps everyone, because that is good, even a demon) makes him an interesting character to watch. My favourite of the main characters was the witch, Ylith. She was funny and realistic at the same time. She added a much needed touch of human common sense to the book. The cast was very well balanced.This is a light book and generally a pretty quick read. I enjoy it a great deal and defiantly recommend it to anyone else!
a good and humorous look at the way we look at language and how we learn it.
hysterical! a perfect understanding of the fantasy genre which succeeds in poking fun in a very dry manner.
The Sparrow stands so very well on its own, it's hard to imagine a sequal. And yet this really does complete the story from the other side - and what happened afterwards.
Though interseting on its own, primarily a reference for medieval fiction, along the line of "The Name of the Rose".  Has more random  information than you can shake a ploughshare at.

Though some think Sayers can be drawn out in her novels, she writes a swift and through short story, highlighting both the comedic and dramatic elements seen in her longer works.  A fair introduction, even, to Lord Peter.

Furiously researched biographical index and concordance for the Aubrey-Maturin series - up and including The Hundred Days (spoiler notice!) The best reference work on a series one could hopefor, although sometimes lacking in general history - no entry on Trafalgar, what?There is a second edition which was published in June 2006, promising 200 pages of new material and corrections.

Along with the fact that I prefer the younger Russell novels (thus far), this again has got some great characters and the single most connections to the other books in the series.  The one problem with this book I would say is that there's not quite an obvious villian - or rather, a reason why things happen the way they do.
One of my favorite Mary Russell books, I think in part because of the wonderful continuation of characters from O Jerusalem - and the story of Gabriel.

Excellent introduction to problems in philosophy of mind, particularly problems relating to consciousness, which foregrounds J. S.'s own opinions explicitly, making it easier for you to know where he stands and, thus, where you stand. Some arguments are better than others (the argument about free will is especially weak), but that's true of philosophy of mind in general. Entertaining, interesting.
Excellent source of "herregårds mat". Good source of haute bourgeoise Russian recipes.

This is a great book. The program requires some homework on your part - I've chosen to read through the book and then go back and follow all the step listed to really get going. The main idea is to live within your means by determining what is truly important in your life. Maybe your current job is standing between you and fulfillment.
A light history read, perhaps too light. Of interest to me, since I've written a paper before on the topic, and for chess, of course.
One of my favorite, if not my favorite non-fiction book.  An easily accessible, non-mathmatical these on coding.  And for the historian in me, lots of information on the people involved.
Special volume as includes land regained from USSR in Winter War. Fine detail. Detail map of Viipui/Viborg Shows most farms.
Published 2 years after Finland's independence from Russia. First such after 1918.
Ode from an obsessive mother, daughter of the founder of Carmel-by-the-Sea.

This is an unusually well-written autobiography, and one is left feeling rather sad that Hawthorne died before he could read the excellent reviews it attracted in the press and from readers.He takes time and care over the childhood sections, something too many actors gloss over, and paints a fascinating picture of the young man he grew to be. Moving from South Africa, where he'd spent his early years, to Britain, at the end of his teens, he strikes a good balance between emotions and facts, skipping over some details ....but evoking a strong sense of the person he was. Similarly he doesn't dwell overly on his most famous roles (Sir Humphrey Appleby, for instance) but has some interesting insights into the arts of acting, directing, and writing. I was intrigued to find that "Father and Son", the Cat Stevens song covered by Boyzone, came from a musical Stevens and Hawthorne were collaborating on!This book contains an unconventional love story (not just because Hawthorne was gay and not "out" for most of his life, but because he lived in a truly complicated domestic tangle that took some years to resolve), a heartwarming account of finally finding happiness, and some very funny, interesting or otherwise worthwhile stories about a well-loved actor who adored his chosen career.

This is a great romp through familiar DW-J territory - alternative worlds, and magical families. Arianrhod (Roddy, one of the two narrators) and Grundo are part of the King's Progress, the travelling Court, but have to travel alone through the Isles of Blest (a "squished and stretched" British Isles) to stop a plot to take all the magic in the land and use it for evil. The Little People advise Roddy to raise the land to stop the plot, but she has little to go on until she figures out her inherited magic "database".Meanwhile Nick, the other narrator, already a refugee from one world, gets drawn through a few other worlds looking for Romanov, a man who might just have the power to solve the mystery of who is trying to kill whom and why. He promises to help Roddy as part of a journey quest, befriending an elephant on the way, and encountering a malevolent goat named Helga.The plot's intricate but all comes together in a satisfying ending as Roddy works out just what "raising the land" involves - dragons, Stonehenge, and all her extended and rather mad family...

I really do love this book, with its envocation of the departed medieval world and characters within.  I probably reread it once a year, though I mean to take a latin dictionary with me my next bout to understand all of the text.

Carefully researched, and drawing upon many original interviews, this examination of the American and Australian soldier's experience of the ground war in the South West Pacific during WWII is a deep book and very good. (His other book, "Fire in the Sky," about the air war in the same theater, is also excellent.)I read this at the same time as "Gates of Fire," the fictionalized story of the battle of Thermopylae, and I can't decide which men fought in  worse, more inhumane conditions.

The book is a labor of love: there are typos and some stylistic inconsistencies. However, these are counter-balanced by an obvious enthusiasm for the subjects and love for the topic.Since the nine second-person stories are based on interviews and whatever documents the veterans possess so many years on, they vary in detail and length.Still, I enjoyed reading these stories for the way they touched on common threads (many related to the common location where they enlisted), and as an antidote to the overly-polished work of Stephen Ambrose: I like Ambrose, and I value the collecting work he did, but this book has a simple, homespun charm. I give it two thumbs up.

In which it is discovered that TH White honestly really did have a political mission.  A mixture of passages from the Sword in the Stone and other animal adventures mentioned but not seen in the Once and Future King, I'm not sure that the tale would have been better ended where it did after all.

A collection of essays by Bart Sutter, a guy from Duluth. My brother gave this to me, but didn't tell me anything about it to prepare me. I laughed out loud at least once during every essay, all of which are about three pages long: easily enjoyed over a cup of hot, hot coffee during a cold Minnesota winter (or over a beer, on a cool new England summer night, for that matter).

Everyone loves Alton Brown: the shocked hair, the espresso-aided delivery, and the Harold McGee-grade scientific foundations for his explanations of how food behaves between his kitchen's four walls (and outside on the grill!) are concise, entertaining, and even practical.

It's hard to disagree with the common sentiment that this is the best introduction to skepticism yet written. It's an impassioned plea for reason, for the inherent virtue of truth and the power of skepticism. Along the way Carl Sagan demolishes, politely and eloquently, tales of alien abduction, ghosts, telepathy and other popular fictions. But more importantly The Demon-Haunted World is an ode to wonder. Carl Sagan was primarily an astronomer, and more than anybody I’ve read he manages to evoke in words a fraction of the feeling you get when looking at the stars. It's quite the read.

I got this book after reading an excellent article about the author in Bitch Magazine.  It's part history of women in spiritual traditions (Buddhism, convent life) and part an analysis of the relationship between a) women and spirituality and b) violence against women.  This is not a straight academic work as Flinder's autobiographical experiences appear within the text, and I found this to be a wise stylistic choice as it made for a page-turning read.  Reading this book is invigorating , and I hated that it had to come to an end.

All Philip K. Dick novels are about the nature of reality, and I think this is his best. Completely mind-blowing yet still comprehensible, it has the incomparable PKD style that I find so hard to pin down - it's some combination of brevity, the unexpected and a sense of the alien, but there's still something entirely Other about the way he writes that I find unique. Hard to describe the plot (not much of a review, this), but as with anything PKD it's completely unpredictable.
