This old book is one that endures despite its age.  It is a humorous look at how statistics can be used, manipulated, and twisted to say just about anything that you want.  In the larger sense, it is important to understand how facts can be spun to represent or create the reality you want to portray.
The ideas expressed in the book make sense to me intellectually; in practice I have been unsuccessful in implementing them.

This is a no-frills, basic introduction to HTML coding.  While it is unlikely that it will, by itself, direct you to produce an award winning web site, it should at least guide you through the foundational elements and get you well on your way.  Or, if mere understanding of how web sites work appeals more to you, then this would be a decent place to start.
This is a pictorial overview of India, obviously the merest sampling.  The pictures are of course delightful.  As a book for children, it is ok; its appeal for adults is quite limited.

George Mosse explores contemporary western culture’s concept of Masculinity or Manliness in The Image of Man:  The Creation of Modern Masculinity.  Mosse argues that masculinity, as an established and widespread notion, is relatively new in western society, solidifying around the time of the French Revolution.  He presents his material chronologically, beginning with the origins of manliness as a desirable ideal; he traces its applications and dissemination, examines the counterexamples, which he stresses are essential to reinforce the ideal, demonstrates how the ideal culminated in the era of the fascist dictators and finally, offers a brief overview of the current state of the concept.

The Divine Comedy epitomized medieval attitudes.  From historical perspectives, this work serves as a window into the mentality of late middle ages in Italy, on the brink of the Renaissance.  Scholastic thinking informs Dante's approach.

A primer of information systems for managers.  In the fast-paced world of technology and information systems, this is about as dated as a book on how to operate an abacus or organize one's file cabinets effectively.  Interesting as an artifact.

This Greek primer seems like a useful and workable method of bringing young scholars and the Greek language together.  I can not fully speak to its effectiveness since I have not used it to any degree nor do I personally have enough knowedge of Greek to evaluate it otherwise.  But judging from my Latin, French and German intro books, this one seems very much in the mainstream.
This book teaches philosphy by examinging basic (Universal?) problems then exploring the writings of various thinkers on these subjects.
This is a Euro-centric compilation of important Western philosophical texts.  Good for exposing readers to the Western canon.  Should definitely be supplimented by addtional readings.

This is a fascinating book that offers selections of Pliny's writings on the strange beasts, creatures, and hanf-humans that he believed populated the world.  Lovely illustrations accompany the writing.  Even if you do not read Latin, the English translation and the pictures make the book a pleasure
This is a guide that teaches you to teach your dog.  You learn how to bond with your dog in ways that a casual pet owner would never have thought possible.  It is a wonderful book.

With Gorey, the pictures more than make up for the text.  His drawings manage to convey so much.  His ability to capture the fine details, and the little elements that go into everyday things, combined with his proclivity for the gothic place him among my favorite artists.

I suppose this book is (or was) good for those who need this or are really interested.  I have to say this bores me completely.  I would rather read the phone book.  However, this book may actually be quite well done.

While Viorst's poetry will probably not stand the test of time over the centuries, it does spotlight and encapsulate life of the late 60s.  Her self-deprecating humor, her barbed insights always charm and usually hit home.  When you need a guick sophisiticated chuckle, turn to Viorst.

Although the scholarship is a bit dated, the contents hold up well.  Akrigg's is a decent assessment of the English Court under James I.  James was a deep, complex individual and Akrigg goes far in analyzing the intricacies of James, as a poltical being primarily but also as a husband, a father, and as a person.  Akrigg's primary focus is on political events, but we get good glimpses of cultural and economic developments as well.

This was assigned in an undergrad Stuart history class.  I was incensed that we were having to read a NOVEL!  Well, I was stupid, indeed.  This is a fine, revealing look at the horrors that people experienced in 1666.

I studied Latin for four years in high school.  Additionally, I was always terribly interested in history.  So it came a complete shock to me when I read this book - a fairly significant uprising, a minor war Rome fought, that I had never heard mentioned.  Fifteen years later, perhaps I understand why this is so.  I can hardly recall anything of the details though I remember finding it pleasant enough to read at the time.  For anyone interested in Roman history, this is worth reading.

This is a magisterial work on the functions and forms of the actual and extra-judicial system as it operated in Southern-Central France in the final days of the Old Regime.  Writen my the director of my PhD dissertation, it is by definition a work for which superlatives are inadequate.

While only the most naive today would contend that the European coloni-zation of Africa occurred for purely altruistic reasons, atrocities and subterfuge on the scale presented by Adam Hochschild in King Leopold’s Ghost give even the jaded cynic pause.  That such base greed carefully done up as humanitarianism managed to inflict so much suffering for so long almost takes one’s breath away.Hochschild presents the story of King Leopold II and his determination to establish some sort of empire for himself.  Hochschild makes clear that Leopold’s ambition centered upon himself; if Belgium or his family profited as a result, that was secondary to the King.  Leopold emerges as a master schemer and con-niver, adept at seeing a profit where most would pass by and skilled at manipu-lating even the most damaging turns to events to suit his own agenda.Writing more as a journalist than as a traditionally trained historian, Hochschild spins a gripping story that compels the reader like a novel.  Had the work turned out to be a roman á clef, it would not have been surprising.  Indeed his cast of players offer fascinating insights into characters that Dickens would have been proud to have created.  Besides Leopold, Henry Stanley is the villain on the spot, whose cruelty and butchery mesmerize with the macabre lure that the cobra holds over its prey.  Furthermore, Lèon Rom appears as the real life monster on whom Joseph Conrad based Mr. Kurtz, in The Heart of Darkness.  Unfortunately, what makes brilliant villains in fiction, makes for genuine horror in reality.Despite the often grisly and lurid information Hochschild has to convey, he manages to do so as tastefully as possible yet still impresses the reader with the grim conditions that prevailed in the Congo.  The beatings with the chicotte and the severing of hands burn vividly in the reader’s mind.  Besides Hochschild’s descriptive skill, the various illustrations make clear the tragic plight of Africans who failed to comply with Belgian demands.However, as promised in the subtitle, the story has its heroes as well.  Jo-seph Conrad personally saw European cruelty at work and voiced his horror of the situation in The Heart of Darkness.  E. D. Morel, who crusaded tirelessly on behalf of the Africans caught in Leopold’s web displays sacrifice and altruism on a vast scale – the only scale that could possibly match the iniquity on the side of Leopold and his agents.  Sir Roger Casement, the Irishman with a fondness for lost causes and martyrdom, managed to aid the Congolese before getting him-self embroiled in even more hopeless causes like Irish independence and un-closeted homosexuality.  Hochschild also presents blacks as heroic agents for resistance, notably George Washington Williams, Hezekiah Andrew Shanu and Reverend William H. Sheppard.  These men fearlessly proclaimed the wrongs being perpetrated in the Congo and insisted that it not be ignored.Hochschild contends that only through the efforts of men brave enough to speak out against Leopold and his tribe did the evil system of oppression yield to more humanitarian methods.  Leopold, he asserts, would have continued his sordid ways as long as possible and abrogated them only when the scrutiny of the world’s attention made their continuance intolerable.In the final section of the book, Hochschild addresses the larger issues, which are:  why is any amount of atrocity tolerable at all, and how are atrocities so easily forgotten or ignored?  Regrettably, his answers do not reflect favorably upon humanity.  Self-serving ends combined with guilt or complicity lead to col-lective forgetfulness and, eventually, ignorance.  The harsh light of self-examination seldom appeals to any but the most saintly of us while politicians offering salves to assuage our shame easily convince us that it is better not to dwell upon it.  Fortunately, writers like Hochschild force the mirror before us and reveal humanity in both its ignominy and its heroism.Alex Hunnicutt

This is a fine book of plans for the garden and lawn that are not beyond the reach of the amateur home owner.  While clearly some are ambitious, the majority of these plans are well presented, and achievable by the person modest talents.  If nothing else, these plans offer ideas, suggestions and inspiration.

This is the culmination of the Narnia series.  As the earlier works are based on aspects of Christianity and the Bible, so too is this work conceived around themes found in Revelations / Apocalypse.  Here we find Lewis making some of his strongest pronouncements of right and wrong.

This is a fascinating book, primarily photographic, that reveals the world of European royalty at the beginning of the twentieth century.  These were the final, heady days of the bazillion descentants of Queen Victoria and Hapsburgs and others.  Everyone was related to each other and all was glittering and beautiful.  These pictures seem especially poignant or bitter knowing that World War I was just moments away.

This is a biography of Kaiser Karl, the last emperor of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, who followed Franz Joseph II in 1916.  He only reigned until November 11 1918, when he abdicated in the general turmoil that resulted in the catastrophic loss of the war.  Karl, of course was not the last Hapsburg.  The family still lives, and the political climate of Europe has changed somewhat.  It is possible his grandson could resume a position of power.  In any case, this book recounts the tale of the Karl up to his days as emperor and to some extent, his brief life afterwards.  He did not long survive the fall of the empire.

This is a fascinating glimpse into the world of the very rich, the ultra elite in their glory from around the late nineteenth century to the mid-twentieth century.  Amory especially focuses on their get-aways - their personal cottages and the communities that they established exclusive and sheltered.  While this is not a rigorous, historical work, it is still quite useful and interesting.  Amory is an insightful writer who can turn a phrase and usually attach a barb.
NA

This book is an excellent introduction to Latin  for young students.  It proceeds slowly, building on previous lessons for a cumulative and comprehensive course in the Latin language.  It uses many classical readings for its sources.

This book is an excellent introduction to Latin  for young students.  It proceeds slowly, building on previous lessons for a cumulative and comprehensive course in the Latin language.  It uses many classical readings for its sources.  This book, even more than the first volume, uses primary source readings - most notably, Caesar and some Ovid.

I admit that Bennett Cerf may not have been cutting edge, satirical comedy with a rapier wit skewering all and sundry.  But he was always fun and funny and a personable human being that I would have been honored to know.  His jokes and stories still amuse, decades later and they also offer a glimpse into the world of Hollywood and Broadway, literature and the arts in a sophisiticated way that gossip shows today can not come near.
If you imagine The Book of Lists, then take that concept and make all the lists gay-oriented you will have this book.  It's fun, entertaining and informative.

I am not a Civil War historian.  I read this prior to taking up history as a grad student and have not had time since to revisit it - so my remarks are by memory.  Flood presents a very likable, respectable Lee.  One is drawn to him.  We want to like him and cheer for his small victories after the war.  But Flood presents a lop-sided, hagiographic view of his subject.  Indeed, there was much to respect in Lee.  It would have seemed the more so if Flood had addressed some of the very real issues that are inescapable in dealing with Lee, first and foremost, his role in perpetuating slavery.  Also, I recall not liking the lack of documentation.  It seemed there were no notes or sources at all (I could be wrong in this.)
This is a small handbook for identification and classification of common shells to be found around America's costal waters.  This is not for the serious collector of shells.

This is a book of letters - fonts, so to speak - that are specifically designed for use in the fabric arts.  These can be used to include lettering in embroidering and needlepoint.  While it is a good idea, I found I wanted far more than this offered.

I found this to be quite moving, extremely inspiring.  I was very open to Lewis's point of view at the time, so I am sure that helped.  This book is a series of letters written to an American woman who was experiencing personal troubles.  In these letters, Lewis seeks to comfort and guide her, but also chastise and correct her when necessary.

What a delightful book.  It's great fun to be led along by Mr. Fry on this tale that takes us accross Europe with some mystery, uncertain identity, and a heap of espionage.  It's guaranteed to keep you guessing.  Along the way, there is plenty of sex and humor to keep things fun.
I found this book an interesting exercise in critical thinking, debunking, and plain historical comparison.  This book should be assigned to undergrad history students.

Jackson relates the perils of raising children and delivers some of her best writing in the process.  She is an unusual combination of average, stay-at-home mother and nationally celebrated author of horror and mystery books.  The result is an interesting blend that may have been produced by Erma Bombeck, Jean Kerr and Edgar A. Poe.  This is an under-appreciated work.

Prior to reading this book, I had never heard of the Dakota.  Since then, I see it everywhere!  I wonder how I remained ignorant of it so long.  The building is architecturally fascinating and its inhabitants not one scintilla less so.  It's not great, but it's a good, gossipy page-turner.

Bennet Cerf never fails to amuse and entertain.  True the jokes are sometimes corny, but on the other hand, they're timeless too.  Indeed, reading these one can easily hear today's comics delievering the same material with the window-dressing updated enough to seem au courrant.

What interesting books this series turned out!  When I first read this I was in the throes of militant Catholicism with the liberal, pacifist view of Jesus fixed firmly in my head.  Also, I had at that point no exposure to Spanish or Italian life or their application of Catholicism in daily practice.  My first reading of this left me horrified and yet hooked.  I was scandalized that Jesus could be an advocate for fighting!  Haha.  Well, I still don't believe he is, but at least I understand how other don't see it the way I do.  All that aside, this book and its successors are just little gems of uplifting good fun.  They are mildly inspiring and certainly calculated to make you feel good.
This is a fascinating book and one that is underappreciated.  It can make you re-evaluate your idea of yourself and what is it that makes you, YOU.
I dislike this translation very very much.  This seems like a watered down version.  It might as well be named, Bible of Dummies.   Hmmmm, there's more truth in that than meets the eye.

A practical guide with specific suggestions you can actually use in everyday life to help get through those early, shakey days of sobriety.  While the AA Big Book undoubtedly has its place in maintaining and deepening one's long-term sobriety and quality of life, it is a moot point if one can not get sober and stay sober in the first place.  It is not an exageration to say this book is a life-saver.

What a surprising and delightful book.  This is about a woman who does not conform, does not fit the respectable mold, and who manages to persevere and even flourish as a result.  This is not a typical "be true to yourself and everything will work out alright" tale, even though there are certainly strong elements of that sentiment to be derived.  The supernatural aspects of this novel caught me completely by surprise and were, therefore, more effective.
Besides being full of good tips for good grooming, this work features stunning eye-candy.  Hix used remarkable models who probably sold the book.

I read this book back in high school and I swallowed its premise hook, line, and sinker.  I suppose it was around here that I first began getting some inkling that perhaps not everything that is printed is true!!!  It was fun being so naive.  I have not had the heart to re-examine the book.  I daresay I would be abashed at the garbage I accepted so readily back then.  More importantly, I need to remember what garbage is accepted now - by myself and by others.

Cadbury blends modern science and forensics with narrative history in this exploration of the progeny of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette.  Mondern day descendants of claimants to royal lineage are subjected to DNA testing in order to determine the physical veracity of the claims.
Cronin's biography is chatty, anecdotal, quite readable, but light on analysis.  Wolf or Dunlap's biography of Louis XIV would be better choices for a serious scholar.

McIntosh chronicles the drive and passion of Ludwig II of Bavaria.  Ludwig threw himself in the financially ruinous building campaigns that resulted in stunning pieces of architecture.  His castle of Neuschwannstein remains the iconic epitome of Germany.  He also had a passion of music, specifically that of Richard Wagner.  Again he devoted his time and money to financing the composer.  Ludwig also harbored a predeliction of low class men who could only be disastrous for his reign.
This book contains the lyrics to almost every song Coward ever wrote, or at least published.  This is an excellent resource to examine the brilliant and clever words Coward penned.

This collection of satire from Mad Magazine derived from the 1960s evokes memories for those of us who were fans at the time.  I bought every issue (I only wish I'd had the foresight to retain them) and these articles and drawing let me relive those days.  I can only guess what these must seem like to someone unfamiliar with the magazine, more especially to someone who was born after the sixties.  What would really be a great book would be an annotated collection of MAD through the years!
A whimsical and wonderful collection. Reminds me of Roald Dahl in some ways, because there's darkness as well as light in these poems.

I actually am a fan of self-help books.  I do not dismiss the genre out of hand.  But this one seems poised to help only those who are most susceptible to  spiritualism, or religion, or maybe hypnosis as the answer to their problems.  He uses for examples a woman who drove without stopping for traffic lights, confident that her belief would render all the lights green for her direction; and a person who was convinced they could win the lottery and did so.  I do not say that these things could not happen.  But I do contend that the individuals' beliefs had nothing to do with the outcomes and that it would be foolish and dangerous to live that way.
Hilarious, especially for those who know something about the Bard. I'd love to see a performance of this someday.
These are short detective stories by the author of The Scarlet Pimpernel.  These little gems delight and amuse.
Great fun, especially for those who have read "Phantom of the Opera".
If you like The Daily Show, you'll love this book. It's like taking a stroll through the mind of Jon Stewart with a picnic basket and some little juice boxes.
'Mrs Doyle' (Father Ted) writing pretty good female-detective noir. A lot of fun.

Tagged 'argh' because I almost can't believe I have kept hold of this copy. It drove me mad. I like to find *one* good thing in any book and the tip about blackout blinds did prove invaluable, but most of the rest made me want to throw it at the wall. Or better still at Gina Ford's head. I am not a fan.

This seems like a good, direct guide to the intricacies of Dutch grammar and syntax.  Since I have only use it sparingly, I can not truly attest that it is the best or worst, etc.  But it sufficed to get me through some translation.
This is an interesting and useful look into the effects of the great plague on Europe.
This is a look at women who faced infamy and notoriety as they became unwilling public figures due to their trials for murder.
Some of this is laughable, some more serious and appropriate.

This is perhaps the best thing ever created for television in English. It's out on DVD, so there's no excuse for your not seeing it. Give it time; things become clearer as you go, and the wonderful swing soundtrack helps the hard parts go down.
One of the best American novels of the '90s, and Powers is perhaps my favorite American novelist now writing (well, except maybe Philip Roth, but that's a whole different kettle of gefilte fish).
I read this in college, so I have forgotten the details, but I remember it being a very good book.

Anyone who is even slightly familiar with Perl presumably knows about the Camel Book (Programming Perl), but this indispensable companion is somewhat less well-known.  That's a shame, because I find myself reaching for this more frequently than for the Camel; once you know the basics of the language, the Cookbook is a wonderful time-saver when you need a particular trick or technique.  More than once I've spent an hour or so working out the details of a finicky regexp (a completely generic number-recognition expression, allowing for scientific notation and the like, is the first example to come to mind) only to find them helpfully supplied as examples in the Cookbook.  Very highly recommended.

This was a major disappointment.  Penrose has made very good contributions to physics, but this is not one of them.  The book can be summarized as "we don't understand consciousness, and we don't understand quantum gravity; they must be related!"

This is one of my very favorite books.  It's difficult for me to articulate just why I love this book so much; there are so many reasons, and I end up sounding like I'm gushing mindlessly.  The characters are wonderful, the plot is charming, it's funny and heartwarming and heartbreaking by turns, the writing is wonderful, the scenery vivid and imaginative, and it's filled with fantastic (in both senses of the word) folktales and marvelous (and recurring) supporting characters, many of whom are redeemed in surprising ways.  All I can do is list superlatives.  The plot seems simple enough, a quest for a powerful ginseng root to save the children of a village, but gradually it piles up into something rich and beautiful, with ghosts and labyrinths and evil dukes and magical trinkets and the wisest man in the world.  Every time I read it, I cry at least twice (always at the same places), and I rarely cry at books. The two sequels, I should add, are very good indeed but cannot possibly compare to _Bridge of Birds_.
companion to Managing Yourself Creatively.  This work  outlines practice techniques that can be used in the workplace to improve productivity, efficiency and morale.

A guide to fashion and grooming, this book is only partially appropriate today.  THe grooming techniques may still apply but the fashion tips are best taken with a grain of salt.  However, as an artifact of the past the book is fine.

A fine work that guide the user to success in creating papers of suberb quality - at least in form and format.  Every kind of note, reference, quote, etc. is addressed here.  Later versions are updated to reflect the electronic resources now available.

I became entranced with L'Engle's writing back in the 60s.  I first read A Wrinkle in Time in jr high and thought it was delightful.  Even now, as a non-believing adult, I find that her work holds up well.

Fraser hit a gold mine when she wrote this book.  She managed to produce a work that is scholarly enough to gain and retain academic respect and yet readable and popular to the reader outside of academia.  No doubt some of this is attributable to the subject herself.

Ny examines the connection between the need to maintain a show of honor and a show of masculinity.  He makes the case that both honor and masculinity are fragily contructed concept.  He shows that in a society where honor must constantly be defended, masculinity itself is always suspect.

I'll admit I was really looking for the technical details when I picked this up.  There's just enough engineering geekery to keep me from being entirely unsatisfied, but it's cluttered with ridiculous conjectural drama.  It's a slight book, too; I probably would have been better served by this book's bibliography than its text.

To say that it's better than the movie doesn't do justice to the movie. To say that the movie is better than the book, however, is to discount the wonders of editoral comments, half truths, backstory, and conversations that could only come from the pen of such a genius as Mr. Morgenstern.

Salerno's poems form a quirky and marvelous meditation on the persistence, fragmentation, and revisionism of memory, consciousness, and longing, as well as the mutability (and flexibility) of language.  Best read as a whole, this slim volume repays re-reading, and deserves more.  (*** 1/2)
Short of the full OED (or the compact microprint version), I would consider this the bible of the English language. Though I do intend to supplement it with an unabridged Webster's one day.
This is a well written biography of Queen Mary.  Edwards recounts the events of her life with plenty of interesting anecdotes yet does not fall entirely under the spell of her subject.
Collection of short stories, delightful to read.  These little gems sparkle in their economy and brilliance of language.  Greene's sophisticated humor consistently charms without cloying.

Drawing from previous lectures, Lewis compiled his thoughts into a coherent. logical case for Christianity.  He tries to make his case for the non-believer and therefore avoids using biblical support for his arguments.  All his reasoning is based solely on reason, logic, and empirical evidence.  He begins by positing that good and evil do exist and that must be something higher, something apart from and above good and evil which can make such a distinction.  This something is God.  Lewis builds from this point.  It is by no means conclusive that he proves his first point, and therefore everything built upon it is questionable.
The Da Vinci Code is a lightweight, fun and shallow read masquerading as something much more significant. Read it, enjoy it but don't take it too seriously.

Stanley Marcus writes an insightful story of Nieman Marcus as a leader among stores that cater to discerning shoppers.  Marcus pitches his store as one that did not necessarily aim for the wealthy, but more for the discriminating and savey shopper - many of whom were wealthy.  Marcus was a brillian man who knew how to sell; more importantly he knew how to educate and lead his customers into cultivated tastes that his store would satisfy.

Fascinating tale of malaria and its treatment.  The discovery of the use of quinine and the ability to mass produce it makes for fine reading.  Rocco does an excellent job of organizing and presenting her material.

Writing in the persona of Miss Manners, Judith Martin manages to be simultaneously tongue in cheek and in deadly earnest.  Throughout her book she skewers pomposity and snobbery, while fighting for the maintenance of gracious and generous good manners.  She shows that one need not be wealthy to conduct oneself well.
This read very much like a rehash of the plot of the Karloff movie.  While that's not entirely bad, one just wonders why that needed to be written again.

This is (was) an excellent reference to mystery stories as they were in the late seventies.  There are all sorts of interesting facts, trivia and diversions inside.  The habits and foibles of the detectives and the authors are sure to entertain.
This is a good Jane Marple mystery with an interesting beginning that hooks the reader quickly.
One of Christie's very best.  This one has a surprise ending that puts the others to shame.

This is among Christie's finest - and that says a lot.  Here we have Hercule Poirot pitting his wits against a train full of smart, sophisticated, people.  Any one of them seems to have had the motive, desire and opportunity for committing murder.  But who actually did it?  Well, I have to say I never would have guessed this one!

This is a fictionalized account of an adviser to King John of England.  It was John who was ruler of England while his brother, Richard the Lion Hearted was away at the Crusades.  It was John who as King, was forced by his nobles to sign the Magna Carta.  James Goldman had already proven himself a master of the time period in his earlier work, The Lion In Winter.  John, of course, is the son of Henry II and Eleanor of Acquitaine so Goldman is still very much in familiar territory.  I read this book 30 years ago, but I recall it as engrossing and engaging.
Christie's first mystery, or at least Poirot's first appearance.  Great fun.
Christie's first mystery, or at least Poitrot's first appearance.  Great fun.

Entertaining and informative, with lots of insights and advice that are helpful to those wondering which film field to focus on. I especially like that while this book has the usual interviews with the stars of the filmmaking process (producers, directors, writers, actors, etc.), it also throws the spotlight on other players like animal trainers, accent coaches, prop designers and caterers.

This is an excellent book that not only provides a detailed look at science and medicine as it was practiced in the Third Reich, as well as how that government institutionally directed the focus of science, but it also raises important questions about what constitutes good or bad science.  Is valid science performed for evil intent good science - good in the sense of usable and valid for other purposes?
Informative, candid interviews that generally avoid repetition. Belongs in every editor's collection.

This is an excellent survey of imprisonment.  It examines punishment before imprisonment and why imprisonment came to be used instead.  It probes the successes and failures of the penitentiary and looks into efforts to find alternative means of punishment.

Does a good job of explaining all the various tasks that directors and producers need to do in order to make a film happen. The comments by three director-producers, about specific issues they ran into with their films, are especially helpful.

DIana Rigg compiled as delightful collection of scathing reviews.  No one cares about reading good reviews expept the actor and his mother.  It's the bad ones that are the most fun and these are guaranteed to amuse.  The remarkable ways critics find to skewer their subjects prove the extent of the human imagination.

This is a chatty, anecdotal account of Noel Coward's life told by former lovers.  However, as Coward himself did, they remained so discrete and reticent to delve into the really juicy bits that they omitted everything of the least sexual nature.  Coward, who was obviously gay, was just never openly gay and these authors have respected that policy, to the readers' loss.  Otherwise it is a perfectly adequate book and has many good pictures.
As the title suggests, this book is a collection of horror tales, some old, some new.  In general, it makes a nice assortment of pieces one can read in short installments.
A well-organized and meticulously researched history that belongs in every Red Sox fan's library.

If you like playing solitaire, this book should be right up your alley.  There are many variations and styles of solitaire games.  Even the most die-hard shut in should be entertained for a long while with these games.

I admit I've never read this book all the way through, but it's a great book to dip into, and Bola told me himself that that is how he meant it to be read. Bola was a tutor at my Uni, and he was in charge of the hall I lived in. As well as teaching at the uni Bola drives a taxi, I think he likes meeting people. Apparently he was going to write a book about taxi driving too. He signed this book and gave it to me one day after driving me back up to uni.
Brilliant satire from the Onion.  They manage to skewer the folly of those who let themselves be led too easily by the news, those who become too packaged and processed.

The Divine Comedy epitomized medieval attitudes.  From historical perspectives, this work serves as a window into the mentality of late middle ages in Italy, on the brink of the Renaissance.  Scholastic thinking informs Dante's approach.

Saki (H.H. Munro) writes with a facility and style that guides the reader unerringly to the surprise denouement in which propriety is set on its head.  His bitingly clever turns of phrase are made bearable by his eagerness to challenge and thwart the norms of society.

Juster writes a charming tale of a bored little boy who has plenty around him that should hold his interest.  Milo received a tollbooth (quite mysteriously) and it leads him in to a world of words and numbers where he learns what a fascinating place the world can be.
Garrett offers concise practical advice for lawns and gardens in the Dallas Fort Worth area.  This book is a must have for anyone interested in having a good relation with their plants.

plenty of slightly bawdy humor.  What passed for racy in 1970 seems almost quaint today because of the change in standards of decency as well as the change in the relationship between the sexes.  Nevertheless, the jokes are still amusing.
Hilarious.  Absolutely hilarious.  A book you should get on tape to hear Franken read it.
This is standard Christie fare, which of course means great fun and plenty of false leads as to the identity of the killer.  We find an interesting puzzle built around a poisoning.

How can anyone who loves classics not love this play? "There is truth and falsehood in a comma. ... By taking out a comma and putting it back in a different place, sense is made out of nonsense in a poem that has been read continuously since it was first misprinted four hundred years ago. A small victory over ignorance and error. A scrap of knowledge to add to our stock."

tr. of Golos iz khora (1973). A mixture of excerpts from letters to his wife, some amounting to literary or philological essays, and quotes from other prisoners: "An informer even sleeps with his ears pricked up." Highly recommended.

Patricia Cornwell wrote an interesting and at times compelling book.  The gist of her argument is that Jack the Ripper was a relatively minor artist who provided clues to the killings in his paintings.  While her argument is plausible, it seems by no means to live up to the "Case Closed" label touted in the title.  Hers is merely one of several possible explanations.  Meanwhile, Cornwell has purchased and defaced more than one of the artist's paintings in her efforts to prove her point.

Winchester combines the story of the origin of the Oxford English Dictionary with an individual's tale of murder and insanity in a fascinating way.  Not only does the reader gain a sense of how the dictionary was compiled - this is more or less a matter of public record - but we also are granted access into a Victorian asylum.  The erudite and discerning doctor unfortunately suffered delusions and was dangerous to himself and others.
Very good introduction to the concept of stage lighting. I like that the book relies on anecdotes, quotes and clear, understandable English rather than specialized technical terms.
A family epic told in one-sided conversations, working backward from 1982 Israel to 1848 Athens. Highly recommended.
Well-delineated characters, a wealth of historical detail, and incredibly complex webs of intrigue -- in other words, a typically stellar work for Dorothy Dunnett.
Very beat-up and out of date, but I can't bring myself to deaccession it -- I loved this book, the first good atlas I owned.

Bizarre fantasy based around a very sexually repressed man who is befriended by a ghost giraffe called Jim. Dark, weird and intriguing. Can't say I enjoyed it as such, but would recommend to some (not all!) friends.
Maltz posits that actions can shape thoughts and perceptions.  He argues that you can act your way into a good self-image.

The Divine Comedy epitomized medieval attitudes.  From historical perspectives, this work serves as a window into the mentality of late middle ages in Italy, on the brink of the Renaissance.  Scholastic thinking informs Dante's approach.

I read this book as a child.  It was enchanting - delightful.  This was one of the first times I ever saw something written as a future history.  I was enthralled by the device.  The gentle humor combined with the environmental and social message has proven eerily accurate and precient.
Thought-provoking theories from a veteran editor and sound designer. A must-read for folks in postproduction.
A thorough and detailed listing of all the offspring from Queen Victoria.  Fun for royal-watchers.
silly, and poorly executed cartoons.  Hardly worth the time to turn the pages.

Rasselas is Samuel Johnson's vision of the world as a place where things do not always work out well.  Johnson shows life at best as something to be endured.  The situations encountered by Johnson's hero seems almost the opposite of those encountered by Voltaire's Candide.  Time after time, things seem to be promising, even ideal.  However, inevitably reality sets in and tiny, then major, chinks in the facade appear.  All is not perfect.  Perfection is shown as ultimately unattainable yet still desirable, leading to guaranteed dissatisfaction.  All written in fine style by a superb master of the language.

This atlas was my first atlas as a kid.  I think I got it in jr high and I was taken by it, absolutely captivated by the maps.  The extraneous info was nice, but it was the maps that I poured over.  I think atlases become more interesting with time; indeed they are little time capsules and now, forty years later, this atlas offers a vision of how the world has changed since then.  The British and French colonial empires were just ravelling then.  The Soviet Union and the Iron curtain were firmly ensconced and the disasters of Viet Nam lay in the future.

These writings are among Gertrude Stein's last pieces.  She died shortly after World War II.  The observations reflect a sharp lucid thinker still quite well attuned to the ramifications of the war, the bomb and the U.S. hegemony.

I must be one of the two or three people who don't get The Little Prince.  I've read it but it just doesn't do anything for me.  I don't see it.  But, as one interested in Latin, I take what I can get.
Charming, sophisticated cartoon, yet down to earth in their presentation.  Booth delights in music, dogs, cats, and the elderly.

Although I enjoyed reading this book, I was also disappointed in that Cole avoided the issue of Coward's homosexuality.  We get a fleeting cursory acknowledgement and that's it.  While in some ways that is sensible and consistent with Coward's own approach, it seems that one of the duties of a biographer is to discuss aspects that the subject himself may have skirted.Other than that, the book reads well; it's full of inside information and backstage glimpses of a very smart, sophisticated set.  Coward managed to be acquainted with the highest ranks of entertainment as well as old aristocracy - royalty itself.  It's worth reading but we must hope for a "real" biography from other sources.

This book seeks to guide business people through the uneasy waters of cultural diversity.  It does a fair job at this task; it succeeds in offering short encapsulations of various cultural 'types', profiling is what I would call this.  I think my complaint about this book is not just that it's a bit dated now, but rather its entire premise or point of origin.  The book tries to give tips on avoiding gaffes and faux pas, and advice on how to be more culturally sensitive - to avoid offending potential customers / suppliers.  I think it would be more noble to try to promote genuine cultural appreciation and understanding as a goal.  Improved business would be a secondary, by-product of this.  But the cultural understand should be the true goal, not the means.
A superb study of the role of and importance of ritual in Early Modern Europe.  Muir's is a probing analysis of varieties of ritual and their numerous uses.
A dazzling piece of prose that's as funny as it's heartbreaking (or the other way around).
Bloch presents historical scholarship about as good as it gets.

Farago presents nineteenth century history as if the dynastic politics characteristic of Tudor/Hapsburg/Valois times were still in operation.  While it makes for interesting reading, the actual influence of royal families by this time seems substantially less than Farago would have the reader believe.

In the 70s, jogging and running became a minor craze.  Happily, I was spared this addiction.  The book however, seems like a good guide full of handy tips and suggestions of ways to avoid injury and maximize the benefits.

Published by a Catholic press, this work delivers a high-level summary of a particular saint for each day of the year.  The summaries are invariably clean and pure, rarely giving much genuine detail of the person's life and background; instead we see only a sanitized, ready for mass consumption (no pun intended) version of the saint's life.  Completely insipid.

Boswell contributes a view of same-sex unions / marriages which if not entirely objective is at least not overly polemical or impassioned.  This book offers a calm voice of basic information in the context of the culture wars.

Boswell contributes a view of same-sex unions / marriages which if not entirely objective is at least not overly polemical or impassioned.  This book offers a calm voice of basic information in the context of the culture wars.
Of far less use now than it originally way.  This may acquire interest as an artifact of the time.

In Santeria from Africa to the New World, George Brandon examines snycretic religion, Santeria, with an eye on how the process of syncretization occurred.  Brandon is as much, or more, interested in the process as he is in the religion itself.  Brandon sets out to show that a syncretic religion can be valid on its own terms despite the dismissive attitudes of the ‘pure’ religious adherents.  Brandon takes an anthropological look at African people:  in their original homelands, in the forced transplantation to Cuba and in the subsequent migration to the United States.  He traces their religion as it evolved from Yoruba through Santeria into Santerismo.
A well-told account of Dr. Barry, definitely worth the read for the details of Barry's secret.  An interesting look into details of Victorian colonial medicine.

Although there are many interesting and a few useful phrases and terms inside, this book also contains serval pitfalls and gotchas.  My experience with these terms has been that is best to avoid them entirely.
Tuppence and Tommy Beresford together for the first time. Good fun as Dame Agatha keeps us guessing.
This work provides useful original source material for Marie Antoinette.  It does not serve as a biography of the queen.  Edited with commentary.

This is about the methodolgy of project management.  Not just the detailed specifics, the the general organizing approach.  The ideas are good and helpful.  Much of the content is dated in regards the many many great software tools that would replace or supplement the statements and recommendations of this work.
Ziglar's motivational technique is infectuous.  He laces his information with a heavy dose of Christianity.

Gerturde Stein is one of my favorite writers - as long as I avoid her "hard" pieces.  I can only take those in very small doses.  But the Autobiography of Alice Toklas and Everybody's Autobiography are wornderful - life transforming even.  I read those at an impressionable age and they opened my eyes to other kinds of literature than I had previously known.  I remember at the time feeling like I had leapt onto a fast moving train from a dead stop.  It was breathtaking and unsettling but so exhilerating too.

I like this Christie work because it features neither Poirot nor Marple, although I enjoy both detectives very much.  Instead we have Tuppence and Tommy Beresford.  It was through this book I first learned about Seven Dials in London.

This is a highly effective book for getting your life turned around and on a path toward professional and personal success.  This is certainly no a cure-all; no promised panacea here.  You have to make a sincere and sustained effort.  You have to apply what Covey teaches.  But even failed attempts, even imperfect applications should result in improvement.

This book was eye-opening to me.  I was astonished to learn about the berdaches among the Native Americans.  This book causes me to challenge what I think about sexual orientation being born.  Trexler's scholarship is masterful.  I e-mailed him and he was very friendly and willing to discuss his book.  He died in 2006.
This is a manual for care, feeding, and grooming of a Shih Tzu dog.  It offers good, practical advice in comprehendible terms.

As a guide to food, brand-name food at that, this is a fairly useful book.  The problem is, it's too big to be convenient to carry, and who can remember it all unless it is handy?  The other problem is that it is subject to change.  Manufacturers have responded to consumer concerns and a lot of change has occurred since this book came out.  It is on those cavils that I rate this book low.

What a lovely book that I put off reading for far too long.  Eliot weaves important themes through her tale of Silas and Eppie.  We see human and earthly values put into perspective and we see humanity in its frailty and in its strength.  It may have a bit of a saccharine element by twentieth century standards, but sometimes a little sugar is nice.

I firmly believe that there were good reasons why Tolkien did not publish this book in his lifetime.  While this work may have been of some interest to him in his interior universe, it seems of little use to anyone other than the most die-hard Tolkien fan who has too much time on his hands.  Having read Tolkien's principal works many times over, this dismissal does not come from one who dislikes the author or his works.

Anecdotal gossipy biography of one of New Yorks literati of the early twentieth century.  This book is an easy read and a decent introduction to anyone who is unfamiliar with Alexander Woollcott.  It is not a deep or scholarly book; nor does it pretend to be.
These little writings by children show the innocence and pluck of the uninformed in the ways of the kitchen.  These are laugh-out-loud funny as one imagines trying some of these gems.
Latha.  She's at the heart of Harington's Stay More and this is her story.  It's crazy good.

I will rate the book high, even though my personal success does not match the rating.  I'm willing to accept that the fault is more mine than the book's.  This book proposes a low-carb ("right carb") approach to eating.  Its thesis is that carbs are what cause most of our dietary imbalances and that fats and protiens are much better and easier to maintain and monitor.  It's the carbs that are addictive and pile on the weight.  The book has good recipes and easy to follow instructions.

This was the gay answer to the Hite Report that was published just a year or two before.  This book reveals counts and amounts of homosexual activity as it was measured in the mid 1970s.  It would be interesting to corelate this with the AIDS epidemic and post-AIDS measurements.

This is an examination of the British Empire in the late nineteenth even early twentieth century - the Empire after it had become overripe.  Morris shows the Empire at its height, when it had already begun to decline though few, if any, had yet perceived that to be the case.  Britania seemed poised to dominate the world for another century or two and yet within another half century, the empire had diminished in size and prestige to a surprising and shocking degree.  Morris provides lots of photos illustrating the blazing afternoon sun of the empire before the nightfall encroached and sent it into darkness.

Masters created a town of Spoon River and lets us look into the goings on there.  This is nothing unusual in fiction.  However, in this case we see the town through the voices of the dead.  Every piece in this collection of free verse is that of one of the former inhabitants speaking from the grave.  Some are funny, some of gut-wrenchingly sad, some are inspiring.  Some connect together so a bit of a story emerges; many stand along.
These are Daily Devotions, sanctioned by the Catholic Church.  It is an interesting look into early twentieth century American Catholicism.

Lots of characters: dead, imaginary, alive... author IN the book but not narrating (that's done by the ghost)... definitly a response to Nabokov, Lolita in particular, a little Gabriel Garcia Marquez maybe...  Lots of reference to Harington's other Stay More adventures.  So you see, it requires faith.  Not for the faint of heart that want, like, a linear narrative.  It has the wonderful ambition, originality, humor, style and incredible skill characteristic of all Harington's work... just pushed a little farther over that WTF? line.  (see also: Some Other Place) Fabulous.

This is a good overview the history of Stay More, and an excellent novel on it's own, but it's a little blander than the usual Harington fare.  There's structure and order and less crazy sex with ghosts, for example.  I love his outrageousness, I think the farther he goes over the line, the better he gets.  So this wasn't my absolute favorite.  But I did enjoy it very much.

Breathtakingly irreverent and laugh out loud funny in that wonderful tall tale sort of way.  Particularly of interest to people with a bone to pick with Christianity, but not mean spirited.  The cockroach characters mirror their human Stay More neighbors... so it stands alone but does improve with more context from the other books.  Definitely recommended.

I think this is one of Harington's most impressive stand alone novels.  Breathtaking as only electric chair humor can be.  It shouldn't work, shouldn't make any sense.  But it's marvelous.  Grim and sad, sweet and darkly funny.

Another impressive Stay More novel that stands well alone or with the group.  It's got that great Stand By Me/I'm Not Scared summertime thing going on.  Boys at play in the sun with dark things lurking underneath and behind.  Sharply written... absolutely no wasted words.  One of my favorites.
The title essay is outstanding.  An excellent argument for the importance of art.
This is an old-style missal, pre-Ecumenical council.  It's interesting and useful as a historic artifact of mass prior to the reforms of Pope John XXIII.

This novel is a pedestrian tale posing as something shocking.  It is the story of the Starr family who own an exclusive chain of department stores.  This roman a clef is a thinly veiled story in which the story is based on Nieman Marcus, although there appears to be no connection with the Marcus family.My own copy is a First Edition, which was recalled in Texas due to similarity of character's name to local big-wig here in Fort Worth.  Since she has since died, her name was Georganne Carter.

This is a great favorite of mine.  I read Virgin Suicides, but thought this was far far better.  Touching and fascinating, it explores the question of identity in the context of family and upbringing, sex, gender, political events, religious teaching, general environment... How much we get to decide for ourselves and how much is inescapable.  In retrospect, it seems so appropriate to write a coming of age novel with the voice of a hermaphrodite.  All these big picture thoughts came after I had finished. While I was actually reading the novel I was totally drawn into the lives of the characters (particularly Cal) and was incredibly satisfied with the ending.
A fabulous plot expertly written.  With irresistable characters.

Covers more ground than its model, Studs Terkel's "Working," but seems much less personal somehow. I remember (vaguely) what people said about the nature of their jobs, but I don't remember the people themselves.
A bit dated (it was published before the Age of the Computer), but still worth the read, thanks to a variety of colorful characters and Terkel's presence as story collector/interpreter.
Beautiful- with pointed observations on the world and life in general and an amazing main character.

American storytelling at it's finest and particularly southern, perplexing, vivid, bizarre, fantastic and real- O'Connor is one of a kind.  This is a great collection to dip into now and then to satisfy cravings for really excellent writing.
This is (all at the same time) a great novel, a great mystery, and a wonderful discussion about what's most important when the world falls apart.
A semi-autobiographical novel that perfectly captures the pleasures and pains of childhood. My favorite Bradbury book, bar none.

Well-written, extremely sobering, and at times frightening account of the mountain lion situation in Boulder. Does a particularly good job of explaining the human politics involved in the response (and, for a while, the non-response) of authorities in Boulder, Colorado.

This book is/was right out of the seventies when macrame was terribly faddish among a certain element.  I did not do macrame at the time (nor since, really) but I vaguely admired it.  Reading this book takes one back several years.  It's fun to remember all those plant hangers and owls and so forth that one used to see so much several decades back.  As it is, I can not imagine actually engaging in macrame any more unless it be a form a therapy.  Still, if you wanted to do so, here's your beginner's guide.
A lovely and interesting story about regular people making something extraordinary work.  Also a fascinating traveler's portrait of Vietnam.
Just amazing.  Beautiful, subtle, humorous, joyous... a relaxing book to spend time with.

Hector, Achilles, Odysseus, Zeus, Athena, Priam... it doesn't get any better.  Some mornings I look out the window and still think "rosy fingertips of dawn".  This translation is very vivid and readable, though not as precise as the Lattimore... or at least that's what I remember from college.
ugh. the only book in recent memory that i have wanted to physically destroy.

This is indeed, amazing.  But no one ever told me it was also hilarious.  Extremely readable, compelling and lively, the embedded philosophy is both fascinating and very easy to take. One of the very best books I've ever read.
One of Austen's subtler books, and quieter heroines.  This is my favorite... although Pride and Prejudice runs a close second.
Fascinating man - and there's a moment in here that's expecially beautiful if you've read Swann's Way.
University reading; I do have a second copy somewhere with notes in. Loved this book -  despite its length and complexity it's a good comfort read.

I HATE THIS BOOK. Well, ok, it has its merits, but gah, it bores me to tears, and I've had to read it three times now for academic reasons. I can write about it, I can appreciate its themes and style and Eliot's prose and all but I HATE IT.I didn't like the TV adaptation either.

This is a fine, scholarly guide to Stuart England.  It is brief, readable, and well-researched.  Anyone who needs a good solid introduction to England in the seventeenth century could do worse than consult this book.  Certainly it is not exhaustive; but that is not its goal.

This is a basic, foundational book on practical management concepts.  It is not overly abstract; instead it is full of ideas that can be applied.  At 2 decades old, some of the specific details of today's technology are absent - some things seem quaint.  But the ideas in general retain their applicability.

While Mitford's may not be the most scholarly work on Louis XIV, it certainly figures prominently among the most readable and enjoyable.  Mitford writes well; she can pack a great deal of information in a well-crafted pithy phrase.

I found this to be the most enjoyable of Rice's Vampire series after the Interview.  I felt that Vampire Lestat and especially, Queen of the Damned got bogged down.  Rice seemed to regain her abilities in this work.
I came late to Ashbery, as to Cecil Taylor; better late than never.

This is a so-so book about the great social/labor disturbance that rocked Pennsylvania in the 1860s-70s.  The story is fascinating but this book does not do it justice.  There are far better ones that have been published since this one.  See Kenny's for a better work.
NA

I read this book within a month of its initial publication.  I read it almost straight through and found it, at the time, quite motivating.  Like many self-help books, it has little original to say; its power lies in the compelling presentation.  I confess, I have not revisited the book since then (1976) so I freely admit I could be misremembering and I may not react to it in the same way today.  I do however still recall several specifics from the book and find them useful in everyday life.

My partner bought this book, recommended by a doctor I thought was a quack.  I still think that and I think this book is a bunch of baloney!  I do not believe that all somatic and psychological symptoms are attributable to yeast.

This is a no-nonsense, practical text for X-ray applications in dentistry.  The book was current and useful originally; it is now 40 years past its publication and it no longer reflects current practices or knowledge.

This is a study guide for those in pursuit of radiological license - especially for those seeking a 1976 license.  No doubt the technology and the specifics are terribly dated.  The book is probably of no use to anyone in a practical sense any longer.  It served its purpose well originally.
There is SO much available on World War II.  This book does a fairly decent job at amassing a lot of information, and pictures in a single volume.  It is very USA-centric.
This is an interesting, thought-provoking book that leads you toward better writing without driving you crazy in the process.  Annotated examples help the instruction here.

This book condenses the basics of good business writing.  This is not an attempt at creative writing or fiction.  This is a non-nonsense approach.  It is a little bit dated but not too bad since the practices of good business do not change that fast regardless of the specific technology.

I read this as a child in elementary school and loved it.  It was one I reread multiple times.  I recall laughing aloud in many places.  I dare say I would react a bit differently now, but I bet I'd still like it.  It was set in the Great Depression, so I wonder if children today would understand in the same way.  My parents lived during the depression so I heard it discussed enough to know something about it even as a little kid.

This is an enjoyable collection of short stories ranging through various great authors of western lit.  Anthologies frequently raise questions of the discrimination of the editors; this one is no exception.  But that too is part of the enjoyment and learning process.

This is simply a collection of many of Charles Addams's best known, and most cherished drawings.  His skewed, macabre world seduces us into enjoying that which we probably shouldn't.  His dark but humerous point of view is irresitable.
NA

I keep old almanacs around as a reference for previous information.  I buy an almanac ever four or five years.  These days, with internet information being so accessible, I doubt I'll ever buy a current almanac again.  And used ones go SO cheaply.  As a child, I devoured the almanac, reading about disasters, mountain heights, river lengths, most populous cities, etc.  Though I no longer just read an almanac, they still fascinate me.  There's something in the neat tabular presentation of data that implies that all knowledge could be captured, tamed and presented rationally.
