Neither one is either entirely impossible, nor credible. The emphasis on instances of 'licentiousness', lynching, drug use, suicide and abortion attempts, infidelity, drunkenness and madness seems to go a bit beyond demonstrating the universality of human nature, the relevance of the past, and possible reactions to tragedy. Nor do they always grow organically out of the characters, so much as seem to be merely allotted to them. Brooks is an impressive wordsmith, vividly imaginative, yet lacking in equally rigorous judgement. The impression left is that a meagre stock of historical fact, research, and period reading was used for elaborately imaginative embroidery: promising, but flawed. It's a colorful and even lurid dream with insufficient underpinnings to support it credibly. Touted as an inspiring story of people's diverse reactions to tragedy and the emerging strength of one woman in their midst, in that guise it is no better than middling. Year of Wonders affirms that suffering and horror can have a beneficial effect, not a merely destructive one. The timing may have given this message more immediacy and widespread appeal than it had pre-9/11, but it is not news. This truth, essential as it is, is portrayed without fresh insight or profundity. - Perhaps with less than I feel it deserves. Year of Wonders is disappointing precisely because of its virtues: it could have been, and was hailed as, a much better book.(Rated three stars for the quality balancing its faults.)

Understated as it is, this fictional 'documentary' of the Plague Year is gripping. Compelling and eminently readable, it gives an almost businesslike account of the Plague's imagined horror.As birchmore pointed out, there are fascinating authorial techniques at work. Early in the story, the saddler establishes his claim as a truthful source not only by his sober and skeptical tone, but by his constant reference to the actual Bills of Mortality. Then, as the story progresses, the narrator, firmly established in the reader's confidence, begins to cast doubt on their legitimacy and accuracy - realistically heightening the fears of catastrophe. Even as a modern reader, it's difficult not to succumb to the Journal's appearance of truth. As far as I'm concerned, that's an extraordinary testimony to Defoe's brilliance.

Digressive, dear sir?  Yes!   Bizarre, madam?  -- Why, yes....    Bawdy?  Well -   Just read this passage quickly, madam, once through, without thinking --- and...Is it: Better in the first half?  Sure.   Sentimental?  Certainly.A witty, whimsical, comic gem?  - Absolutely!!!

If you think you know your Bible, this book will make you re-evaluate your knowledge level.  It has questions on all kinds of interesting topics, such as "who said this?" and "what book ends with this verse?"

If you study Biblical Hebrew, using BHS, and have ever wondered, "What is that thing?"...this book is for you.  This is a fairly short and to the point reference manual for explaining how BHS works, including its symbols and critical apparatus.
Excellent primary source for the study of Napoleonic uniforms.

This is the only non-fiction book I stayed up all night to complete, it's that gripping. Although I don't actually own it yet, I need to and want to, so I felt I should include it, and perhaps someone may pick it up for themselves based on my recommendation.Its an absolutely amazing, harrowing journey through a very dark period in the author's life, on the course of which the readers are introduced to a cast of vividly colorful, highly damaged individuals as the author is proceeding through rehab. Even if you do not normally read non-fiction, as I do not, this is well worth checking out. A startling, horrifying, amazing look at what its like to be an addict and the dreadfulness of the recovery process.

Readers first met Frey's friend Leonard in his previous memoir, 'A Million Little Pieces,' which recounted his time in rehab. in 'My Friend Leonard,' Frey continues his story, telling of his release from jail and the subsequent severe hardships thrown his way. All along the way, Leonard is there to support him in his darkest times, and we learn more about this unique, colorful character. Although the author's narration style occationally may be irritating, the depth of feeling and range of emotions he conveys in surprisingly simple words and the absolutely vivid, amusing and touching portrait he paints of the man who came to call him son make this an unforgettable book, even for those disinclined towards non-fiction.

It's not an allegory. It's a disaster novel. As was Camus' Plague which it's usually compared with. The sequel (Seeing) IS an allegory (in part.) So with 47 reviews to the contrary, I just can't stand the allegory talk, esp. when "it's hard to read so my inability to read must be part of the allegory." Good grief. If I tried to read the Portuguese original I'm sure I would have the same problems: would that make it twice the allegory? Seriously, would it? Who is this librarian who's an expert on allegory?

On cataloguing my books, I find I have a lot of post-apocalyptic material - I'm not really pessimistic, but perhaps it is a reflexion of my anxious personality! This originally dates back to late 50s/early 60s (the hey-day of the Cold War and paranoia about nuclear war), and it is slightly dated. The story shows America (specifically Florida) in the aftermath of nuclear war. It is a good story, but perhaps a lot more optimistic than the reality would be. This may be an indication that A bombs at the time the book was written, had a much smaller yield than modern nuclear weapons. The optimistic way in which it is written, and the way the community survives and pulls together, reminds me of the "cosy catastrophes" of John Wyndham.

This is a fascinating novel of lurid, over-the-top prose that appealed to readers in earlier times.  Corelli writes of a young man's descent into addiction to absinthe and the destruction he wreaks on those around him.  While presented as a cautionary tale, it allows the reader to indulge vicariously in the seamy side of life in Paris's underbelly.

This book is an amusing mystery / detective story.  Braddon keeps the reader guessing who-done-it in this nineteenth century tale of greed and madness.  It's a lot of fun and well worth the time to read.

This was a fascinating novel that was assigned to me in a graduate level British Lit class.  It was not a happy story - one hopes this is not truly the plight of the modern woman.  It reflects the begining of the thaw of Victorian morality and women who sought independence.  Although it did not paint a rosy picture of women as independent beings, neither did it dismess them nor offer a morality-laden, cautionary tale.

Bill Bryson putting his writing skills to science this time - written form the layman's point of view. This is a really thick book full of all sorts of science from the Big Bang, to dinosaurs, supervolcanoes, genetics - you name it, Bill covers it. Although he is not a scientist, he has done his homework so that the book does not come across as lightweight, but is very readable (I couldn't put it down).

An encyclopaedia for confirmed Tolkien enthusiasts - includes references to Silmarillion and Unfinished Tales as well as the better known trilogy. Many beautiful illustrations (not Tolkien's, though).

These writings are the reflections of a man in a position of great power.  Yet he revelas himself as a man possessed of human frailties and vulnerabilities and certainly not one who is over proud or consumed with his high status.  Instead, his goal is to be a good man.  His ordinariness is more important to him than acclaim as an emperor.  His thoughts inspire and challenge me to be a better person.  His strength and simplicity are models to emulate.

A really helpful cookbook for Veggie mums and babies. As well as the recipes (all easy to make and balanced and nutritious), there are general helpful pieces of information throughout on general childcare.

An easy going and slightly whimsical trip down memory lane (particularly if, like me, you are of an age with Francis Spufford and grew up with the same books he did). This is described as an autobiography, and certainly contains many biographical details, but is centred on the books he read. Much of the book can equally be read as a series of essays as book reviews. I read this and enjoyed it so much, I recommended it to my book group. We read it and it generally had a good reception.
A fat collection running from Argentina to Zulu, with all poems in the original as well as translated.

The second book in a two book series (the first is "The Weirdstone of Brisingamen"). Set in the NW of England (close to where we live, so it is great to be abel to explore some of the countryside mentioned in these books). Alan Garner drwas heavily on themes from Celtic mythology to create a magical, frightening and wonderful world, into which two mortal children are drawn. A fabulous retelling of the eternal "good vs. evil". One of those children's books that is still possible to read in adulthood.

A classic book of advanced Lisp hackery, especially involving macros.  Contains much stuff that is available nowhere else.  If you want to understand why Lisp can do things that no other language I know can, this is the book.
Has Persian in calligraphy and transcription along with translations; oversize, bottom of poetry case

A sequel to The Straw Men this is an interesting continuation of the paranoia and conspiracy.  The serial killer is interesting as well.  Some of it is a bit farfetched but I found it a compelling read.
Not quite as good as the other one, since 'happily ever after' equates, it seems, to boy sleeps around well, not really, but kinda.. and eh? Still, funny in its parts, and better than the movie.
It's Harry Potter. It rocks. Best one yet. Darker and more sinister than any of the previous books in the series. Things are gearing up for a blast of a finish!

"A Yearly Report of the General Sanitary Sciences Throughout the World, Edited by Charles E. Sajous MD and Seventy Associate Editors, assisted by over two hundred corresponding editors, collaborators, and correspondents, Illustrated with Chromo-Lithographs, Engravings and Maps." One of the best parts is the collection of advertisements on the back pages.
Strong, awesome photography from all over the world. There is nothing bad, I can say about this collection of masterpieces. A must own for all who has an interest in photojournalism.

Michael Connelly has yet to write a bad book. This one's a hate-crime, cold case story that has the usual Connelly mix of great characters, whodunnit and hardboiled action. Slightly on the standard-formula side, but a good read nonetheless.

"A Yearly Report of the General Sanitary Sciences Throughout the World, Edited by Charles E. Sajous MD and Seventy Associate Editors, assisted by over two hundred corresponding editors, collaborators, and correspondents, Illustrated with Chromo-Lithographs, Engravings and Maps." One of the best parts is the collection of advertisements on the back pages.

A classic conspiracy thriller. Not the most original material, since I already knew a lot of the information on which the book bases it's conspiracy, which took away a little excitement along the way. Still, about half-way through, I got sucked completely into it and could not put it down.

This book is a good guide for people wanting to play limit poker, expecially if you like playing with your friends or going to casinos. It introduces the basics of the game and touches on some of the more interesting aspects, such as tells and bluffs. Although it does contain all the mathematical data, emphasis is put on having a feel for playing the game, and that makes the book a good read. The only thing missing, is a chapter on online playing, and I would have liked a little more comparison between limit and no-limit poker.
Meh. Never really caught me. The main problem was the secondary character - the young man whom Alex Delaware sets out to save. I never cared or even liked the guy.

Though I also own a Japanese edition, my Japanese is not up to anything more than recognizing some Kanji and verb endings. As for the English version, I must say it was nowhere near as frightening or as engrossing as the Japanese film version. But I couldn't put it down which is saying something since I manage to put down many books I start.

It took me a couple of chapters to get into the main character of this book, but once there, I was hooked. The story is well composed with a good feel of urgency and the badguys are truly evil. Pretty good, recommendable.

Extremely dry and boring, even for a book of this kind. The example programs are too few and not very interesting. Still, there is a lot of valuable information for readers who are willing to put in the effort.
Very well researched and insightful, except for the language section which embraces all kinds of proposed superfamilies roundly rejected by the majority of linguists.

This was the first book I completed in French though I had previously tried with Le petit Prince. Though my vocabulary was not quite sufficient, the pace of the story balanced perfectly with the level of the language for a French learner. I found at least one change from the English original which makes me think there must be more: an aside where Harry is dissecting a rat in one scene is missing.
Beautiful presentation but doesn't cover the range of topics I had hoped for.

Does a good job at explaining the ins and outs of managing a fantasy baseball team. Would be even better without all the "processed meat products" jokes (earth to author: women play fantasy baseball, too).
I actually really liked this one. And I agree with DukeStreet that the jump was disappointing (more details please Mr Weber). It was quite a fun read and I was sorry it was over when I finished.
Interesting if a bit dated. The advice is sound but the contacts etc a little out-of-date.
Frankie, Clay LeGrand's wife goes missing for 2 years, when she returns there are more questions than answers.
Tons of beautiful illustrations. A must-read for any Tolkien fan.

I originally read this book as a 10 year old, but have begun rereading it critically when I stumbled across it for a children's literature class. The social criticism angle looks especially promising with this book, but it is a fantastic, epic adventure as well. I have probably read this book literally two hundred times.

I'm still not sure about this one. Although billed as Fantasy I'm not sure that it is, it does use prediction as a method of trying to change the future but I'm sure people of the time believed that it was possible. The characters were interesting and well rounded but some scenes were a bit off for me.

In spite of the title, this book has very few racy bits, and focuses instead on the social culture of the geisha in the 1920s and 1930s in Kyoto. This was a window to a world that I had no familiarity with whatsoever, and I found it highly detailed and yet never boring or bogged down by minuteia.

Kohl takes a long hard look at the wisdom of censorship in children's literature. This book is surprisingly entertaining, and it definitely caused me to think long and hard about Babar. A great encouragement to reading against the grain.

A good, personal account of Jim Crow-era life in Mississippi. The author's family life, schooling, and social situations are painfully recounted, and she gives an excellent insider's chronicle of the Civil Rights movement. Moody was a pioneer.
Love Palahniuk's style. Skaz narrator and the uglier sides of human nature. A fantastic book, just like all his others, with characters that entrance and repulse the reader. This book is tight.
brings up some interesting points about living as a couple that ring quite true, good stuff to think about.
Readable, but difficult to get into, story about england in the time of shakespeare where the Spanish managed to invade.
readable but predictable Vampire novel, I fell for the main character being the same name as myself trap.
The echoes from other series do sometimes leap out but it still retains a certain freshness that makes it a great read.
Very readable urban fantasy. Witches trying to save NY from being sucked into the otherworld.

Starts off in Dublin! Scarpetta is investigating a serial killer who appears to have killed in Dublin as well as Richmond, possibly starting in Ireland. And then another victim turns up. But all is not what it seems.
don't remember being this bad but I probably was Guy from Essex is the first person in his family and area to go to college, this is the story of his life, loves and mistakes.
Pretty ho-hum, but readable vampire novel. Had elements which could have led to a great read but ended up falling back on stock vampire issues, even when it was trying to be different.
An interesting sequel to the series. Concentrating on Nicholas Sayre and the aftermath of what happend to him and his future

A fairly inaccurate cover, a story that does read like a nearly first novel, it's not her best but it is early work by her and I prefer it to some of her later stuff. I'm going to have to read it again to see if I understand it properly. A fantasy romance now billed as a young adult book.
Great blend of mystery and fantasy and makes me want to search out some of the authors to read more.
Story about a group of lawyers in a barristers chambers. Interesting but a bit scattered.

It's about the 60's or 70's and Daisy is an academic, when Min walks back into her life and Daisy agrees to visit Min. Last time they met Daisy was in bed with Min's boyfriend and they hadn't talked for 15 years. When Daisy goes to Min's house Min injures herself so Daisy takes on Min's work. A cosy story that tries to be Miss Reed but fails. Everything is wrapped up neatly at the end.
A very interesting thriller with psychics and a small amount of romance thrown in for variety with plenty of red herrings.

readable story but didn't quite grab my attention and I didn't really care or get involved in the characters. It did read like how my father tells stories all the same, wandering around and eventually getting to the point.
sequel to Seer and the Sword and a great read, new cast of characters and new struggles.
Readable murder mystery but I didn't really feel for the characters.
Pretty predictable and wouldn't induce me to read any of the three authors.
Fairly obvious readable eddings standalone novel. Characters are par for eddings and situations fairly telegraphed.
A fun read, completely frivilous and plot low but fun all the same. SK finds love for Alexion but as he's dead how will be be able to keep her?
Fun look at life through the filter of thinking about coffee.
some very interesting points about the why and how of weight issues. Worth a read even if you discard half the ideas.

Nita has to face up to her mother being very sick and Kit has been distracted by other matters.  She's convinced that their relationship has trouble, but it's those troubles of finding places in their partnership and how they work with each other.  The Lone Power offers her choices but what are the costs of those choices.I like the solidity of this series.  The charcters are interesting and the world consistent.
The lives, declines and falls of several famous actors. Sad and gossipy all at the same time!
another epistolary novel from Meg Cabot, again aimed at an adult audience its a fun, light read.
mildly annoying in it's sexism but of a period. Still I don't quite understand why it's been reprinted!

In some places fatally flawed and in others worth reading for the ideas she has a good theory about some things that cause us to act irrationally and with fear (black holes) and people and things that take away our energy (energy pirates) and how to cope with both.
sequel to, and needing the previous book, next couple get involved, which was telegraphed in the first one
very readable alternative world fantasy with Lord Darcy as a detective and his forensic sorceror Sean O'Lochlainn.  Quite enjoyable with almost a Sherlock Holmes feel to the period and the stories.
This is a slim volume which remains focused on the subject its title suggests.  Unlike many works on execution, it rarely strays into the lurid details of sensational crimes and criminal biography.

I am no philosopher.  I have no formal training in the matter.  Russell's work astounds me.  I drink it in thirstily and still want more.  He has the facility for explaining without condescending or diluting.

This is a decent college freshman level survey textbook.  It is basic and without frills.  It attempts to steer a middle course between conservative and liberal interpretations and succeeds fairly well.  It is not my first choice as an instructor.  I find there are several others that are superior in their coverage and detail.

Although the book is interesting in some ways, disappoints more than it satisfies.  Robert Elliot served as executioner in numerous high-profile cases in the early twentieth century.  As often seems the case, he chooses to focus almost entirely on the criminals and the criminal cases rather than on himself and his own experiences as executioner.  While that is understandable and forgivable, the worst part of it is that he recounts the stories of his involvement almost as a mouthpiece for law-enforcement propaganda.  He sounds like a government documentary designed to gloss over any inadequacies or deficiencies, the intent of which is to supress criticism and reduce fear and doubt.  All sounds glib, facile and rehearsed.  Admittedly Elliott had a ghost writer and no doubt that accounts for some of the lack of personality and humanity.

One would think that executioners would be in a position to provide interesting memoirs.  Invariably it turns out that they only want to write about the criminals and cases they are involved with.  Their contribution, in the larger picture, is quite small - a matter of minutes in a life of crime.  Not surprisingly then, if the tale of the criminal is to be told, it must be almost entirely without reference to the executioner.  What would really be interesting is a work about how execution works, how the bureaucracy and administration of death operates, how executioners come to practice their calling and how do they live in day-to-day world among people engaged in more mundane professions.
This is a beautiful book filled with lovely photographs.  It gives a stunning view of Ireland.  Having never been to Ireland, I can only hope the country looks as good as it photographs.

Berghahn squeezes an amazing amount of information and analysis into the relatively few pages that constitute this book.  The period of late nineteenth century through World War I is one of the best-documented, most written about in all of history.  Nevertheless, Berhahn manages to clarify and explicate elements that others have missed or at least manages to bring them together in easily accessible ways.

Susan Dunn explores the implication and meaning of the death of Louis XVI in the French collective memory.  This event may be roughly equivalent to the signing of the Declaration of Independence or the Assassination of Lincoln or a handful of other pivotal, defining moments.  Such events grow and assume a life of their own.  Dunn examines how the death of the King at the hands of his own subjects has shaped French politics, arguably to this day.

Although this book is interesting, it is NOT an actual memoir of the Sanson family.  There seems to be a strong desire to have accounts of the Reign of Terror from Sanson's point of view.  But there is no such work in existence.  All of the so-called ones that have surfaced have been shown to be fake.
No, nay, never. One of the very few books I've every seriously considered burning out of spite.

I absolutely devoured this book. Within three days of receiving it from the Sci-Fi Book Club, I was done, licking my chops and waiting for the Well of Lost Plots to arrive.If you didn't like the first book, my advice is don't waste your time and money with this one. The jokes are similar, the attitude toward literature is the same, the characters (and most of the characterization) are the same.This is an easy world to get lost in. I've found myself wondering, as I read other books, about what the characters would do if they were in our world, or how they would interact with other fictional characters. The idea of Jurisfiction is brilliant, and there is no limit to the adventures that are available in this universe. Add to that the potential plot lines with the ChronoGuard ....No plotline givaways here (you can read the other reviews for that). Just a few comments:I LOVED the names of the expendable SO-15 agents. Slorter and Lamb were my favorites.Ascheron's sister seems to be unbeatable. Should make for great drama later on.I HOPE Thursday gets better at jumping from book to book -- although she SHOULD get a medal or something for jumping solo into Poe.Through it all, Fforde displays the same wit that made me love The Eyre Affair. I'm ready for the next one.I just wish there was a contest that fans in the States could get in on! By the time I got my book and looked at the crossword puzzle on the back, the contest was over!

This book is NOT literature. This book IS, however, a great light read that I thoroughly enjoyed.The premise is classic sci-fi -- alternate universe, detective work, chaos caused and averted. The details are what make the book.Anyone who has no taste for literary classics will not understand the majority of this book. Set in an alternate world where classic authors are revered the way rock stars are here, the literary one-liners, puns, and casual references abound. Since classic literature is treated fairly casually, perhaps I should also caution those who take their literature too seriously -- especially Bronte fans.Thursday Next, as a character, is fascinating. I was a bit disappointed with who she wound up marrying (no spoilers there -- the chapter titles would give that one away), but enjoyed the way that it came about. The rest of the LiteraTechs are fairly shallow in this book -- I have hopes that they will be fleshed out in later books.There is a problem with point of view -- the book seems to shift from 1st person to 3rd person omniscient for no apparant reason, and that bugged me abit. Some of the characters were a little stereotypic -- uncle Mycroft is a great example of this, Jack Schitt is another, Asheron Hades himself a third.My favorite part of the book was Thursday's father. I looked forward to each of his appearances, and would LOVE to see him get his own series of books.All in all, this is not a perfect book, but it IS a great beach book, and I recommend it.

The world has changed dramatically since the classic, internationally bestselling The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People was published, influencing tens of millions. The challenges and complexity we all face in our relationships, families, professional lives and communities are of an entirely new order of magnitude. In order to thrive, innovate, excel and lead in what Covey calls the new Knowledge Worker Age, we must build on and move beyond effectiveness...to greatness.

Having read Invisible cities around a year ago I was expecting great things from another Calvino. However I was somewhat disappointed, this work is far more surreal and lacks the intellectual layers of Invisible Cities.
Like Al's radio show, the information is a lot better than the humor. Al's a funny guy when the flow is natural, but he tries way too hard at times. Still, there's a lot of great information in here.
pretty predictable story about a woman worrying about her long-absent cousin's return and creeping weight issues.

I really hated this book. The essays were superficial, self-conscious attempts at snarky humor, and offered little insight. Most of them seemed to be written solely to bemoan the latter two seasons--which I happened to love, so I am clearly not the target audience. What really killed the book for me were the inaccuracies: if these people are truly all fans, as they claim, then mistakes such as referring to the AU portrayed in "The Wish" as "Vamp World" (with the parenthetical assurance that this is the accepted term in fandom) are quite perplexing.I'm glad to be rid of it.

Another good visit with Eve and Rourke. A young girl is the only survivor of the murder of her family, hiding out with Eve who's trying to find out who did it before they find the girl and kill her too, taking a lot of other people with her.
does show some age but an excellent read. One of the better vampire novels.
Not as good as the other two, this one seemed to have some very contrived situations happening and a leadup to a sequel or two.Good but a bit disappointing.

Interesting book, I know it's been debunked by several people but some of the points she makes are actually quite good! Little and often would appear to be the motto, quality over quantity every time!
interesting story about a man who is dying, his grand-daughter coming back to visit and discovery of ghosts that are haunting him.
Readable but just barely pretty ho-hum cliched 80's spy novel with cookie cutter characters.
Not the most exciting book but a piece of life for a therapist Natalie, Carter her boyfriend and Finn the man who sparks her interest.
This is a very thorough, well-organized guide to HTML.  Although the technology has changed some since its publication, the core elements remain valid and therefore the book remains useful.

I tried and I tried to get somewhere with this book and could not do it.  I have been a programmer for 20+ years, so I'm not a complete beginner.  This book seemed pitched at someone who already knew and understood everything.  I felt like if I had used it in conjunction with a live instruction to whom I could pose questions, that I might have gotten something out of the book.  As it was - zilch.

I acquired this book as a result of a course I took.  I have never really had the opportunity to use UML on the job.  But the idea sounded great.  This book supports the excellent ideas inherent in this approach.
Interesting if vaguely disturbing book about murders aftermath.

I used this in a course I took and found it to be useful.  It seemed understandable to me, a seasoned programmer in general but a novice in java, yet it was also accessible to others in class who were much newer to the whole process.  It is arranged in easy to follow steps, each lesson building on the previous.  It is well indexed.

This is a good introductory level book for VB6.  Of course, in the world of technology, that means almost nothing now that VB6 has been superseded by Dot Net.  I may be alone in preferring VB6 but that has little to do with the merits of this book.  As a Microsoft publication the book reminds me too much of their help.  It's good up to a point, but it rarely takes you into those little nooks and crannies that you really need to get the serious job done.

This is a technical book aimed at teaching the reader how to understand, write, maintain, and deploy com objects using Visual Basic.  I believe this book is written with VB.6 in mind, although it might be earler; it certainly is not written for the Dot Net version, and therefore is out of date and has been for at least a couple of years now.  A couple of year is a LONG time in the world of technology.  Rating this on its own merits, the book was useful and thorough as a guide though singularly uninspiring to me.  Perhaps it was I who was unmotivated, but the book did not stir any excitement or interest in the process and consequently I used it but little.

This is a good manual for beginners to get up and going and get a sense of accomplishing something.  I like this book a lot as a beginner book.  It has projects that a novice can actually complete.  It is well indexed.
Planning and corruption in Ireland. A look at some of the issues raised by the Flood Tribunal. Interesting and scary because it's still ongoing and they're still finding out about the issues.
An interesting read about a few months in the life of poor cotton farmers in Arkanasas. More slice of life rather than the usual thriller from Grisham.
A little dated but an interesting read. A guide for life after cancer with some of the side effects and nastiness that can happen!

Interesting look at the perception of wealth and poverty in several different countries around the world. He's looking at the different systems - none of which he shows to be perfect but many of which have both good and bad points.

This is a photographic collection of individuals involved in the aftermath of the events of 11 September 2001.  Not surprisingly, it is a highly charged, emotion-laden work.  THe photos are well done and evocative.  I think this may be an interesting part of the historical record much later.
Readable but barely disguised christian allegory. Mediums channelling badness - tho they could channel good - good guys having to find god to help them defeat this bad.

Dogs who have been moved from owner to owner can present special problems or at least have special needs.  This book teaches you how to help a dog adjust to its new home and environment and how to make the transition less painful for humans and canines.

This is a photographic essay, a memory book of the World Trade Center.  I usually do not go in for the mushy, overyly sentimental, reactive sort of book.  I always loved the WTC; thought it one of my favorite spots in New York.  Every time we went to the city, we went to WTC at least a couple of times, usually to eat at Windows on the World and always for the half-price tickets for Broadway.  So in addition to the tragedy, the place already held a unique position in my heart.  The book is well done for a hastily assembled photo montage.
Readable but I didn't find that I had any sympathy for the main character who is a shapechanging Dragon.It's basically that the Dragons of myth are real and their prey is Humans.

Theres a murder of an elf and LA prosecutor, sleuth and forenisc Ianthanomancer Lee Enfield; with her partner Gelert whose a Fayhound, are investigating but there's more to this murder than is obvious.
This starts off quite obvious and then starts to become interesting. Interesting read.
Interesting read about a remarkable group of sisters whose lives spanned France, England and Ireland.
Interesting, particularly with some insight into his relationship with his father.
Interesting book about how sometimes it's small changes that make the big changes happen.

This book is essential for understanding the growth and development of instituions that create, maintain, and even impose order on modern society.  Rothman suggests connections between the asylum, prisons, schools, factories, and hospitals.  His work couples nicely with that of Foucault but Rothman's is by far, more accessible.
as a companion to the series it scores a 4 without the series it would get a 3.Doesn't go into any more real depth than the channel 4 series of the same name but an interesting read.
a bit christo-centric but interesting all the same. The kind of book you'd have beside your bed and read one of in the morning to get yourself in the mood to deal with everyday inanity and insanity.
Set in the now and the past, this story of psychic ability and magic is interesting during the now but the past part is a bit forced.
This was a great read. A Prince and Princess from different societies meet as slave and princess and through the bonds they forge here later events are shaped.
now a film. this is a fun read, pretty predictable but the path is fun.

You know I wouldn't have read them in a newspaper, reading them in a book was fairly painful, I couldn't recommend this book. I just didn't care if the characters dropped dead between one sentence and another, I kept hoping it would improve, to no avail!

I read "Too Many Blondes" first and it was a better read, this is good, just not as good.One of Sam's ex-teachers and friends turns up dead, she knows almost everyone at the party and although the cops call it accidental death she's not sure. Once she starts to pull the strings several things start to unravel.
This is a fine book containing thoughtful, useful insights into the nature of crime in England.  The superb analysis is backed up with thorough documentation.
This is better than Geoffry Abbott's books though it certainly suffers from a similar pandering to the lurid and sensational.

Elizabeth (Betsy) Taylor is having a bad week, first she's unemployed and then she gets killed by a car.And then she wakes up. A vampire she doesn't want to be cliched, thats being courted by some vampire groups, that can go out in the light, isn't allergic to holy water and other typical vampire moments, so the other vampires believe she's the Vampire Queen prophesied.Fun.
quite readable memoir of life in Egypt and France, every time there is food mentioned you get at least one recipe!
Dated now story about some women whose careers are taking off while their husband's careers are starting to flounder.
Interesting but I think her energy levels would be scary! Very much a wake up and smell the coffee (and give it up!) type of person.
A great series with believable characters who beat Anita Blake hands down for sheer believability.I want to know what happens next!
ho-hum horror, druids bad with transmigration of souls taken to a new level where instead of being born into a new body some people are taking over peoples old bodies.

Possibly not quite critical of some of the detractors and without too much information about the aftermath, the final chapter felt a bit rushed but an interesting look at the before and after of the Irish ban on Workplace Smoking

Very good read, tho sometimes you wonder if it would have been better if just one timeline had been used, I liked the characters and it was quite good in an oldfashioned murder mystery way where you didn't know the identity of the villian until the end!
plods quite a lot but the historical detail is interesting, not enough to make me really care about the characters tho.
An interesting idea and a clever conceit, but I really didn't care much what happened to the characters and wanted to slap Nicholas!
Jared is a pleasure slave being sold on to a notorious queen. Demon has a cameo and Dorothea functions as an interesting villan.
Interesting ideas. Will have to think about a lot of the ways of change he proposes.

Readable yarn about Tara, an astrologer to the stars who used to be Scarlett an overweight teen with few friends and a mother who, to be frank, abused her emotionally. She reinvents herself with the help of an old teacher.

Geoffrey Abbott delights in titalating his readers with lurid tales designed to elicit the maximum sqirm factor.  He usually avoids straying into technical inaccuracy.  But somehow one comes away from reading Abbott with a sense of mistrepresentation by ommission.  Still, at a primitive level, he can be great fun.  As a former Yeoman of the Guard at the Tower of London, I bet he was a HUGE hit among the customers.

As an instructor who uses The Jungle as an assigned text, this book is useful so I can keep up with what not to ask students on exams or identify specific phrases from the study guide itself.  Over all, this is a decent guide and explanation of Sinclair's book.

I find this a valuable guide to have around as I grade essays on by students.  These days, the internet is a more useful tool for searching for plagiarism but good old cliffs notes are still useful.  As for the book's real use, it is a good means of interpreting and studing the novel.  I always find these notes helpful for checking and verifying my own understanding as for a guick summary.  They should never be used as a substitute for the actual book.

Excellent resource, if you're learning Japanese.  I use this dictionary more often than any other when reading text in Japanese.  In conjunction with a good online dictionary, there's very little I can't look up in one place or the other.
I loved this story of several girls and later women who are involved in the complicated world of a slightly alternative medieval imperial China.
Although I don't necessarily agree with all of it it does make you think!
The first two were good but this was great, really enjoyed this but kinda wanted more about some of the other characters!

Fascinating book.  I knew next to nothing about China's history before reading it, and I usually have difficulty reading history at all, but Fairbank handles the subject quite well, and adds the occasional dash of dry humor (which I was entirely not expecting).

Still unsure about this one, it didn't flow as well as I would have liked, it made me quite annoyed at the style and not at all enthuastic about reading anything else by him. It's written in both a modern way and a style from the 18th Century and it just feels "too" clever. As if the Author was trying to perform a creative writing exercise.

I preferred this one to the first one. Jaenelle becomes fleshed out and matures. I really liked this and can't wait to start the next one!  Jenelle and Daemon have to fight their way out of their respecive mental prisons.  Jaenelle also has to embrace her life as a dark queen and do her offering to the shadows while also fending off Dorothea and her plans.

Interesting blend of the paranormal and war. The second world war leaves Clare alone and pregnant, newly come to a sussex village where there is darkness lurking, but with the dark there is also light, light that wants to protect her and her child, and incidentally England.

Interesting, I did feel like I was part of the way into a series with this one but it was an interesting read. Very dark and it's not too obvious who the real bad guys are.Janelle is young and powerful and her stories have led to her being regularly institutionalised.  Her family don't understand her and the power she wields is such that trying to train her is beyond the power of her teachers who blame her for their inability.  Frustrated she finds Seitan the the region of hell and gets him to teach her.  He's facinated with her as is his son Daemon. When a powerful witch comes near her power she attracts powerful friends and powerful enemies.

Interesting look at Breast Cancer and what it means to have a breast in the western world. Her decisions were brave and interesting.Her fears about recurrance hit close to the bone while I'm waiting to see my oncologist later this month!
Two people turn up dead, one of them was in therapy with a woman who has got on the wrong side of Alex Delaware before. Interesting and very readable.
Fun read about a architect and a writer who find themselves in a house together and have to learn to live together for a while.
Two murders, one of a Child and one of an adult, one the reader knows who dunnit, the other is up for grabs, interesting with very human policemen.
Until recently I'd forgotten how much FUN Dick Francis could be. Interesting adventure with missing money, missing treasure and a missing race horse.

Interesting but a little forced. Geraldine Frances' heart is broken by her cousin and she decides to get her revenge. She gets extensive plastic surgery and diets and exercises her way to a different outside, she hires Jake, who's blind, to teach her about pleasing a man in order to get her revenge on her cousin. Jake is also looking for revenge on the drug pushers who killed his wife.
Henry travels through time, Claire is one of his fixed points throughout time, this is their life story. Very very cool and original idea.
Although the technical references are WAY out of date still a good read.Kate investigates Missing Conservatories, Crooked Land Deals and problems in a pharmacy company.
Interesting, if a bit christo-centric occasionally, papers from a conference on where Ireland should go from here.

A young theology student is found on a beach and is thought to be an accidental death until other people start dying.Interesting moment where knitting provides a clue that not all is well with one of the deaths.
Readable story about a psychologist who finds himself in the middle of murder. Unsure who is doing it and having plenty of suspects it's still a shock when the actual culprit is unveiled!
Interesting read about a man with cancer who takes a chance to visit the stars knowing that that will shorten his life.
The story of a nuns past. Live, Loves, and medieval Florence.

GAH! Pretty much disliked this one, manic depression and child abuse rolled into a package that seriously had my teeth on edge.I prefer Daphne du Maurier for the same kind of atmosphere and would much rather lose myself in a Jane Austen for a period piece.
First book in the Kate Brannigan series and a great read. Kate tracks down missing song-writer Moira Pollock and shortly after that Moira turns up dead.

Boy was this book difficult to find. The Bird family, it is rumored, had most of the print run bought up and destroyed. Described as a benign dictatorship the Bird family plundered the treasury of Antigua as if it was their own piggy bank. As usual the good ole USA let it all pass with a smile and a wink.
Many years ago I read this, and re-read this, and lent it to a cousin who never returned it.It was as good now was before!Italian romance during the time of Garibaldi.

Interesting but not her best.Ranira is a bond-servant, saw her parents burn in the town square on suspicion of sorcery. In this town Women are veiled.Mist is a sorceress drawn to the city because there is magic that has gone wrong. Accompanied by Jaren and Arelnath - both fighters.
Sex, Drugs and murder with bikers. Readable but not a writer I'd return to.

A more adult Meg Cabot. A light romance where Cartoonist Jane Harris is helping her best friend elope with her boyfriend. The best man is causing sparks to fly.Format similar to Cecelia Aherne's Where Rainbows End.

Vintage Meg Cabot, she just keeps getting better!Luke Striker is a hollywood teen who is researching high school for a role, Jen Greenley is the school confidante. She is supposed to help him pretend.Love, Life and high School.

This went through several stop-starts and I didn't care, for the characters, plot anything, just didn't interest me. The odd snippets of Orthodox Jewish stuff was more interesting than most of the rest of the plot.13 people killed in a posh restaurant, Peter Decker investigates and gets immured in some pretty shady accusations.

Readable story about a family where everything seems to be coming apart at the seams. The Parents appear to be in a happy marriage but what you see on the outside isn't always the whole story.Their three grown-up daughters have to deal with their own issues and lives as well as their parents'.

Passable but a bit annoying message wise.This tries to be several things and fails. Louise is a lecturer in college with a committment free relationship with Toby, another academic, who's married to Miriam, Louise's best friend. Rose comes along to stay in her orchard, who's 80, and starts stirring things.Best bit:"You read novels?" she asked rudely."Sometimes. Mostly I listen to them." he smiled. "I've got a Walkman and I like to listen to novels when I'm in the tractor cab. I like Jane Austen best I think, but I like them all."He did up the buttons on his jacket. "George Eliot is good for a long field," he said. "And Henry James is the best for harrowing. But that post-modernist fiction I just can't get on with. It's no good for ploughing at all." He shot a mischievous grin at her astonished face.

I really enjoyed this one. Kate Brannigan is a great character and I laughed out loud on a few occasions with this one.She's trying to capture a couple of fraudsters preying on recently deceased people. Wondering why a doctor died and how that has implications for a friend and her girlfriend who's expecting and to add to her burden her partner has fallen in love and is moving to Australia.I'm going to read more of these!

ou would actually need to know something about yoga to follow this book and it's not all that accessable for beginners, it shows the full blown poses rather than the yoga for starters poses. Interesting

Interseting travelogue of a man who lived and came to admire the mujahadin of Afghanistan during the Soviet  occupation. Provides some useful insights into todays (2005 / 06) troubles. Good discriptions of Tibet and interior China
Probably would be a better read if I had read the first story.

Dalrymple,s writing syle is a delight to read. He lived in Delhi and travelled the subcontinent immersing himself in Politics past and present as well as the social cohesion and mores of this large complex society.

Wrote review for the Journal of American Studies. Hopefully they publish it. Wide-ranging and impressive look at panAmerican literary history between 1820s to 1850s. Great at making connections, new views on classics and rescues some more obscure literary work. On the whole a bit too ambitious in its scope although is bound to be influential in the offshoots it produces.

I remembered the story "The wings of Courage" from my childhood and bought this hoping for for a good translation into English. Alas, this isn't it. I expect if you turned it back word for word it would come out in good idiomatic French. Its jazz age illustrations are the best part.
Wonderful witty tales of the post-classical and medieval world by Dr Garnett of the British Museum Reading Room; foreword by TE Lawrence (of Arabia).
Publisher's daughter meets rural life and learns a few things they didn't teach her at school.

This was one of the few books I've read this year that made me shake after I was finished. Beautifully written. Not sex crazed like her other books. (Although I don't mind the sex books she writes) I look forward to the sequel of this book because it's set in Charlotte where I live now.
The book is out of print. A pdf is available at Woody Vasulkas website for free.

This was a great read, a bookbinder can read things out of books, swapping with items from this world, and one of the villans from a book is after him to get gold and power. WOW!Nearly scored a 5 but missed due to some dragging.

This was SO PAINFUL. I could nearly feel my braincells committing suicide as I read it. This alien KIDNAPS this woman, marries her in a ceremony she DOESN'T undersand and then procedes to force himself on her, despite her repeated no's, which she comes to ENJOY!The ending was rushed and trite and it's got to be one of the worst reads I've had in a while.Gor for women. And without the laughable, dated sexism either.Not reading any more Dara Joy without severe recommendations from people. I am so glad that I bought this in a charity shop, that's the only mitigating factor with this.
An older book on the GI diet, half explaining how it works and the other half with recipies, some from Restaurants.
Three women living in a small village in Dublin all friends. This is about their lives and loves.

I'm torn with this one, a quick read really for all it's over 1000 pages it's full of detail and interesting moments but a lot of it stretches my disbelief a little too far. An alternative historical Laurel K Hamilton with a bit more plot and detail.
This series just gets better and better. The Emperor is dead, Pyrus is about to become emperor and then his father turns up alive, or is he? A good kids series of books.

Readable but just barely. Juddery, it reads like a series of short stories held together by a central theme.A family have a recessive for twins and shapeshifting, mix in shamanism, magic, hunters and some other paranormal. Turn of the 20th Century USA.
A good read but not really to my taste, reminded me a lot of secondary school books
Maybe my favorite sports book of all time. The ABA was a crazy place and this book tells the story through the words of the people that lived it.

An interesting book of the use of deception by the world's intelligence agencies. This book shows that the KGB is the master of using deception to further Soviet Union's national interest. According to the author the function of intelligence agencies are not only gathering information, but also to present information AND passing disinformation to adversaries in such ways that the adversaries will react accordingly.
this is my favorite book ever. if you've ever felt marginalized, you'll identify with... well... all the characters in this book. it's mind-blowingly strange and amazing.

this is a grat book for use by students or others interested in thinking the actual stage of the human presence in the world.some topics like sustainability and eco-development find here some very important lessons.I used this book in my research works (I am an environmental engineering student)and I noticed it presents many up-to-date texts,wich contributed very much for my understandig of a lot of the relations between humans and the world and life itself.Great.
Creepy ring of changes on the alienated young-person motif.  In this case she finds her way to a wonderful place within her own house only to discover that it is perhaps not so wonderful. Superb.

A true Victorian novel in Japanese drag.  Interesting, purportedly accurate representation of life among Geishas.  It is probably accurate enough from a Western point of view, but the Japanese themselves do not seem to so highly regard much of the profession
fun read with a woman time-travelling to roman times from regency england to find her love and then is suddenly thrust back into recency england.

number 11 in the Stephanie Plum series, someone is trying to kill her and after leaving her job as a bounty hunter and a couple of false starts with other jobs ends up working for Ranger while nursing Morelli's broken leg.

A Sequel to Along came a Spider and very interesting. Two serial killers are competing and talking to each other, one seems to be a collector and one of his collected beautiful and intelligent women is Alex Cross' Niece.
Tom Holt does the gods better. The Gods are facing some millenium issues, combined with boredom and a computer with ideas about changing the paradigm.

Readable mystery. Kept me guessing even with the clues throughout. Some people have gone missing in a small English town. No bodies have been found and Detective Sergeant Freya Graffian thinks something is going on and keeps at it. Some discussion of Alternative medecine as well, as they find that this is one of the common denominators.
Oh this was fun. Valerious is the Angsty Dark Hunter, who is formal, and Tabitha is a vampire hunter who is a live spark, and the two of them are thrown together when she almost kills him.

Fun read, immortals abound, Zarek is a dark hunter, immortal, soulless, exiled. Astrid is an immortal who is supposed to judge him.Complete Vampire slash but a fun and compelling read, I couldn't put it down!

A different slant on the vampire legend, detective story with two strands, the vampire strand and the detective strand. Honestly I wouldn't hunt down any more in the series, the vampires were way too powerful and really they weren't careful enough.

An interesting mix of history and speculation, just like his Sister Fidelma stories. The story of Bran, an exiled Irish warrior from the time of Cuchullain who ended up sacking Delphi in the name of love.
Readable but sometimes overly complicated and involved, multi-layered story.

This book is an amazing, really coffee-table work that shows the uses Needlepoint has been put to over the ages and some modern slants on the craft. Pictured so clearly you can see the stitches it has no patterns, just pictures and some text. Shows some famous people stitching away and mentions the people the works were created for. Shows everything from Slippers to Heraldry to seat-covers.
Another fun Eve Dallas book. This time the unsub is mirroring famous serial killers and Peabody sits her Detective exam.

Translated from the french this kids book is a good read with well-developed characters and left me wanting moreRobin Penmarch lives on the lost Isle, where they know about our world and about the Uncertain World but try to keep away from both.Magic works in this world and Robin finds that he has skills in this area. When his school bully is kidnapped mistakenly for him, he feels he needs to rescue her.

Readable chick-lit.Emma works for a legal office and is married to Tony, who seems to be going nowhere, as is the marriage. When she's offered the chance to start up the Dublin Office of the firm with the acerbic Jack she jumps at the chance. Mills & Boon style plot.Favourite character is Jeremy and he regularly gets the bad end of the stick.
Readable but not really cyberpunk and not comparable with William Gibson, more J D Robb.Keeps you guessing throughout.
Very readable. Moves the story on and matures the characters quite well. There is a Dragon introduced.
Interesting apocolypse story starting with the pope resigning because his vision of the end is more than a little uncomfortable for the rest of the hierarchy.
Fun read. She's a Air Traffic Controller and he owns and runs some health food stores. They meet on a plane to the US, fall in love and marry, then they have to learn all about marriage and love.

I liked this one. A group of people from this world are transported to another world and have to work together to save it, could have done with some more info on the training they went through but it's a fun read.

Quite a readable story. The layers of the characters is quite interesting and often assumption will get you in a wrong mindset!Kerry is 16 and a runner, Lorraine is a detective inspector and they're brought together when one of Kerry's sisters is kidnapped. This scrapes the underbelly of UK society. The end is a bit pat and wraps things up a little too nicely but the characters are decently drawn.

Oh wow, I'm really enjoying this series and need more of it! Great characters a plot that seems to be getting more complex and you're just not sure who is the person in the right.Book 2 in the Black Magician Trilogy and Sonea's training continues, here she has to live with the bullying of her classmates and the knowlege that the High Lord has some very dark secrets.
Rather mundane haunting story where Grace buys a serial killers' house and starts to have things bump in the night.

The preachy tone of this one managed to annoy me but it had some interesting ideas. Even though the cover implies an inclusiveness it's a very very christian book, so I'd probably give it a 2.5, maybe a 3 for some of the ideas about living a thoughtful life but for the inclusive implication it gets a 2.All about finding grace in the everyday and being at peace with it all.

Beckmann makes math history entertaining by setting it in a larger historical context, and liberally lacing the story with his own political opinions. As one of the most important numbers in mathematics, π really does need its own history, and Beckmann gives a good overview of mathematicians' attempts to approximate or calculate π throughout history. His story is not just one of abstract mathematical endeavor, however; he sets those mathematical advances in their social and political context. His history is geographically complete, at least as complete as the records are available; aside from the Near Eastern and Greek attempts at calculating π, he discusses Chinese, Japanese, and Mayan knowledge of π, to the extent that there are surviving records.Beckmann's writing style is clear, and while he does include a good deal of math, the story still flows if the reader skips over the harder parts.
honestly I didn't like this really, I thought the race issue was belaboured and the twee dialect moments overused. It was a good story without the sledgehammer.

Not sure I can add much to Birchmore's review. The selection is excellent, covering old and new. A great pick me up, as you find yourself laughing out loud at many of the poems. Although everyone's sense of humour is not the same, there should be something for everyone here.

Fun and interesting story of the murder of a Jewish Feminist Rabbi who has managed to accumulate many, many enemies, Orthodox Rabbi Daniel Winter gets involved in the investigation. A murder mystery reminiscent of the golden age of murder mysteries.

Even if you are not really into reading poetry, this is likely to appeal to most people. It gathers to gether all the poems voted by BBC viewers, I think around 6 years ago. Consequently, a dip into the book is a trip down memory lane.
Very readable, once you get past the first few pages, and it drags you in with very little effort and had me guessing right to the end. Good read.
Fun sequel to the original, the next summer for the four girls where they learn more about life and love
Readable story about a Glassmaker who is friends with a jockey. When the jockey dies he leaves a parcel for the glassmaker, however other people want that parcel, willing to kill for it.

A great mystery from Barbara Vine. I did guess the answer before the end, but it didn't spoil my enjoyment. The eponymous doctor is a Victorian physician specialising (and obsessing) in haemophelia. A fascinating study of the characters and the science involved, using a modern day descendant of the doctor as a vehicle for the story.
A pair of perfect trousers and a summer of discovery, a good teen read.
What happens when the head of MI6's head of station in Berlin falls in love with the wife of his Russian opposite number?
Interesting story about a woman who is haunted by her past getting caught up in a murder that rubs some raw wounds.
3 women trying to find marriage on a bet before they turn 40. The best fun is guessing which one will get which guy.

Readable mills & boon. Ginny Marlow is a lawyer chasing her sister who needs bailing out, Quint Cutler is the Sherrif who decides that her sister needs to learn some lessons and that Ginny is someone he's interested in.

Readable story of a woman's life from girlhood in India to adulthood nursing in the Chrimea, live, love and losses in the interim. Very proper and nice but although the character has hardships they don't seem to impact in real ways.
Readable and often very funny a lot of this went completely over my head cause I'm really not a sports type.Much discussion about the 2002 world cup and the Mick McCarthy vs Roy Keane fiasco.
Count Nikolai was annoying, rude and took over, Lisa didn't kick him where he deserved it, repeatedly

Interesting read, Matt Scudder is an ex-cop who isn't a private detective but still does odd jobs for people for pay. Like the saint he gives 10% to charity but a lot of his stuff is a lot less nice.The twists are good too.

Readable doorstopper of a beach book about a female journalist who inherits a part-share of a foodball club, (this is on the back so no spoiler but doesn't happen until half way through) and has to fight her past and present to make things work.Written by a woman in a similar circumstance.
Actually kinda worth reading for the fact that it shows what happens when two people in a relationship don't talk and don't admit to problems.
Morgan was supposed to be dead and four years later she was starting to get her life together and date again, and then he turns up.

An interesting read. The Dark-Angel is a vampiric character that kidnaps women as his wives draining them of soul and blood. Aeriel is the maid of one of these who goes looking for her mistress and finds adventure and courage.A skilful blend of Fantasy and SF in the grand tradition of Andre Norton.
readable romance. Ginny van daun is a research botanist, Logan MacAllister is an enigma, they find themselves sharing a house.
Readable quick teen fiction, the continuing adventures of Devon March Sorcerer, Demon Fighter and teenager.

Nicky Piper remembers a kiss that haunts her life, no-one else has affected her this much, Esteban Tremain reminds her of this man. Will he be able to release the passion inside her? Not badly written this one and fairly engaging.
Readable and with some nice twists but it took forever to get into the story and I nearly abandoned it in disgust!

Vaguely disturbing and intensly gripping.In Summer of 1954 US Marshal Teddy Daniels comes to Shutter Island to investigate the disappearance of an inmate. But there are rumours of strange procedures and nothing is as it seems, not even Teddy Daniels.

Actually quite readable, even if I did want to slap the characters silly sometimes!Reclusive Millionare Widower strikes up friendship with the woman who passes on his answering service calls. When disaster strikes he feels compelled to help, the rest is predictable.

Fran meets Andre, thinks hes a monk, guilt trips about liking him, writes article, finds out Andre isn't a monk, guilt trips about her father being unfaithful. Rest left up to reader to fill in before author.
Tries way to hard to be clever, getting in Shakespearean quotations even. Good Mythical creatures, stupid bad mythical creatures, nasty men-folk. I won't be looking for the rest of the series.
He speaks to dead people, this is the story of how he ended up on TV
Three friends who have been together since forever in Ireland now live in Ireland and have to deal with their complicated love lives.

English and Irish Doccuments from the period pointing out that the fault was in both houses and that it's more a question of how people managed to survive than die that we should be asking, though it could be an embarassing one to answer!
Interesting read, more mystery this time than social commentary. One of the early books in the series in this one Qwilleran is still struggling.
Readable story with plenty of twists and turns to keep you reading.
I have some minor annoyances with this one re: typesetting but apart from that it's a great look into Irish Scientific Endeavours.

I can't recommend this one, it suffers from the Louise Hay school of dis-ease. As if cancer patients didn't have enough to deal with!Inspiring in parts with the ideas of taking charge of your life and changing things so that you're happy and living a full life instead of just surviving.

This is just simply dire. The stories are cookie cutter, the details are exasperating (needles to do crochet, help; a character who was into victoriana who felt "liberated" by modern clothing) and I wanted to slap most of the characters. The last two were tolerable, which moved the rating from 1 to 2, Sinderella by Kimberly Randell and Leather and Lace by Maggie Shayne were, in particular, the least offensive.

I honestly don't know who in the era managed to annoy Ngaio Marsh with their magick but this book is in response to it. I have my sneaking suspicion that it was Crowley. There's a polemic against magick and such superstition in this modern era and the most appaling mishmash of magickal types. The villans are painted very black with no redeming features and the good guys very very good. Even nastier practices are hinted at but not actually comitted.A good read but very, very biased.

It is a long time since I read this (for my A Levels, and if I said how long that would be giving away too much!), and it probably merits a reread.On a par with Mme Bovary and Anna Karenina (in period and theme), it is the story of a fallen woman, a victim of her class and the patriarchal society she lives in. She is seduced by the caddish Alex D'Urbeville, and subsequently cast away by her fiance, Angel (and on this basis he is the more dastardly, as Alex at least tries to atone for his sins). A tragic ending.
Written with the apparent connivence of Leslie Charteris, and before his death, this is a humourous and touching fan biography and Bibliography of Leslie Charteris.

This book had me torn, it reads more like fiction than fact, chopped and changed between characters and depressed the hell out of me about the treatment of women and their own apparent connivence with it. The mindless acceptance of the treatment they got was heartbreaking, the assumptions of the men, particularly Sultan was scary. You could see how, through peer pressure and assumption people could perpetuate the tragedy of both sexism and terrorism. How easy it is to keep a partially educated population afraid and how ignorance could be literally dangerous for all involved.
Bar that escapes from nuclear descructions of several worlds by moving in space and time. Interesting twist in the end.
I know it's teen fiction, but it's damned good teen fiction. In a world where dragons are small almost mindless pests a girl freams of something more, her quest takes her into peril and on to love.
Strange book that deals with the love lives of two people one of which looks very simple but isn't. Somewhat sensitive subject matter as there is some incest involved
Interesting but very light.  Kids dealing with parents dying in Ireland during the famine, somewhat too easy and glosses over some of the nastiness.

A haunting account of the true story of the Jews rescued by Oskar Schindler during the Second World War. Moments of extreme heroism and courage, coupled with demonstrations of the depths of cruelty to which humans can stoop, show the range of human experience and emotion.I would suggest this is one of those books everyone should read, not only for its craftsmanship, but also for the events it witnesses.

Actually an excellent book, but really for someone a little more into Yoga than I am at the moment. Goes through each Asana and explains how allignments should work, also explains how to ease yourself into each one.
Sister Fidelma in Rome, investigating a suspicious murder, interesting stuff.
An interesting read about an elf hunting a sword that turns ordinary humans into grendel's or cannibalistic monsters. Some ordinary humans (including some library students) try to deal.
Some great stories, especially Mercedes Lackey's story where she is being confronted by her characters! Fun reads and some good introductions to some writers in the DAW fanatsy stable
Interesting read with an interesting twist, some of the characters love-life complications are due to fairy intervention.

Interesting series of thoughts for changing your life, some of which may or may not be applicable to everyone's life but all of which will make you think about how much time you spend on yourself and how you should and could make your life a better one.
readable, interesting and makes you wonder about the effect you have on other people's lives.
Interesting but mostly if you actually *know* whats causing the problem.
Tiny font and some of the stories are a bit lame but the last two were interesting.

Probably a good book to give someone leaving home for the first time or a smelly friend but, and this is a big but, they leave out info like what the alternatives to Biological Washing Powder is, and what to do if the stain won't come out and you have allergies, and how to spot that that's what's making you itchy. Not a bad book but not wonderful.

Another Eve Dallas story where Eve finds out that having friends is a good thing while she investigates a nasty serial killer, while being fed information from a psychic. A great twist in the tail as well!
Quite readable story about murder, gangland killings, and a pair of detectives who are interesting people with lives!

The first of the series by Andre Norton and Mercedes Lackey, an interesting read about a human world where elves and dragons have invaded, dragons almost invisibly and elves as human slave-masters. Half Elves possess possible power to take down the evil masters, so they're killed, one survives and is found by Dragons.

Reads like a college essay where the title is "Compare the Irish Serial Killers phenomena to International Examples" not "Serial and Psycho Killers in Ireland" which is the sub-head on this one. Interesting read but sparse in the details about actual Irish Serial Killers.

Has the energy and verve of some of her earlier work. A good yarn.Kindan has several talents and has to find his future in a minehold. He ends up working with Watchweres and learning more about them than has been known before.
Bones: some human, some animal and many of them from different bodies.
A little off whack but very very insightful. Well worth reading particularly for the couple stuff.
Beautifully illustrated this one is so fluffy it's not funny.

Interesting read but sometimes tries to be a bit too clever. Twists and turns and a world that I'd like to see more of.Musician finds magic harp, legend has it that there is a price to pay if you use it, lots of people around him want him to use it. Fights and magic and love.

Shocking but compelling story about how one man found victims online after spending years preying on people in real life, Douglas points out that some intelligent manipulative people know how to convince psych people that they've reformed, but that there are people that truly don't want to reform and our society isn't geared to deal with them.
Mmmm, interesting read if possibly a little paranoid. Brings up a lot of questions but not a lot of very viable solutions.
Readable pseudo-x files stuff. Secret Cabal trying to keep humans from advancing too fast and killing themselves.

Scary. What happens when your father all but admits that he killed a contemporary of yours? That you start asking questions to find that a lot of things were quashed, including the fact that he molested a lot of children in the area.Scary but enthraling!

Severly formula fiction. Lauri is the young teacher of the deaf, Jennifer is her student that she's asked to privately teach, Drake is Jennifers Father who's still mourning his dead wife. If you can't guess the plot, you need help!

This is strongly chick lit and made me grind my teeth a few times. One of the characters, the main character Cara, is a witch, a "Charmed" type witch and sometimes is a bit annoying. It does namecheck "Spirit and Destiny" within the first 20 pages 8)I understand the worshiping Dionysus, but you don't invoke him before a JOB INTERVIEW!Cara is a Nanny, who goes to work for Nick and Andie Wilkins whose marriage is starting to crumble while their child has started school and Andie is starting to look at her life. Next door is the handsome Irishman Sean whose living with his old letch of a grandfather. Her mother doesn't approve of the match, many spells and catastrophies ensue.Don't get me wrong it is readable, it just has moments of wrongness about Wicca and witchcraft

Having read other books by this author this mills & boon-esque romance is pretty standard fare and sub-par for this writer!Actress is tricked into pretending to be engaged to her ex who's a producer. No prizes for guessing the rest of the plot.
Faith wakes up from a coma and discovers that Dinah, her friend is missing and passing messages on in her dreams. Good read with a good twist in the end.

For me this one has a mixed feeling there's shedloads of maths in it but not as much as in others of that ilk. There's leaps of faith, but again not as many, it still left me sometimes with a feeling that it's a too symplistic view of the world but also left me wondering if some of it could be true.
A plodding genre novel with no real insight to any of the characters, fairly yawn really. Two murders seperated by time show similar evidence, maybe they're the same murderer.

Interesting read, largely skimmed parts of the Gazetteer, but the section on the goddess in the landscape is a good read to remind that modern beliefs and the original landscape can be two different things.
A Psychic sherrif who's in denial about her abilities, a FBI team who use their psychic abilities to find murderers and a serial murderer who's targeting teenagers.

Interesting fare about the definition of humanity. An explorer visits a planet where everything is silicon based and their world is based on individual roles. He has to try to survive both the world and the people who want to exploit it.

Yes, sometimes the heroine has Way Too Much Angst, but this sucked me in, kept me up way past my bedtime and kept me guessing until the end!A burnt out successful psychic retreats to a quiet North Carolina town to find that murder is stalking her, and maybe she's next!
I struggled through this one. I really didn't see the point. Disappointing

Been doing a binge of Sister Fidelma books. This one is a great read with an attempted murder being branded as an attempted political assination, it is but not by the obvious culprit. She has to find out before it all leads to war.
An intersting read about a man with AIDS who loses a friend to suicide and then begins to get signals that his friend is trying to contact him. Heartwarming.
The Culture shock was well written. This adventure of Sister Fidelma has lots of twists and turns and a few murders, as well as a lot of political manouvering.
An interesting fantasy story with complicated and complex characters, not all of whom are either good or bad but both. Shapechangers and magic, dragonfolk and revenge. A good read.

Sometimes I wonder about stuff like this, maybe they're right, maybe we all should be vegan or breatharians but then theres a healthy thump of scecticism that tells me that maybe they trust too much in the nice.
A series of short stories and an interesting read in some incidents, others are a bit blah.
Interesting take on the Robin Hood story concentrating on Marion as the healer in the woods. This covers 3 books and is about three generations of forest wives.
The finale in the Galactic Milieu Trilogy - both the past and the future of the saga of the exiles, an excellent read.
A marginaly above average story about a housewife who writes bodice rippers, and the messes she gets into with her family. It's almost written like a Blog...

An interesting melange of The Secret History, Da Vinci Code and The Name of the Rose. A book contains secrets, some college students are studying it, crooked college politics and murder affect events.
And Mercedes Lackey once again hits her stride. A great read with some of her regular features including anxty teen. New world.
I read this pre-cancer and it was heartbreaking and funny and poignant and post-cancer it's even more of those things cause I can empathise.

A book that still has me wondering, a polemic look into the future where the issues are more important than the thriller aspects, a story of love and tragedy and near-future nastiness. Written before 9-11 but some of the points are quite poignant!
Not his best but an interesting story of some women who join the army of a repressive country where they're losing the war(s) badly. Fun.
Facinating look at the world of the Geisha by a woman who started off studying them and then became the first and possibly only white geisha.
How Waco meets Beth and Doc Leroy Lynn and how Waco with the help of his friends cleans up a town.
One of the finest reference books on Heraldry, this resource is a "must have". Wonderfully illustrated and easy to understand.
Above average fun readable romance with a portion of thriller mixed into the brew.
Another great resource for the aspiring herald, or lover of this ancient art-form
