I plan to reread the entire series again, with the hope of adjusting this rating accordingly.

Klosterman travels to various sites of rock deaths, such as the field where Lynyrd Skynyrd's plane crashed and the club where Great White's concert ended in flames.  Along the way he throws out his usual continuous stream of pop-culture references and contemplates the state of his love life.  Light and breezy, it's entertaining reading.
I really didn't understand the appeal of this book.  Charlie was not a particularly gripping character and the plot felt trite.

A glimpse into the life of an art dealer.  Polsky describes the people in his professional circles and the process of finding art for them.  Meanwhile, he's looking for the perfect Andy Warhol for his own collection (and budget).  An interesting look into a world most people don't know much about.

This is a great thriller. It's partially told by a young Englishwoman who has an interesting past which leads her to be obsessed with the Nanking massacre, and partially by the journal of a survivor of Nanking. Going back and forth between modern-day Japan and 1937 China, the story unfolds unhurriedly but also unrelentingly. Terrific storytelling.
Try-to-keep-from-laughing-in-public-places funny at times, but uneven.

A girl finds a strange old book in her father's library, containing only a woodcut of a dragon. She asks her father about it, and he begins telling her the story of his research on Vlad Tepes, also known as Vlad the Impaler, or Dracula. We track back through his adventures and those of his mentor, who disappeared while following the same historical path. When the girl's father disappears suddenly as well, she follows along after him. Well-written especially considering the many jumps in timeline and POV. Lots of fascinating historical detail makes the story come alive.

I might have been more interested in this if I'd read it when I was in college and reading things like Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance and Way of the Peaceful Warrior. All I can say now is that it's a good thing Santiago found a woman who was willing to wait while he went off to look for a treasure.

I found the vernacular a bit hard to read at times, I had to slow my reading pace in sections where there was a lot of dialogue. But it was worth slowing down for. The story is one of practicality and hardship giving way to confidence and self-assurance. Some passages were so beautiful I had to stop and read them again, particularly the section from which the title comes, and the following one."The familiar people and things had failed her so she hung over the gate and looked up the road towards way off. She knew now that marriage did not make love. Janie's first dream was dead, so she became a woman."

The 101st Airborne was an elite group by virtue of being paratroopers, but Easy Company was the elite of the 101st. The portraits of the leaders are well-drawn, particularly that of Dick Winters, who comes across as larger than life and almost too good to be true. The bond that was drilled into them by training under the merciless Sobel and then fighting in some of the most challenging conditions of the war (notably Bastogne) turned these ordinary men into people who could be trusted with others' lives.

Looks at the science of everyday life -- does toast prefer to fall butter-side down? how do rocks skip across water? can you really feel someone staring at you?Conversationally written, with science kept on a "Physics for Dummies" level, which was perfect for me.

I'm not what one would call a fan of baseball, so I learned a lot about Lou Gehrig and the world of baseball in the 20s in particular. Easy to read, interesting, my main complaint was the way the author went off on flights of fancy that involved lots of statements like "he must have" or other things that the author had no way of knowing.

Fascinating and full of information, interestingly presented. The weakest part I thought was the portrait of the modern beekeeper, but the historical aspects and the explanations of bees and bee life were eminently readable.

Originally read somewhere around 2002 probably. Reread in 2005. I liked it better the 2nd time around. Still don't like the Wizard of Oz finding its way into the book, but the rest was pretty good even if it really is mostly one giant flashback.

The characters in this one are just one-of-a-kind. A strange nobleman finds a baby and decides to raise her as his daughter. The major problem with this course of action is that the baby is actually a boy. This is a good one.

I can't attest to the correctness of the conclusions Krakauer draws (I intend to read Boukreev's book eventually), but this account draws you in completely to the experience of these expeditions to Everest.  People who weren't really qualified to make the climb, but could pay for it, people who have made multiple attempts but failed for a variety of reasons, people who lead the expeditions, and the omnipresent sherpas.  It's a gripping, fascinating story, as well as being tragic in many parts.

Brilliant book about Lia Lee, the child of Hmong immigrants in Merced, California. The clash between American and Hmong worldviews happened over her hospital bed, with tragic results. It's a fascinating study though of the Hmong and of the types of problems that can happen when two cultures simply don't understand each other.
Some insightful moments, some funny, some sweet, some easy to relate to, but overall not much substance. Interesting interactive aspects with the website, but as a book not very engrossing.

A bright young woman fulfills her lifelong desire to become a spy. What makes this book less than enjoyable is that once she gets through training, she really seems to dislike her life. She didn't seem to have enough perspective on it to keep it from being dreary for the reader as well.
Useful information but terrible editing and proofreading. Nice to get an overview of political climate, ship life, ranks, battles, and how things worked.
A memoir of a hard childhood, and the resourcefulness and determination that can come from those circumstances. Funny sometimes, sweet sometimes, heartbreaking sometimes.
Decent thriller about a blind attorney and the young man who may have killed him.

As chilling a depiction of a downward spiral as I think there could be. Your breath catches as you cross that moment from which there is no going back -- only to find another moment farther down the path which is another turning point.
Promoted as Pretty Woman meets Nick Hornby, and it is in a way. I thought it derailed at the end a bit like High Fidelity did, but it was overall enjoyable and quite funny at times.
Self-conscious, self-referential, self-reverential at times.

Five stars aren't enough. An instant favorite, an instant recommendation to everyone I know. What a beautiful, tragic, and amazing book. It made me cry in a number of places, and that almost never happens. It's simply brilliant.

A female MI5 agent is trying to find a suspected terrorist who is attempting to enter England for purposes unknown. She must also try to find the "invisible" (person who blends in) helping him and determine what their target and purpose are. There are quite a few characters to keep track of and it can get confusing at times, but overall it's a good espionage thriller, and reads a bit like a good episode of the "MI-5" tv series.
Beautiful writing, sweetly handled story about a man with OCD, the limitations on his life, and the ways that people find a way into his world in spite of his many restrictions.

This is a story about one of the more obviously psychotic families out there, with everything you can imagine thrown in -- affairs, guns, diseases, drugs, pregnancies, and much, much more. Sometimes it all became a little much to deal with, but overall it serves to illustrate the point that you're tied to the people to whom you are related, and even though you may think you have nothing in common with them or you hate them, that bond is always there, as real as it is inexplicable.
Quite a good little thriller. Lots of twists and turns, and a likeable main character in Bobby Dodge.

Howard's life was blown to hell and gone in Vietnam 16 days after arriving in country, when he stepped on a landmine at 18 years old. He's learned to live without the ability to talk, read or write, and he's settled into a routine, but things are thrown off when his ex-girlfriend asks him to watch her 9-year-old son while she goes into rehab. Not overly sentimental in spite of the potential for such.

The story of a scholarship boy at a private prep school where literature takes on mythic proportions. The boys in school are in love with language, vying to write something that finds favor with (and therefore earns them an audience with) visiting writers like Robert Frost and Ayn Rand. The encounters with these writers are entertaining and revealing, but the real prize is a meeting with Hemingway, which the narrator wants very badly. Sparse but vivid in his writing style, Wolff obviously loves language just as much as the boys in his story, and it's contagious.
Powerful stuff. It's amazing (and not in a positive way) what doesn't get taught in schools in the US.

I read this after the movie came out, and I was shocked to see how much it was written to be a movie. Sure, it was in a completely different country, but aside from that, it was the rare book that's excellent as a novel and also easily translates to the screen. Laugh out loud funny of the "funny 'cause it's true" variety.

I loved this book.  It's written in such a beautiful, haunting way.  The subjects of the book, the Lisbon girls, are seen from the outside, through the eyes of boys in their neighborhood.  It's a simultaneously fascinating and frustrating way to view events, since there's no way to know for sure what's going on with these doomed girls.

Inspiring without being sentimental. Besides telling the story of Joe Simpson's survival, this edition has the added perspective of Yates, who had to make the decision to cut the rope attached to Simpson and move on.
Quite interesting story that combines the story of present-day Mormon fundamentalists and the history of the LDS church. There's so much there they don't teach you in school.

He decides to read the Encyclopedia Britannica all the way through. More than just a quest for knowledge, it's a quest for wisdom. Amusing, a quick read, lots of little factoids to add to one's stores of useless knowledge.

While this has Ender and Valentine within its pages, this book doesn't hold the same grip as the original Ender's Game did. The storyline is not as compelling, doesn't draw one in as well. It does have questions on society, and make one think on the aspects of society vs society, but I think Ender's Game did the job better.

Tom Ripley is an interesting character -- morally bankrupt, easily bored, an incredibly ego used as a bluff to cover his intense insecurities. I'm looking forward to reading more in this series. You can't exactly like him, but you have to find out how he gets away with the things he does.
Fascinating and only rarely shudder-inducing. All the things that your body can be used for after you die, as well as some history on things like embalming and bodysnatching for anatomy classes.
Meticulously researched like Gabaldon's longer works, but less satisfying as a story, especially since the mystery is not so much solved as explained by the culprit.

I'm glad I read this, if only to prepare for the next one, but it took almost all of my willpower to keep going. There are too many characters, with the four main ones taking turns at sharing their perspectives (fine for a two-hour movie, very hard for a long novel). And there are too many plotlines, including threads dragged in from previous books. I hope "A Breath of Snow and Ashes" moves along much more quickly.

The back of the book has a Kevin J Anderson quote about a mix of Lord of the Rings and Buffy the vampire Slayer, I would disagree, it's more medieval fantasy world meets Buffy, including the main character who is "fated" to fight the vampires and has to learn about her powers from a mysterious man who steers her career from behind.A readable romp and it could have stood on it's own if you left out the epilogue.There are sequels and although I'm curious I'm not sure that I'll be actively hunting them.

Overall, an interesting account of Brinkley's "on the road" undergraduate seminar. At times, though, I wished the reader got to spend more time with the students. When it was just Brinkley talking, I felt like I was being lectured to, instead of being allowed to share the experience of going to all these places.
Some cute patterns, and EASY knitting instructions.  I taught myself to k1, p2 using this book.

"Lars Porsena of Clusium, by the nine gods he swore / that the great house of Tarquin should suffer wrong no more!"  ... and so on ... There's also a wonderful one on Verginius' murder of his daughter to keep her from becoming the illegally-enslaved concubine of Appius Claudius, too. Macaulay has her catching Claudius' eye whilst skipping merrily to school, as, I guess, all Roman girls ... did ... when exactly would this have been?  Even the first time I read this one I remember thinking, but maybe she would rather have been a mistress than a corpse? Her father never gave her that choice.  Nor did Claudius of course in the poem; and perhaps the point was more the illegal enslavement than the intended concubinage.  Anyway, great, red-blooded, sexist, classist, name-a-variety-of-political-incorrectness-and-find-it-herein Victorian stuff; I love it.   I seem to have collected 2 copies, one without a cover.
I've never been able to wrap my head around genetics, but I have something of a handle now on DNA thanks to this book.

"The Dance of Death:  The Legend of Saint Julien the Hospitalier" figured in an old Dragnet episode which I saw in childhood, and I tracked it down decades later.  An early example of the theme of decadence in French literature...?
The book is easy to read, but can be difficult to absorb.  Great subject matter--makes you think carefully about your life.  Movie will premier in Spring 2006
A followup to Celestine Prophecy.  The narrator and Wil go further with the insights.
The narrator puts all of the insights he's learned about thus far to use.  A tad bit unbelievable at times.
Very touching book, partly a diary written by a mother to her son.  Have lots of tissues ready, as it's a tear jerker.
I actually had dreams about Watchers.  I love Koontz and his ability to keep me totally engrossed in the book.  It may not be a literary classic, but it's definitely enjoyable.
One of my favorite books of all time.  Love and war.  What more can you ask for?
One of my all time favorites.  Just proves that you can't change fate.  Classic!

Cast the pretentious subtitle aside and rid your mind of Sufis; the enneagram uncovers more than a few defense mechanisms.  Personally I'm a 4w5, which is largely congruent with the Myers-Briggs' INFJ.
This book was a little slow and hard to follow at times.  I couldn't really get into it and struggled to finish it.

Touching story of a pregnant girl left at Wal-Mart by her boyfriend and her fight to overcome all of the disadvantages she's had in her life.  Friendship, family, love, death--there's a little bit of everything in the book.
Surprisingly, this is one of my favorite books.  I love Yossarian and his sense of self.  A must read for anyone.
Sequel to The Notebook.  A man's attempt to get his wife to fall in love with him again, while planning his "daughter's wedding".
The precursor to The Wedding.  A tale of two lovers torn apart and brought back together.  A page turner and a tear jerker.
Popular guy meets plain girl.  She forces him to open his eyes and realize that there's to people than their looks.  Good story--emotional, if you're a sap like me.

The best of all Grisham's books.  Adam, a rookie lawyer, takes the pro bono case to get his grandfather's impending execution delayed or pardoned.  This books goes a little deeper into the character development than most Grisham books.
Typical Harry Potter book.  Boring for most of it, but then it picks up towards the end.
One of the best books ever.  I don't know that I could ever part with it.
Another easy read.  Starting to think he's got something against the Catholic Church.
Sweet book showing that the slightest thing we do may have a huge impact on someone else's life.
Very inspirational book, dealing with life, death, and everything in between.
A collection of essays and speeches by author of Hitchhiker's Guide.
I recommend this book for any military, military spouses, or just military family members.  Heartwarming stories.
I didn't really like this book.  I stayed confused and disgusted most of the time.

Bernard Goldberg takes swings at every loudmouth liberal, obscene rapper, and just plain ignorance in this book.  Thankfully, while landing some low blows, he's able to support what he's saying with quotes and facts.  He's highly entertaining with his dry humor.  A must read for any conservative.

I found this book for a buck and it was well worth it! A story about a women who's feed up with getting set up and goes and makes up an imaginary boyfriend, then hires an actor to play it out. It was laugh out loud funny. Many quotable lines as well.
Couldnt put this one down. Dysfunction Junction at its best! Hey, I can relate.
I got this book for a buck and it opened my eyes to the world of Jonathon Carroll. Bizzare is the only word to describe Carroll.
Probably my favorite from King. Really enjoyed The Running Man. Must read.
Finally read thi safter having in my to read pile for years. Drugs, humor, hitchiking, whats not to love!

I recommend this book for all young girls. My sister got it for me when I was younger and its great. The book is colorful and helpful and entertaining. Contains quotes from REAL girls going through what every young girl goes through. Must read.

A young woman is hired as a nanny for a freak of a rich lady. The kid is almost completely messed up because of it. It had its laugh out loud moments. It was one I couldnt put down. As I nanny, I really enjoyed this book.
Various foster children with very different backgrounds come to live together and finally become friends. A childhood favorite.

I found this book at the library while searching for Jack Kerouk I think. I checked it out and loved so many of the poems. I started coping the ones I liked, then I realized, I'd end up copying the whole book! So, I had to add it to MY library. I love anything to do with bad boys.

When Tigre's father is badly injured in an accident, the family is thrown into turmoil.  Who will plant and harvest the corn that they need to survice and to please the Mayan gods? Twelve year old tigre has never done a mans work before.  Can he shoulder the burden on his own?, and take his father's place?
Great homecooking recipes.  I particularly love the Black Pepper Shrimp and the Vialia Onion Pie.  The epitome of southern.

In high school my friends and I had a wonderful time with the "If" books. Basic comcept: a book of random questions like "IF you were an animal what would you be?", stuff like that. Hours of enjoyment to be had.
I hated this book.  I guess I missed the whole point behind it.  To me, it dragged and wouldn't end quickly enough.
Great book!  I actually began to pity the Wicked Witch of the West.

This book paints Cinderella as a spoiled brat and the ugly stepsister as the worker in the house.  The stepmother is just trying to earn a living while wrangling a wealthy husband.  Interesting adaptation of a classic fairytale.
The story of Snow White, from the Queen's perspective.  A good read.  Unfortunately, this book doesn't compare to Wicked.
An interesting but twisted book.  Maguire was constantly one step ahead of me.  It took me a while to grasp what was going on and the ending was a surprise to me.
A young girl gets diagnosed with juvenile arthritis. Her life is severly changed since she was a dancer/cheerleader. I've read this book over 10 times.

Katie.com is a true horror story. A young girl meets guy online. Girl goes to meet guy in real life. Guy is not who she expected. Luckily the police intervined, this time. All young girls should read this book so they are aware of the dangers of meeting strangers from the internet.

So much better than the movie. It delves deeper into the characters and you see more of what is going on. I liked the novel better than the movie, and recommend people read the novel. Even after you've seen the movie. It will fill in those lost details that the movie just could not give you.
The mystery was a bit too long in the unraveling for me, but I would pick it up again in certain moods.  Very much a story about process, so to speak.
Not Gibson's best work, but even his mediocre stuff stands out.  Could you live as a professional trend-spotter with brandphobia? A semiotic whirl of a novel.

While the book describes locations millions would like to see, most can never afford to do it.  It's a nice dream to visit all 1000, but highly unlikely to ever be accomplished.  I'm also disturbed by the lack of American places.
Gives a little insight into the madness of Jim Morrison.  Maybe he was too intelligent, too sensitive, or too insecure.  Nicely written.
Definitely theological halvah for St. Jerome's "scandal of particularity" freaks!  The other persons of the Trinity don't get as much press.

A lot of interesting recipes.  If you like a lot of different types of sauces and/or salsas, you'll really enjoy this.  Biltmore tends to use a lot of mango or peach salsas.  Nice change from the ordinary.

Promising beginning to a splashy new fantasy series.  Has some good writing, great political intrigue, and things move along at a nice clip.  Suffers from badly written female characters and some "attack of the cliche" moments.  It's not quite at the peak of the large, splashy fantasy (think China Mieville) and it lacks the subtle maturity of writing present in some of my favorite authors.  But give the author time...

If you can't get to Biltmore, located in Asheville, NC, this is the next best thing.  Beautiful pictures (without the heads of your fellow tourists in the way) of the home, inside and out.  Brief history of the family and their claim to fame.

This book consists of brief excerpts from first-person accounts of major historical events.If I were a teacher, I would freely borrow from it to spice up class; in high school, I'm pretty certain I used it as a primary source more than once. Anyway, it's a fun read.

Senior year of high school, I took a team-taught class combining religion and literature. I have mentioned my english teacher, Mr. Rob Peick, in another review ("Rivethead"); Mr. Mark Syman taught us religion, and he was a huge fan of Zinn. He also felt positively tortured by guilt over his ugly, woven leather shoes, as they were produced in South America, probably by peasant labor.

The story of rich, rich men who played finncial tricks and the common laborers who executed their grand dreams. A departure from the style of first-person interviews that typified Ambrose's WWII books.
A fun, light read, especially entertaining if you know the Cambridge, Mass., area.
I really ought to get around to reading this: my smart friend, Lori, said it was good, and that was like a dozen years ago.
It's tempting to say something like "seminal" about this book, but it's really just a fun read without all the mental heavy lifting that makes a Neal Stephenson book stand out (and be so rewarding).
A bit thin, as it's more about the John than Thomas.  The subtitle was the publisher's idea, and the title itself has a double meaning.
Saints 24/7?  They're actually much more interesting human beings than sociopaths.  This modern-day Book of Hours brings them back to the fore.
Very entertaining stories, some based off of very old southern folk lore.  I love this collection.
The scripts for one of my favorite television shows ever. I think I've nearly suffocated laughing every time I've heard him ask the old lady, "Is this a piece of your brain?"

As God is my witness, I've tried and tried to read this book. Sober or with drink; sitting outside on Bloomsday listening to parts of it acted out at Boston's Custom House or reading alone; I just can't do it. And I even bought it at St. John's College in Annapolis, MD, where I hoped some smarts would rub off on me: too bad.
How the world was discovered, strata by strata, discipline by discipline.
Great theory, but AFAIK it hasn't borne fruit.  We do owe it to the Sumerians for having invented beer, though, so let's hear it for the voices of the gods!
Fischer's argument is not a little overdrawn, but is nevertheless of considerable pith and interest.  A welcome and hefty addition to early American history.

Its pages are warped and moldy now, but this is the book which introduced me to Eisley, Ballard, Best and Zelazny ("For a Breath I Tarry,)"  Silverberg and Ellison ("I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream"), Leiber, Delaney, and Simak ("Desertion").
Your own, personal, Jesus, and how He got that way.Fascinating sociology.

A narrow focus can yield rich results.  This history of heresy demonstrates that it's the same damn thing over and over again, so to speak.  There's  no heresy without orthodoxy (and quite a few matches).  If you need one book on heresy, this is the one.
I'm a sucker for this sort of on-the-ground-at-the-time read, whether diaries or memoirs.  The Cold War context rubs shoulders with archetypes here.

If you enjoy boundary violations, this is the science fiction trilogy for you!  The world is fully realized, but I'd rather read about it in an encyclopedia than visit it, much less live it.  Vampirism and shape-shifting is the subtext, albeit of a beneficial sort, and humanity becomes a sort of trickster figure in the alien society which rescued it.
If there's a better WWII POW memoir, it's "My Hitch in Hell:  The Bataan Death March" by Lester I. Tenney.

A classic hard science science fiction novel of the old school; archaic, but great fun and quite rigorous.  Clement's Mesklin were the first science fiction set on a planet "set outside the solar system on a planet believed (then) to actually exist,"  acccording to the Wiki entry on Mesklin.  And apparently anyone can set scenes there, which would make it the first shared universe as well.  The pages are yellow, the characters are cardboard, and it has as many female characters as Norman Spinrad's "The Iron Dream," if that, so if anyone wants to try their hand at crafting a retro blast, go to it!
Still the standard work on on the first irruption of populism in the U.S.

I participated in the National Genographic Project in part to give my father and brother a unique gift for Father's Day.  (Apparently our ancestors had wandered in off the steppes after the last Ice Age.)  Engagingly written, "The Journey of Man" provides one some sense of, and a greater appreciation for, everyone's deep ancestry.  A must for any genealogy library.
A rather uneven collection of short stories by various writers. I enjoyed Nick Hornby's and Colin Firth's stories the most.
Uneven collection of essays about songs that are meaningful to Hornby. Insight into his feelings about and relationship with his autistic son was very interesting.
Well-written, very involving story of Henry's wives. It was particularly interesting to get some insight into the less-famous wives like Catherine Parr and Anne of Cleves.

I know the story is not great or original. The story was completely secondary to the way Martin writes. Very rarely does a writer make me stop and reread a passage just because of the beauty of the writing. Martin does exactly that.

I wasn't that excited about reading this because I'd heard it described as "touching" and "empowering." It was indeed touching, but not in an emotionally false way. There was just enough humor, enough heartbreak, enough tragedy, enough warmth and understanding.
Friends at Princeton try to solve mysteries contained in the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili. Basically a standard-issue thriller. The story was all right but the characters weren't well-developed at all.

This was a tight little novel about a professional killer in Japan. Half Japanese, half American, he has decided to leave behind a rather dark past in the US and make his home in Japan. Very atmospheric and smart.

Summary: Good historical information on the Viet Cong tunnel systems of the period of the US war in Vietnam. Excellent resource for inspiring deadly underground environments for various roleplaying game genres.Game Masters, ever want to make those underground venues more gritty and realistic? This is a great book for painting a picture of a kobold or goblin warren. Make your players shiver with dread at the prospect of assaulting those "wimpy" short humanoids.The book has pictures and descriptions of the "Iron Triangle" region of the Vietnam war. This area had deep clay soils that provided an ideal environment in which to build storehouses, factories, bunkers and tunnels under the jungle. The Viet Cong tunnel system was extremely effective for protecting their troops and material assets from the US military assaults.
Great, although depressing, book about Schindler and his transformation from greedy businessman to risking his life for his Jewish workers.
If you're trying to make your husband, boyfriend, friend, brother, etc a little more sophisticated and refined, this is a good start.
This books gives a brief biography of every Vietnam Medal of Honor winner.  A lot of touching stories of bravery and courage.
The story of McCourt and his trials of growing up poor in Ireland with a drunk for a father.
Wonderfully told story of Ia Drang as one of the most important battles during the Viet Nam War.
Not surprisingly, Morrison's poetry tends to be pretty deep.  You can see where some of The Doors' most famous songs came from.

An interesting collection of dark fantasy stories for young adults, including a Terry Pratchett non-diskworld story.  Some of the stories are quite scary, but they're all compelling.  Quite a quick read.

Grendel is a marvelous book that uses the original myth as a starting place for an inquiry into the need for external evil in the formation of societies. Along the way it digresses into examinations of various philosophies, from the most basic to the most profound (and even post-modern). And -- most surprisingly of all -- it is laugh out loud funny.

I had high expectations from the book's title.  However, this is aimed at a grade school level.  While that may be fine for the targeted audience, as an adult, I would enjoy a more sophisticated and thorough look at Lincoln's humor.

This is to accompany Thud! and in it's own right is a wonderfully funny, almost children's tale as told by Vimes to his child.  It starts off as a story about someone who had lost his cow, half way through vimes thinks "why is young Sam's nursery full of farmyard animals anyway? Why are his books full of moo-cows and baa-lambs? He's growing up in a city.  He will only seem them on a plate! They go sizzle!"I can think of a more useful book.  A book with streets in it, not fields.  A book about the place where he'll grow up."And then several staple characters show up.I laughed until I nearly cried.The illustrations are wonderful and quite apt.

Mulengro is unusual for an urban fantasy book because Romany people (aka gypsies) are at the center of the story.  De Lint, as usual, does a masterful job of making Romany magic work in a modern world and in the context of a city setting.  One gets a sense of the gritty and some what grim life of modern Rom, and why they continue to be resistant to a "proper" modern settled life.  Mulengro can be dark but is ultimately hopeful.

This is one of my favorite urban fantasy books because of the ways in which the fey are inhuman.  They can easily be dark, cruel and deadly. Also, Bull does a great job of showing how capricious the fey can be and how that can be both good and bad.  I have a hard time describing this book excep to say it's completely amazing and should be read.

At this point in the series, I became extremely frustrated with Anita's prudishness especiallyy given how explicit the sex in the books was getting. This book focused a lot on Edward, a buddy of Anita's, and an interesting metaphoric deal with the devil Anita makes.  Still worth reading, though with some grumbling tossed in.

This book is part of a series in which elves are not only running around the LA area, they race high performance cars.  No really.  Shut up.This particular book deals with the elves and their human friends, attempts to save a young boy from horrific abuse at the hands of a cult.  While I like Lackey's other 'elves in LA' books, this one didn't do it for me.  We all know child abuse is bad, and I didn't need to be smacked over the head with that message.  This is not one I re-read very frequently.

I adore this book and if you find it, but it immediately. It took me years to obtain a copy after re-reading my library's copy obsessively.  At any rate, this is an early work of urban fantasy that has withstood the test of time.  The book focuses on a series of magic workers who live in Seattle.  Wizard, the main character who is among other things obliged to look after the pigeons, has cobbled together a relatively plesant and comfortable existance living on the margins of life in Seattle.  Eventually, a malevolent force comes to Seattle and disrupts Wizard's life and grasp on reality.  The way the story plays out is interesting and things don't happen the way you might expect.

A brilliant book by a well known author that doesn't seem to get the attention it deserves.  The main character in this book, Maryland Long, is a 2,000 Chinese dragon who has gone to San Francisco to find purpose and drive.  He has tea with Martha Macnamara and, well, philosophy and hijincks ensue. The book swings between meditative passages and more action/adventurey msytery plot.  It's a charming book to sit down and read on a rainy day.

This is a stunningly good book I can not recommend highly enough.  Sherman takes some of the classic tropes of medieval fantasy novels and turns them on their ears.  The main characters are queer, in ways that makes sense for the time period and for contemporary readers. I'm amazed this book didn't win a huge pile of awards when it came out.  Buy it, love it, give it to friends.

I don't normally read sword fighting adventures, so when I first picked this up I said "If it's not gay by the end of the first chapter, I'm not going to continue."  Lo and behold, by the end of chapter one our (male) hero returns to his room at an inn he shares with his boyfriend.This book both bucks genre conventions and plays with them in interesting ways.  The society beauties are male, and that gender flip plays out in different ways than it does with women. This book is engaging, interesting and I defied my expectations in all the best ways.

"Bone Dance" is a really great thought provoking book.  It's set in a near future post-apocalyptic Minneapolis, and for quite a while it's unclear if the narrator of the book, Sparrow, is hiding something about a mysterious past, or if memories of the past have been obliterated through nefarious means.  It's hard to describe, but an amazing read even for those who aren't a fan of sci-fi or futuristic books.

This is a child's edition of Tom Sawyer and as such is slightly diluted, sanitized so to speak.  I can just imagine Mark Twain's reaction to the idea of his books being cleaned up for children.Aside from that, Tom Sawyer is a quintessential American story of a boy on the verge of adolescence in mid-nineteenth-century Missouri.  Anyone wanting to learn parts of what is the American mythos could do worse than read this book.  Twain writes so well that it appears effortless.  He never fails to delight; he usually manages to insert gentle gibes at the human condition while doing so.

I find that adding a review to a classic like this is far more daunting than reviewing other works.  Huckleberry Finn may be the Great American Novel; if it is not, then it must be in the top two contenders.  Twain's writing is a delight to the senses; the humor still works; the satire still bites.  He manages to amuse, inform, and guide us all at once and without making a show of doing so.My only complaint with this edition is the minor editorial liberties taken and the lack of notes and commentary.

This is an anecdotal collection of stories about post mortem activities of the bodies of famous people.  The book is exactly as the title describes.  While one could wish it were more scholarly, it is nevertheless, interesting, amusing, and informative.  I would not use this as a definitive source; I would seek secondary corroboration before using these stories in anything serious.

Alice is one of my favorite works of all times.  I found the book profoundly influential as a child, providing as it did a entry into the world of Victorian literature and history, to say nothing of the sheer delight and humor of the piece.
One of my favorite books of all time. Not perfect, as I was bored by the discussions of religion by the present-day narrator, but the story of Owen was amazing.

This book is so great! I reread it 2 more times and watched the movie 10+ times. About a young girl whos mom is a bit quirky and ends up in jail, while the girl gets shipped around to foster families. The book is much better than the movie, of course.
A woman finds out her ex boyfriend is now writing a magazine column about her. Hilarity ensues. Very funny book.
This book was so-so. About a group of women coming together for one in celebration of ones pregnancy. One of the characters is unnervingly, annoying. Ends with a good realization. We dont need men!

What a wonderful book. It's a graphic novel, the story of the Islamic revolution in Iran as seen through the eyes of a girl who's 9 years old when her entire world changes. She's growing up under a constantly changing situation -- protests, revolution, religious extremism, political prisoners being taken, war, closed borders. It's a grim time, but nevertheless, she manages to communicate the good and bad, the humor even in the midst of incredibly difficult times.

I'm calling this one done. I read all but the last 30 pages and just can't bring myself to pick it up again and read the rest. A disappointment, since I loved The Virgin Suicides, but what can you do?

True story of Elizabeth Wurtzel and her battle with depression and self injury. I read it when I first got diagnosed with depression. I identified with Elizabeth. For some reason it helped me imensely.
Beautifully written, intriguing story of a geisha. Hard to believe it wasn't written by someone who had lived it.
Uneven collection of essays. Some were hilarious, laugh-out-loud funny and others were just tedious.

I was truly surprised how good this was. Aubrey and Maturin are both great characters and the interplay between them is just terrific. It probably would have helped a bit if I read up on sailing, but lacking that knowledge didn't hamper my enjoyment of the book at all.
I really enjoyed this when I read it in high school. I don't know that I necessarily buy in to what it says about the nature of humans, but it certainly makes a strong argument for one viewpoint.

Lord, did I love this book. Not just because it's more about the families from "Cryptonomicon," but because it's fast and funny and wide-ranging and smart and -- oh, all the things that literature professors told me that period lit should be.
A book of a hundred-odd line drawings about ways to be cruel. For example, as a man hunches over an open cage next to a table where restaurant diners scream, the caption reads simply, "Release rats."
Quotes about finding Zen in every-day life. Enjoyable enough, but not very deep.

The bigraphy of Vince Lombardi, pro football demigod. My word, what a narrow world view that man had: football uber alles. I sure hope he was happy. I enjoyed reading the book, though I was relieved wheen it ended.

This is a collection of a few essays published elsewhere. I believe it contans the piece he wrote about being a Macy's Christmas elf, which is the sole reason -- and sufficient, thank you -- that I bought it. (The story still wrings tears of laughter from my eyes whenever I read it.) If you like his particular tone, you'll love this book: it's a little less pitiless than he's been since he start appearing in Esquire and on NPR so often, so it's a simpler joy to read.
It's a light read by a former representative of HRM the Queen who travelled all over the world in her service. Very pleasant, no heavy lifting here.
This books has an impressive array of images to illustrate WW II - from the point of view of the U.S.  The book lacks significant representation from other points of view.
More grumpy quotes. Most are well-known, but a few brought a new smile to my face.
Another collection of quotes about love, and more specifically about marriage. A small-format book, it's a close companion to the John Winokur "Curmudgeon" books. Not bad.

A book of cartoons of how the brians of various people are subdivided. (For example, lawyers have a huge area devoted to money and a tiny spot devoted to ethics.) This joke works well a few times, but becomes labored by the end.

Reportedly the longest fiction book in English, it's certainly among the heavist I own. Purchased for a course at Tufts on the 18th Century English Novel -- which was really a great class -- I found reading this book to be so dull that I could skip tens of pages at  time and seemingly not advance a bit. I believe I wrote a long paper on casuistry (the professor's suggestion) based on this book, though I have no recollection of what I said, nor even what the word means. I get sleepy just looking at it, and intend to use it with my children as an object lesson in the need to edit onesself.

I laughed very, very hard at the title essay, about the author's voyage on a cruise ship. Having been traumatized by the movie "Jaws" myself, I took great joy squirming along as he leans over the side, looking for fins. Some of the other essays were less enjoyable, but still it's a good read.
I liked this one better than The Witching Hour. More intrigue with some of the better characters in the series -- particularly Julien.

Here's karma: I borrowed this book from my sister, and I didn't tell her when some freshman spilled my coffee on it during a lecture for a European History course I had to take after I transferred. I ended up tanking the course, and repeating it in summer school after graduation. Ugh. What, the story? I liked it, actually: the main characters reminded me of my friends in high school (minus the whole killing people thing), and I fouind a tale of smart teens a refreshing departure.

Wide topics like this are great for P.J.O'Rourke because he has a great range of things ot be funny about. He takes good opportunity to explain how the U.S. government works (or doesn't), and it even bears re-reading.
One of the few Koontz books that doesn't follow his standard formula. Lives up to its name, a very tight and suspenseful book.
I had a hard time getting through this one. It had some cool ideas, but it didn't grip me and I got rather bored with it. Unfortunate, because apparently it's got ties to the Dark Tower series
This limp story about life in high tech in California in the 1990s tries waaay too hard to be funny.

A collection of little essays about movies that is funny, but maybe like 15% less funny than his friends told him it was. Then again, people from Minnesota are just too nice: maybe he should have had someone from, say, New York read it.

This book is often lauded, and I can't tell why: the protagonist is whiny and neurotic and just not funny. I know that I should be impressed that the author's only work collected such plaudits only after he died, and that it's a prime example of persevering and following your dream -- but I just didn't enjoy it.

This was my first Clancy novel. I found it a bit of a slow starter, but I've been told that Clancy books tend to be that way. The first 50 pages or so were very dense with people and information, but after that, you know everything you need to follow the plot the rest of the way through. Suspenseful, I would definitely read others.
This book, ostensibly for children, has truly ugly pictures, and I have clean forgotten the story itself.

Thsi came out when I was in high school, and I really thought that this Groening fellow must only be 17 himself. He was my hero -- and on the strength of "The Simpsons," he still is. I just wish I knew where the other four books from this box set are...
I know that a lot of people didn't think he wrote a very believable woman, but I enjoyed the book well enough.

A big collection of Fry's stuff, of varying quality. I think he's hilarious -- I even read his novels and liked them, especially the "Revenge" one -- but this many disparate items between two covers guarantees some unevenness.
Bizarre story of a family whose livelihood depends on having freaks. Good, but deeply strange.

Tough going at times, a bit dry occasionally. However, it has some truly fascinating stories in it about the incredible rise of New York into a civilized city. It's amazing how brutal life was at the turn of the century with violence raging nearly nonstop in some areas.

This collection is fantastic and highly recommended.  Gaiman's writing in this has the style/feel of realism, but the subject matter he covers ranges from pleasantly fantastic, too subtle horror.  I picked this up recently in an airport becaue I ran out of books (horrors!).  It kept me engrossed the entire flight and my subway ride home.  I managed to finish the last story just as I got to my apartment.
The account of Gary Gilmore's life, crime and death by firing squad.  Over 1000 pages that I read in a weekend, I was so absorbed by the story.

This is a light hearted take on various tropes in urban fantasy (including Lackey's Diana Tregarde books).  The protagnoist, the Keeper, is in a run down B&B in Canada trying to plug a gateway to hell (which has taken to arguing with itself), deal with an argumentative cat, an interfering sister who is a powerful magic maker and an irritating sibling, and convince her libido to not go into overdrive when dealing with her insanely handsome, polite handy man. This is an amusing quick read.
Involving, detailed story of a concubine in Imperial China. Humorous and warm, lavish in attention to detail. The main negative was that the ending felt rushed.

This book is set in the "Lyra" series: a series of stand alone novels all taking place in the same universe.  You don't need to have read the others for this book to make sense.  A fairly plain Jane inn keeper suddenly has her not at all plain past catch up with her when a magic worker suddenly needs her to return to the Sisterhood of Stars in an attempt to figure out a magical disaster which happened years ago.  I really like Wrede's writing style, and how she incorporates prosaic details into the story in an engaging fashion.

This book is combines a rollicking adventure with magic and the mystery of where is a stolen set of silver located.  Kim is a street urchin/thief masquerading as a young boy.  She is caught trying to sneak into Maireleon's carriage, and she becomes his apprentice in both stage magic and real magic.  Set against the background of regency England, this book is fun and appealing to young and old readers.

This is the sequel to "Mairleon the Magician" and begins soon after the first book ends.  This book delves more into the impoverished world Kim left when she became Mairleon's ward, while also showing us more of the society world she is entering.   Fast paced and quit enjoyable.
I love this book.  I'm not a Steinbeck fan, but I thought this one worked on every level.  A sweeping tour of a family following the Biblical lines of Cain and Abel.  Amazing in every way.

It doesn't seem like the story of the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago would be all that exciting. Even after you learn that half the story involves a serial killer in the city at the time, hearing that the other half is about the architect struggling to build the Fair might put you off. Don't let it though, you'd be missing out. Both stories are equally compelling, and tied together in unique ways.

A story about Dorcas who lives in Dublin after the Blast.  Society has gone to pot and gangs roam the streets trying to stay alive and  take whatever food they can find.  Pretty standard fare for this type of book.  Most of it's interest is in following the action while in Dublin, it's quite fun, particularly when you realise that the headquarters of the nasties Mace's Gang is Dublin City Council's HQ in Woodquay.

One that I always remembered from my childhood, reread since my daughter was reading it.  It was comforting to revisit Deenie's worries about her back brace and her struggle to fit in and accept herself.

To me, one of the most interesting things about this book is that I liked it, having no experience at all with autism, and that I've also had it recommended by people with autistic family members.  That makes me feel better about what I got out of the book, knowing that Haddon got it right enough for people who know to think it's accurate.
Slim novella, classic Garcia Marquez.  Death in a small town.

"What's My Name, Fool?" shatters the image that many on the left think of athletes. Citing both historical and present day acts of resistance by athletes in national spot-light sports, DC area socialist Dave Zirin challenges this sometimes elitist with clear and crisp writing. The title comes from Muhammad Ali challenging white reporters, who made it a point to call him Cassius Clay, his former name, after a dominating victory. From football to baseball to soccer to tennis to boxing to the Olympics, Zirin digs into the history and shines a light into the dark corners that the major leagues would prefer remain unexplored. Zirin discusses racism, classism, sexism and homophobia, and also profiles uplifting examples of athletes fighting the power and speaking the truth.Such glaring examples include the domination of a nazi boxer by Joe Lewis, the smashing of the color barrier in baseball with years of organizing by members of the Negro leagues and communist sports writers, the Black Power salute given after winning the gold and bronze medals by the American Olympic Track Team to protest apartheid and segregation, and current day examples of antiwar women's college hoopster Toni Smith or all-star slugger Barry Bonds criticizing racism and the war in Iraq and then being targeted by the Bush adminstration as anti-american or pro-bowl Miami Dolphins running back Ricky Williams refusing to be used anymore to sell tickets.As an rabid sports fan, I loved this book and saw it as the connect between my two major interests, political action and sports. Zirin criticizes the sports industry by taking solid aim at the ownership who make it their goal to exploit athletes who are mainly working class people of color, sacrificing their bodies in order to bring their families out of poverty. He does a good job at pointing out that athletes are not the dumb idiots that society encourages them to be, but instead many use their fame for good causes. For every Michael Jordan being silent on the issues like sweatshops, there is a Kareem Abu Jabar who the right wishes would just shut up and go away. I also believe it is a huge mistkae to dismiss all sports fans, possibly because of classism, and some of the best organizing can be done amongst sporting events.

This is one of my favorite books ever.  Cynical, funny, sad, it's a little bit of everything.  Some of the most memorable characters you'll find anywhere, and eminently quotable."There was only one catch, and that was catch-22."

Easy to get into, incredible story of the cons Abagnale managed to pull, and of his eventual capture. The only weakness of the book is Abagnale's lack of introspection, which keeps us from really understanding him.
Not as funny as the original novel, but still with some laugh-out-loud moments.
Read this after Illusions and enjoyed it much more. Found the story of love and fate much more applicable to my life.
Great book for hikers in Hawaii to read.  Gives just about any information about the hike as you could want, including types of trees and flowers found along the trails.

A quick read, it's really more of a novella. Quite a number of things were different from the movie, most glaringly the ending. Unsurprisingly, the book leaves it all more open-ended. Although I'm not a fan of Hollywood endings, I think the book would have benefitted from a bit more definition in the wrap-up.
When I read this in high school, I thought it was brilliant. I suspect I should probably go back and reread it to see what I think now.
Another great page-turner centering around Jason Bourne.  Not great literature, but a terrifically fun book.

A fun, page-turning spy thriller with more than a few twists. The movie was pretty good, but the book has a much meatier plot, which makes the character of Jason Bourne just that much more compelling.
I must be worse than an idiot because I sure didn't learn German.

I really liked his style -- he's got a sense of humor, and I loved the way it peeked through here and there. I adored the opening story, and found a couple of the others chilling. Most of the stories weren't that scary to me though, centering around the supernatural the way they did. And a couple just felt way too cute.

I have two quibbles with this book.  One is that I would like her to discuss some of her decisions about how certain items are cut (I can see where she got some of them, but I've been working on 15th C clothing for 10 years now).  The other is a really a problem with editing and layout -- you have to flip back and forth to get all the directions to lay out a particular item, and that's aggravating.  But those are just quibbles; this is a fantastic book.

This book is one of Lackey's re-telling of fairy tales.  This retelling of Snow White is set in turn of the century England and our heroine is an educated 'half-caste' (one parent is British, the other Indian) woman.  Lackey's descriptions of life in India draw heavily from British colonialistic/romantic ideas of what life was like.  Also, Lackey's understanding of Hindu gods is not as sophisticated as I would like.

This book is Lackey's retelling of "Swan Lake."  Unfortunately, the retelling lacks narrative drive.  Lackey does a good job of describing Ondine's life, the swans and their indolent beauty.  However, she does not do a good job of convincing the reader to care.  For Lackey completists only.

In this book, Lackey retells "Beauty and the Beast" and sets it in San Francisco around the turn of the century.  Our heroine is destitute and bookish, so of course takes a mysterious position working for a man who she never sees properly.  Unlike others in her situation, she takes charge of her situation. Enjoyable, though not ground breaking.

This is a stand-alone book in MZB's Darkover universe.  You don't need to have read the rest of the books to read this one (I still haven't read most of the Darkover books). The universe "Hawkmistress" is set in is rich and detailed, without being overwhelming.  The book focuses on Romilly, the daughter of a local lord, who has laran (a telepathic gift that allows her to communicate primitively with animals).  The book deals with Romilly's struggles to be considered a person, rather than as a piece of chattle, a useful tool, a freak, etc.  MZB has her characters react realistically, which is to say some people disappoint you, and others surprise you.
My friends and I did a naval dinner based on a recipes from this book. In fact, it was a bit of a smashing sucess and extremely enjoyable. Highly recommended, in the pratical sense.
This book is so riveting that I had to read it at one sitting even if I was in the middle of a serious crisis at work: deeply moving, helped me keep things in perspective.
This was the first of O'Brian's Aubrey / Maturin series that I read and I really liked it (along with most of the others).
A little girl saves her younger brother with courage, determination, knitting, and the help of her toy horse.  What's not to like?

This book is a combination of folk tale, mystery, and extended comedy routines.  Number 10 Ox is sent to find a learned scholar who can solve the mystery of why a plague has hit the young children in his village.  He ends up with Master Li, a brilliant drunken scoundrely Confucian scholar, and they go on a quest throughout China to solve a mystery, find  a mythical creature and possibly help out some gods.  Wonderful, charming and funny.

I adore urban fantasy and read tons of it.  This book is not a very good example of the genre.  It recycles many tropes from other books and doesn't deal with them in interesting or unusual ways. Our heroine inherits a library from her grandmother, discovers a gateway into faery, it turns out her grandmother was murdered and our heroine must solve the mystery in order to prevent untold chaos and crappiness.  This has been done way better by other authors.  This book was not offensive, but it wasn't great.

Although I really enjoyed this series over all, I found this book to be a disappointing end to the series. For some reason, this book fell flat.  Kel faces some tough enemies, including a mage who steals children's souls to run evil war machines, but I didn't get wrapped up in her struggles the way I did in the past.  Maybe the problem was that the enemies she faced in this book were evil in an over the top way.

I read a lot of high fantasy, and a lot of fantasy series,so I came to this book expecting to enjoy it.  Unfortunately, after reading over a third of the book I found myself bored.  The plot was overly convoluted and the writing was stiff.  I tried to pick the book back up a few other times but I couldn't get interested in it.

This is the first in a series of books set in an alternate North America.  Two of the biggest changes are that British won the Revolutionary war and that magic workers exist.  Card's take on this North America is interesting, and appears to be influenced by Manly Wade Wellman's "Silver John" books.  A great beginning to the series.

Let me say up front that I have enjoyed everything Bright has written. This book is a collection of essays that deal with gender, sex, sexuality, being a parent, privacy, and more.  Bright's writing in this book deals more with issues such as being a parent, which makes sense given that she has a child.  However, this is not written for the desperate housewives set (though they could benefit from reading i).  Bright continues to write in a direct manner, that is honest and truthful without being harsh.  Definitely worth reading.

This book is a must for people with an interest in gender, nature vs. nurture, queer issues, trans issues, fabulosity, and introspection.  If you've ever colored outside of the lines, read this book.  It deals with difficult issues with a deceptively light touch.  You'll find yourself being introspective when you thought you were just playing with quizzes.
A really excellent collections of essays and some poetry about femmes. These are mostly from point of view of femmes, but there are also works by people who appreciate them.
I'm not much for sci-fi, but I really loved this book. The atmosphere is great, the characters, the underlying commentary.

I had a hard time getting into this book and had to start it multiple times. Finally though, once getting past the first 50 pages or so, I cruised through it. I hated a lot of the writing, but I liked the story.
The Latin for all the fallacies are herein, just the thing for you to lose all your friends.
"There is more than one history of the world."  The only book to which I keep returning every few years but have yet to finish!

Pablo Escobar was one of the world's prime monsters and at one point probably the richest, becoming a billionaire on the back of the American cocaine business. I found it difficult to put this book down as it traces his violent domination of Colombia with the fatal (for him) involvement of the Americans through the "War on Drugs". Their clean and dirty manoeuvres eventually wore away his power and lead to his shooting. Mark Bowden has written a great book & I'm surprised that it's not better known.

The only book I've read in this series; I'm deferring the pleasure.  Great crypto-history, and great fun.  (I've given my copy as a Christmas gift, because for some reason Baker's stuff is only published by Tor now, and this title wasn't available.  Drat!)
A nicely drawn criticism of a warped and intolerant fundamental religious personality (in this case 19th century Christian).

The Culture is one of the great space opera creations, and "Consider Phlebas" was where I first tucked into the milieu.  Something of a cross between Vinge and the early Gibson, but Banks has a sadistic streak which recalls Ian Fleming.  An allusive, rip-roaring comic strip for adults.
The science fiction equivalent to "The Night of the Hunter" (1955), and just as perfervid.
Trenchant stories and essays.  I especially liked the explanation for UFO abductions.

Some of the stuff you read in adolescence stays with you forever, some of THAT you can reread without grimacing, wryly or otherwise.  My copy is yellowed, and it's my only example of the series, but the stories (a la the music of the Velvet Underground) have a lingering power.  It's the anthology which introduced me to Schopenhauer, James Tiptree, Jr., the Death of Dr. Island, alternate time streams, and something up there that likes me.
I first read this in high school.  An unusual take on the hoary "first contact" theme.  Good, but not great.

The author is a retired civil engineer who worked for the Provincial Government Roads Department. With this background he brings a wealth of experience from an engineering perspecive and an archival perspective.  Despite some interesing technical detail, the sries themselves about each mountain pass, are fascinatng to read.

A fine post-holocaust triptych, each set many decades apart, and one of the great Spoon Rivers of the genre.  If Olaf Stapledon's "Last Men and First Men/Star Maker" is a symphony, "A Canticle for Leibowitz" is chamber music or a canticle.
The frame story (a lunar bar) is almost as good as many of the stories themselves.  I especially liked the real explanation for the foo fighters of WWII...

It's difficult for me to do justice to the richness of Linebarger's unique mythos.  It's even more difficult for me to get across just how much some of these stories meant to me (some of them with Chinese narrative techniques!); they are eschatological fiction of the highest water.  (Heck, the cover of the Ballantine edition is one of the great science fiction mass market paperback covers -kudos to the illustrator!)  Forest of Incandescent Bliss, was unique; it would take a Hayao Miyazaki to bring the likes of "The Dead Lady of Clown Town,"  "Under Old Earth," "Alpha Ralpha Boulevard" or "The Ballad of Lost C'mell" to the big screen.  A unique treasure.  Science fiction used to have a positivistic click -and to think that the man died in 1966!
Classic overwritten mid-60s science fiction of the down-in-flames school.

An alternate history with a twist which is arguably the most disturbing framing device ever.  The afterward is of a piece with the novel.  Inasmuch as this is the science fiction equivalent of Ichi the Killer (2001), it is perhaps best suited for those with strong dispositions.
Von Neumann machines more common than ATMs shake up a repressive society when the information circus comes to a Russian planet.  A good read.  Not great, but good.

An interesting look at a man who grows to adulthood as a slave and gladiator and when he gets his wooden sword and freedom is offered a chance to be a celtic chief, he's identical to the heir, only the heir has been blinded by an enemy.  He gets involved with the people of this tribe what the future holds isn't always obvious or easy to deal with.
Okay -- didn't find it as interesting as the other two books in this series.
About a young girl who sees her own face on a milkcarton at school. Drama ensues.

I came to this book knowing that Anansi was a spider god, and a god of stories. I'd  seen several people rant and rave about how good it was.  They weren't wrong.  It's a compelling read and excellently put on paper by Neil Gaiman.  I would recommend it to people who enjoy a light fiction read.When Charlie Nancy was younger he got the nickname of Fat Charlie and it stuck.  He never knew that his father was Anansi the Spider God.  He gets the news that his father is dead and he has to go back to America from London to attend the funeral, along the way he discovers his brother and when his brother returns with him his life starts unravelling.
The writing style of this books reminds me of Catcher in The Rye.
This book is very similar to the plot in the movie "My Girl". Best Friends. One dies by allergy to bees. Tear jerker. One of my childhood favorites.
This is the most unsentimental book about personal tragedy that I have ever read. It's an impressive accomplishment, since the topic makes it so easy to tug on heartstrings.
Everything works out well for Catherine Maurice. If your child is autistic, this book gives you hope, then it makes you very sad.

This is my current favorite North American field guide. The illustrations are stunning, and very accurate, and there's loads of text and great maps. All around a wonderful guide, and not too big that it can't be carried in the field (although it is on the large side). Still, when I'm only bringing one guide, this is the one I choose.

A quick read with some of the best quotes I've found."People don't want to hear what really being in love is like, 'cause it sucks. It's like a diamond; it looks pretty from the outside but inside it's hard, angular, and sharp. Truly loving somebody else should never be confused with a good time. Loving somebody is just as painful and disappointing as it is getting to know yourself. It's probably the only thing worth doing, but that doesn't mean it's gonna be a picnic."

Not much to say about this one that hasn't already been said a thousand times.  A remarkable insight into both what it was like to be Jewish and in hiding during WWII and what it was like to be a young girl trying to grow up under such dire circumstances.
A harrowing memoir of growing up in poverty in Ireland and America.  The best out of McCourt's memoirs, highly recommended.
NO WIRE HANGERS! Crazy book. I couldnt put it down. "True" story of Joan Crawfords adopted daughters abusive upbringing.
this book creeped me out. A family tragedy. Then the children are forced to live in secret. Eventually they are left to die. Tear jerker.
This was so beautiful and heartbreaking that I can hardly believe it.

A story about three women linked by an event that happened while they were in high school. I found the story of one of them particularly compelling, the other two not so much. The connection between them was tenuous, really, and seemed a little contrived. A first novel -- I'd give her another chance.
A beautiful, funny book, turned into an equally beautiful, funny movie.

Starts three days prior to the quake and makes the case that much of the damage was preventable even at that point, particularly the devastating fires that swept the city. The picture painted in the book is of a city almost impossibly beautiful, alluring, charismatic -- with city government almost impossibly corrupt, callous and focused on lining their own pockets. The story is told partially in the first person through the eyes of Anna Passarelli, an opera critic for the newspaper (this of course gives the author a great excuse to work the famous visit of Enrico Caruso into the novel). Overall, the book was pretty good, but I got a little tired of the author's staccato writing style toward the end.
A mouse with an usual name finally grows to love it. Cute story.

Touching, awe inspiring, tear inducing book told by a young girl who lost almost her entire family, a leg, but never her resolve.  The story of her life, in Afghanistan and her transition to young American girl.
Nice collection of various recipes.  You can't get tired of eating the same thing all the time.
Gorgeous book featuring photos of cars from the early years right through the 2001 model year.  Photos seem to concentrate on the late 70s through the 80s although all eras are covered.
A space opera of ideas.  "The empires of the future shall be the empires of the mind." -Winston Churchill.  Great sensawunda.
Glorious interviews.  Great minds at a symposium.  Doth teleology dare raise its ugly head?  No matter... Bring on the flute-girls!
Perspicacious essays.  His appreciation of Philip K. Dick, who was a close friend, is of particular interest, but the whole megillah's of considerable heft and interest.
Analysis of the Corps of Discovery's experience at the mouth of the Columbia River.  Attention is paid to tides, dominant weather patterns.  Great maps.
Slaughter's collection of essays question our perception of Lewis and Clark as heroic explorers, casting doubt on their veracity and our traditional views of their achievements.

Fanny Hill is important because of its place in the history of the end of censorship in America, but it's also a fun read. The book takes a positive view of sex generally - the first-person narrator enjoys sex for its own sake, and isn't consumed with guilt over all the sex she has, but she also acknowleges that sometimes bad things happen because of sex or the desire for it. The book is unusual for a book which graphically depicts sex acts in that there are no "dirty words" in the book - the characters don't swear, and the narrator uses coy euphemisms to describe the details.

I selected this book off a rack because I found that it spoke about the environmnet surrounding the game in general terms rather than getting bogged down in specifics.  The author favors selective, agressive play; but above all being aware of the table conditions and adjusting your play accordingly.  Carson writes as a career poker player; that is to say, not very well.  While the sections of the book are well laid out, the flow between paragraphs and items are, in several instances, not so well done.  Phrases and terms are gratuitously used before being well defined.  He jumps into specific examples and talks about them both vaguely and excessively specifically at the same time; as a novice player, I get the feeling that I would need more experience and study with other resources to get the maximum out of this book; however I question whether the book would be a good supplement to the necessary study it seems to require.Over all the book forced me to think about my game in a different way than I had been; however my game was so bad that practically any book would have given me the necessary attitude adjustment I needed.I wouldn't recommend the book to others.

engaging romp of a book.  Basically Buffy as a medium.This is the first book in the series, Suze moves to California from New York and finds herself facing up to a ghost who is still furious about her death, furious enough to be murderous.  She finds a mentor in her headmaster, who has a different style of mediation with the dead.
This is a fine, standard book of hymns used by many Baptist congregations several years ago.  The songs are standard and do not include much that is new.

This is a highly technical book describing and explaining the various degrees, angles and positions involved in getting the proper x-ray.  If you're into to that, this is an essential, for normal people, forget it!

This book is purported to be a translation of tables found by Joseph Smith after being directed to them by an angel named Moroni.  This is supposed to be the story of Tribes of Israel in the Western Hemisphere.  Admittely I do not believe this nor accept it - neither historically nor religiously.  Aside from that, as a book, I was struck by how stiff and boring it is.  It doesn't read at all like the Bible, except it the most superficial (and to my mind, worse) ways.  It has archaic language and repetitive formulaic phrases; but is simply is dull, draggy, and lacks interesting stories.  What's worse, for a religious book, it is not inspiring.

Featuring Edson's Calamity Jane, Phillipe St. Andre, New Orleans and a strangler who's killing prosititues in the city.  Calamity Jane offers to help by serving as a decoy.  Fairly typical, pretty dated fare from Edson.

An interesting story about magic and the costs and a struggle for power that sucks in almost everyone of consequence in the area.  It was interesting but it just didn't really appeal to me.  I did like the idea that magic had consequence, and the hints that the consequences would be played out at an inconvenient time later.
I found this book to be a big so what.  It focuses the work of the journals, but if one reads the journals I'm not sure this book is necessary.

This is the dangerous stuff that lurks behind any weak democracy. Nietzsche lays things out very clearly while deciding for the "Overman" route, so 5 stars are for his analysis not his conclusion.To suppress desire is to be weakened by guilt or bad conscience (subject of the second essay). As he puts it,"- I mean the morbid softening and moralization through which the animal "man" finally learns to be ashamed of all his instincts. On his way to becoming an "angel" man has evolved that queasy stomach and coated tongue through which not only the joy and innocence of the animal but life itself has become repugnant to him-."

On the 16th November 1532 a group of 168 Spanish soldiers led by the conquistador Francisco Pizarro arrived in Cajamarca Peru. The nearest Spaniards were over a 1000 miles away in Panama but nevertheless they decided to set a trap for the Inca emperor Atahuallpa who faced them with 80.000 men. At the end of this historic first day of contact between the dominant European power and the largest empire in the Americas, 7000 Incas were killed with many more wounded. Not a single Spaniard was lost.The Spanish used horses, steel weapons and armour and some firearms to completely overwhelm their opponents.Eight years later in 1540, another conquistador Hernando de Soto, led his soldiers through the south eastern part of North America and was surprised to find abandoned towns in his path.It turned out that Indians had died of diseases such a smallpox, measles, typhus and influenza that had never been encountered before, and which had been accidentally introduced by Spanish visitors to the coast.The microbes were travelling faster than the Spanish troops and they were certainly proving more fatal. It is estimated that between 1520 and 1618 smallpox alone reduced the Aztec population of Mexico from about 20 million people to 1.6 million.Diamond makes the point here that it was the Spaniards who arrived in the Americas and not the Incas who arrived in Europe. Furthermore it was the Spaniards who had the horses and steel, and European diseases wiped out the Indians rather than American diseases wiping out the Europeans .This excellent book starts to become very interesting as he takes the next step and asks why things turned out this way.His idea is based on geography. The Eurasian continent is bigger than America, Africa or Australia and it has a dominant East West axis rather than a North South one. The result is that a lot of Eurasia lies in similar latitudes, and any plants ar animals that can be domesticated in one area have a good chance of being suitable for use elsewhere in a vast area reaching from Ireland to Japan.He also points out that Eurasia was "lucky" in having a larger stock of the ancestral plants and animals that were suitable for domestication. These were much fewer in America and Africa and especially in Australia. People living in the middle eastern fertile crescent (present day Syria and Iraq) around 8000 B.C.could harvest large large amounts of wild cereals in a short time. These were the precursors of the earliest cereal crops, wheat and barley.The mayor 5 domesticated animals were all Eurasian in origin; the cow, sheep, goat, pig and horse probably being domesticated between 8000 B.C. and 2500 B.C. giving Eurasian people plenty of time to develop resistance and immunity to the diseases such as smallpox that arose from contact with them.Further history is more familiar with settled agriculture and the key factor of a rising population. As he says,"size of regional population is the strongest single predictor of societal complexity". It only took time for different technologies to combine to manufacture such things as the printing press that opened wide the floodgates of knowledge and technology.In my opinion this is an important book to look out for.

It's a cliche that Ataturk was the Founder of Modern Turkey but Mango puts some meaning into it by showing him stepping into the vacuum of collapsing Ottoman rule, defending the fledgling country and giving it a new Western/secular bias. An excellent book.

The book is partisan to the German side but nevertheless gives a good overview of the Luftwaffe throughout WWII. It highlights the effectiveness of British radar and the lack of a German heavy bomber in the Battle of Britain + the serious lack of  trained pilots towards the end of the war. Bekker also accepts the decisive role of the long range Mustang in engaging German fighters over Germany. He covers the technological triumph and lost opportunity of the ME 262 jet and has some good sections on the successful use of anti-tank aircraft and night-fighter operations.

A Scottish friend, who grew up in the Aberdeenshire countryside described in the novels, gave me the book as the best portrait she knew of a life which was rapidly fading when she was a child and is largely gone now.The first novel, Sunset Song, is probably the best.  Gibbon succumbed to heavy-handed allegory as the trilogy progressed and Grey Granite especially suffers from being as much a political treatise as a story.

Brian Johnson was a BBC science writer and in The Secret War he looks at the Second World War from the viewpoint of a war between the scientists and technologists of the two sides.Arguably it was the point where science and technology started to clearly dominate in importance the traditional military virtues. There is nothing heroic in the traditional sense about scientists in a laboratory evaluating the possibility of a nuclear bomb or working on codebreaking algorithms but the results or lack of them become critical to the outcome of a conventional war.The idea is interesting and Johnson has covered all the main scientific/technical areas in the conflict showing how technology (more than science) is forced into a rapid rate of evolution and testing.
